Yusuf Alioglu and Mohammad Sio
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
The Palestinian Fatah and Hamas groups are preparing to hold a meeting in Cairo next week to resume national dialogue and discuss challenges facing the Palestinian cause, Palestinian sources familiar with the matter told Anadolu on Friday.
Delegations from the two groups are preparing for the meeting, which is expected to take place Monday following months of contacts aimed at reviving dialogue, said sources.
The planned meeting comes days after Hamas Political Bureau Chairman Khalil al-Hayya led a delegation to Cairo for talks with Egyptian officials and meetings with representatives of Palestinian factions on developments concerning the Palestinian cause.
Sources said the talks come amid challenges affecting the broader Palestinian political system and the Palestinian cause, as efforts are underway to reorganize Palestinian political affairs ahead of legislative elections scheduled for November.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree July 9 setting Nov. 28 as the date for legislative elections in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza Strip. The vote would be the first since 2006.
The Central Elections Commission began voter registration and data updates Aug. 15. Hamas has said it intends to participate as part of a broad national coalition.
The sources said Hamas had invited Fatah to two meetings since Israel launched its war on Gaza in October 2023, seeking to discuss a political and national way out of the crisis. Neither invitation resulted in a meeting, and the sources did not give a reason.
Contacts between the leaderships of the two groups continued later on, holding an open-ended dialogue session, but the meeting was not held, they added.
Fatah and Hamas have remained politically divided since 2007 despite numerous rounds of dialogue and reconciliation agreements brokered by Arab and international parties in the ensuing years.
Abbas previously met late Hamas Political Bureau Chairman Ismail Haniyeh in Algiers in July 2022, under mediation by Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune.
In October 2022, Palestinian groups, including Fatah and Hamas, signed a reconciliation agreement in Algiers committing to hold legislative and presidential elections within a year. The elections were not held.
Palestinian groups, including Fatah and Hamas, signed the Beijing Declaration in July 2024, which outlined steps to end their political division and strengthen national unity. The declaration did not lead to an end to the split.
Palestinian National Council Chairman Rawhi Fattouh contacted Hamas after the legislative election date was announced, according to sources. The two factions had initially considered meeting in July, but the meeting was postponed indefinitely without explanation.
The groups recently agreed to hold a meeting in Cairo next week under Egyptian auspices, said sources.
Cairo has for years played a central role in mediating Palestinian internal dialogue, particularly between Fatah and Hamas, although its efforts have not ended the political division.
The sources said the significance of the planned meeting lies in whether it can “test the possibility of turning the pressures imposed by Israel’s genocide on Gaza into a new internal Palestinian process” that could reshape relations between the main political factions, particularly ahead of the upcoming elections.

Swedish police say 1 dead, 2 injured after school sword attack
An 18-year-old with a sword attacked a school Friday in central Sweden, killing one person and seriously injuring at least two others, authorities said.
The 18-year-old perpetrator at the school has been arrested, Police Chief Tommy Alriksson said at a news conference.
Police confirmed that shots were fired during the arrest. It was not clear whether the suspect had been injured, but he was being held in custody — not treated in a hospital.
The attack took place at the Brinell School in Fagersta, a city northwest of the capital, Stockholm, while classes were in session, with about 400 to 500 students, officials said.
Vastmanland County, where the town is located, said the two seriously injured boys were between 12 and 17 years old, the TT news agency reported. It did not provide details about the dead person.
There was no immediate word on the attacker's possible motive.
"We have no reason at this time to believe that there are multiple perpetrators," said Alriksson, adding that an investigation was continuing.
Sweden's national police said investigators have already carried out two house searches in connection with the suspect. Many witnesses were expected to be interviewed as part of the investigation.
"That's why we can't give out too much information, because we don't want to influence witnesses," Alriksson said.
Police spokesperson Pelle Vamstad, quoted by the TT news agency, said an alarm was received early Friday afternoon and that police rushed to the scene. He said officers would check any available camera footage for their investigation.
The dead person was found as police entered the school to secure the premises, authorities said.
In a post earlier on X, Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson called the attack a "serious incident" and lamented the violence in Fagersta "right after the summer break."
"We do not yet know what lies behind the act, but we know that the police are working very intensively," he added. "Our thoughts are with all those affected."
The Fagersta city government said it set up a crisis center in a sports hall near the school. The Vastmanland County government said "many people" were affected and that police, fire services and healthcare workers were among those caring for them.
Several nearby schools had been locked down following the incident, and roadblocks were set up, authorities said.

Troubled US aircraft carrier heads home after protracted deployment – media
The US aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln is heading home from its extended deployment, multiple media outlets reported on Thursday, citing officials.
The carrier’s deployment began in late November last year and was originally scheduled to end in May, but it was repeatedly extended due to its participation in the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran. The vessel now holds a modern US Navy record for the longest consecutive, uninterrupted period at sea, with roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard and more than 260 days spent largely without port calls.
The deployment has reportedly been plagued by supply and maintenance issues, including shortages of food and basic supplies, a lack of hot and potable water, and plumbing problems. Crew members’ families have raised alarm over what they described as collapsing morale, burnout, and mental health issues. Several crew members reportedly attempted to jump overboard.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao acknowledged last week a “small number of mental health cases” on board that were “treated with no loss of life.”
Reports about the troubled deployment have prompted calls for the dismissal of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who dismissed concerns raised in the media as “completely misrepresented.”
Last week, US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Hegseth “must be fired immediately” over the USS Abraham Lincoln situation.
”When Pete Hegseth was nominated, everyone knew he was completely incompetent. Now our brave sailors are paying the price in a horrific and unfathomable way,” the Democratic leader said.

Russia’s North Korean missiles could threaten Kyiv and six other regions, ISW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
21:13:02 UTC
06:13:02 KST

Russia is deploying six launchers for North Korean ballistic missiles in Voronezh Oblast, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported on 20 August. The assessment cited Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR).
Russia has already used North Korean missiles in deadly strikes across Ukraine, and Pyongyang is supplying more of them. From Voronezh Oblast, the weapons could threaten Kyiv and six other regions, adding to the ballistic arsenal Moscow can use in mass attacks intended to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
Six launchers expand Russia’s missile threat
The North Korean missiles could reach Kyiv, Sumy, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, ISW said.
The unit may eventually field 120 missiles. HUR said North Korea had transferred around 50 KN-23, KN-24, and upgraded KN-30 ballistic missiles to Russia by July.
The KN-30 can carry a 2,500-kilogram warhead, though ISW has seen no evidence of Russia using it against Ukraine. Other North Korean missiles have larger warheads than Russia’s Iskander-M but are less accurate, Ukrainian military expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi said.
Those missiles could join Russia’s combined attacks. ISW expects Moscow to stockpile ballistic and cruise missiles for several days before launching large barrages intended to overwhelm Ukraine’s air defenses.
ISW pointed to the 19–20 August attack as the latest example of that pattern. The barrage lasted nearly nine hours and killed at least 15 people in Kyiv. Ukraine’s Air Force said it intercepted most drones and cruise missiles, but no longer routinely reports how many ballistic missiles Russia launches or Ukraine intercepts.
North Korean missiles have already killed civilians
Preliminary evidence indicated that Russia used a North Korean ballistic missile in a 30 July strike on Radushne, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, that killed five members of one family.
On 10 August, a North Korean missile killed seven Zaporizhstal steelworkers and injured 21 others in Zaporizhzhia, Ukrainian officials said. The workers were heading to a shelter when the missile struck.
Ballistic missiles travel at high speed and leave civilians little time to seek cover. They are also harder to intercept than drones or cruise missiles, while Ukraine has limited supplies of the Patriot interceptors used against them.

Warsaw moving closer to control of Kiev’s Soviet-era gas transit system — spokeswoman

MOSCOW, August 22. /TASS/. Poland is getting closer to taking control of Ukraine’s Soviet-era gas transit system, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.

Sweden’s police order Tiktok and Meta to remove 30 ads for criminal services
- Swedish police ordered TikTok and Meta to remove 30 ads since mid-July offering payment for criminal services, as gangs increasingly recruit youths online.
- New legislation allows police to demand removal of criminal recruitment posts within one hour, with platforms complying but police urging better content monitoring.
- Criminals lure young people with false promises of large payments; Swedish Parliament lowered the age of criminal responsibility from 15 to 14 starting Sept 10.
AI generated
STOCKHOLM - Swedish police said on Aug 21 they have demanded tech giants Tiktok and Meta take down 30 posts offering payment for criminal services since mid-July, as criminals increasingly make use of social networks.
The Nordic country has struggled for more than a decade to rein in a surge in gang violence linked primarily to score-settling and battles to control the drug market.
Swedish gangs often use social media and encrypted apps to recruit teens who are paid to carry out crimes, including murders, knowing they would avoid prison sentences if arrested.
“Since July 15, we have had legislation that allows us to order platforms to remove online recruitment content within one hour,” a police spokeswoman told AFP in an email.
Since then, “we have sent 30 orders... 29 to TikTok and one to Meta,” she added.
The platforms had complied, but police were still calling for greater awareness and for tech companies to step up their monitoring and moderation of content.
Criminals operate with a well-oiled modus operandi: the ads are first posted openly on social networks such as TikTok, Instagram or Snapchat.
When a young person responds to an ad, the conversation then continues on an encrypted messaging service.
“The amounts offered can range from 10,000 kronor (S$1,340) to several million, depending on the crime they want to outsource,” the spokeswoman said.
“These are false promises used to draw young people into crime. It is extremely rare for the money to actually be paid, especially for the fanciful amounts advertised to be genuinely handed over,” she added.
On Aug 13, the Swedish Parliament voted to lower the age of criminal responsibility from 15 to 14, a measure that will come into force on Sept 10. AFP

Bulgarian folklore dance troupes abroad are the "beating heart" of Bulgarian communities around the world. From September 18 to 20, it will "beat like crazy" in Burgas during the second festival of folklore ensembles from abroad. The initiative is of the Association of Bulgarian Folklore Ensembles Abroad (ABFEA) and is a continuation of the first edition of the festival, which was hosted in Veliko Tarnovo in 2025.
21 groups from 8 countries will dance by the sea as part of the event called "Burgas Brings Us Together". Performing in front of a domestic audience brings great excitement and respect for the amateur dancers, Radoslava Nedyalkova, chairwoman of the Association, but also creator of the ensemble "Nashenci" in Milan, told Radio Bulgaria. The idea for this festival in Bulgaria was given impetus by the event „Na Megdana na Drugata Bulgaria" (On the Village Square of the Other Bulgaria) known throughout Europe, which for 11 years has been gathering thousands of Bulgarians from all over the world in a dizzying folklore experience in the central squares of some of the major European cities.
Radoslava Nedyalkova
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
"For us, the whole organization is very exciting. The Association of Bulgarian Folklore Ensembles Abroad has the idea to invite Bulgarian folklore ensembles that perform abroad to show their passion for dance on Bulgarian soil. And I have to tell you that it happened in a very difficult way, because the groups feel an incredible respect for their homeland and for folklore in general. But, thank God, this year we gathered enough participants and we will be able to hold three festival evenings - on September 18, 19 and 20."
Nostalgia as a powerful engine
Life abroad gives rise to nostalgia and folklore fills the void and unites our compatriots.
PHOTO ABFEA
The Association has over 60 Bulgarian dance troupes – from Europe and beyond. According to Radoslava Nedyalkova, there are already over 200 Bulgarian dance troupes in America and there are probably as many in Europe. The interest in Bulgarian dance is there and many of the dancers are not Bulgarians. However, the challenges facing these groups are not few – from finding a suitable rehearsal space to purchasing folk costumes and music. However, this does not dampen their enthusiasm:
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
"We we have no state funding. These are exclusively personal funds of the leader, of the people who are members of these groups. In addition, we are all amateurs – this requires time for preparation, it requires the right choreographer who knows how to teach people."
The rhythm and energy of Bulgarian folklore have the power to create a community
PHOTO ABFEA
2026 is a special year – it marks 10 years since the establishment of the Association of Folklore Ensembles Abroad. This will be specially celebrated during the Fifth Creative Seminar, which the Association traditionally organizes in the second week of November in Sofia. The task of these workshops of the ensemble leaders is to contribute to the preservation of authentic Bulgarian folklore abroad, with the thematic emphasis now placed on the Shoppe folklore region of Bulgaria.
PHOTO ABFEA
The program of the festival in Burgas
The three-day celebration "Burgas brings us together" starts on September 18 with an opening at the Summer Theater. On September 19, a one-hour horo dance will be performed at "Sts. Cyril and Methodius" Square, from which we will also expect impressive footage filmed from a bird's eye view with a drone. On September 20, a colorful parade of participating groups in folklore costumes is planned, which will start from the Municipality and reach the Summer Theater for the gala concert. "There will also be two children's groups from Bulgarian schools who wanted to dance at this festival. Bulgarian security services neutralize powerful GPS jammer in Sofia

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21

News
Bulgarian security services neutralize powerful GPS jammer in Sofia
Friday 21 August 2026 23:27
Friday, 21 August 2026, 23:27
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Bulgaria’s State Agency for National Security (DANS), jointly with the Communications Regulation Commission and the Sofia Directorate of the Interior, have located and neutralized a powerful GPS jammer in the Sofia neighbourhood of Dragalevtsi, the agency’s press office has reported.
The device, found in a heavily guarded complex, was suppressing GPS frequencies across Sofia, including those used at Sofia Airport, by aircraft flying over the city and by television towers.
Speaking to journalists at the site, a restaurant complex that continued operating during the operation, manager Nikolay Ivanov categorically denied that any such device had been found there.
For the time being, the Ministry of the Interior and DANS have provided no further details about the jamming device. It is also unclear how it was detected and how investigators were led to the site. The two institutions said further information would be released at a later stage, BNR reporter Nikolay Hristov said.
Professional pilot and aviation journalist Aleksandar Bogoyavlenski told the Bulgarian National Radio (BNR) that there had been problems with GPS signals affecting aircraft taking off from and landing at Sofia Airport over the past several days.
The Ministry of Transport and the State Enterprise Air Traffic Services told BNR that flight safety had not been compromised, as aircraft can rely on independent ground-based navigation systems that are not affected by GPS jamming.
In connection with the incident, the press office of Vasil Levski Sofia Airport told the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) that airport operations had not been affected and flights were being operated according to schedule.

Trump temporarily lifts tariffs on ground beef imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
21:07:04 UTC
06:07:04 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
US President Donald Trump on Friday announced a temporary waiver of out-of-quota tariffs on ground beef imports, allowing hundreds of thousands of metric tons to enter the country over the next 90 days.
“As we work to rebuild this herd and help our ranchers, for the next 90 days, the United States will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out-of-quota tariff,” Trump wrote Friday on his social media platform Truth Social.
“We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices,” Trump said. “This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.”
The average price of 100% ground beef in the US is about $6.89 per pound, according to US Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.
The announcement comes as US beef prices have risen amid a decline in the domestic cattle herd, which is at its lowest level in decades.
The US cattle industry has faced tighter supplies as ranchers have reduced herds amid high production costs and other market pressures. The shortage has contributed to higher prices for consumers, particularly for ground beef, a staple of US households.
Affordability of groceries and other goods has emerged as a central issue in US midterm congressional elections set for Nov. 3, less than three months away. While Trump is not on the ballot, most polls predict opposition Democrats will make gains in Congress, which could hinder Trump’s goals in the last two years of his term.
Trump’s new measure is expected to increase the amount of foreign beef entering the US market while the country works to rebuild its cattle herd.
The president planned a similar move in May, according to Politico, but shelved the idea after pushback from his inner circle.
The move could face opposition from some US ranchers and cattle industry representatives, who have argued that increased imports could undermine efforts to strengthen domestic production.
At the same time, the Trump administration has sought to balance support for domestic cattle producers with efforts to address food inflation and reduce costs for consumers.
The administration has not yet provided details on how the additional imports will be allocated or which countries will supply the beef.

Ukraine is fielding more drone-hunters than ever. Free simulator now lets operators learn each one before it reaches their hands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
21:02:43 UTC
06:02:43 KST

Ukraine is training the operators who shoot down Russian drones on a simulator, before they touch a real interceptor. The Ukrainian interceptor drones P1-SUN and Bullet were integrated into the UFDS combat-drone simulator, Drone Fight Group reported.
In the simulator, an operator can practice basic control, pursuit, and interception of aerial targets, repeat exercises an unlimited number of times, and train accuracy without using real equipment, letting Ukraine build interceptor-drone crews cheaply and safely as it fields more of the drones that down Russia's Shaheds.
The simulator uses accurate models of real drones
The two interceptors are the first real ones added to the military version. The P1-SUN by SkyFall and the Bullet by General Cherry became the first actual anti-aircraft interceptor drones integrated into UFDS Military, Drone Fight Group said.
The point is to train on what operators will actually fly. For the developers, the collaboration continues the simulator's core principle of bringing training as close as possible to get to know them in a safe digital environment.
It is free for Ukrainian troops
The training version is provided to the military at no cost. The full training version of UFDS is available free for Ukrainian soldiers, while a public version is available on Steam, and the full version is given to units individually through a form on the site.
More Ukrainian drones are being added
The developers plan to keep integrating real systems. The UFDS team intends to add more real Ukrainian drones and other uncrewed-systems solutions, giving makers a way to present their platforms to operators digitally and users a way to train on models matching real systems.
As the country fields an ever-wider range of interceptors and other drones, a simulator that mirrors the real systems lets operators learn each new platform before it reaches their hands.

US Supreme Court allows White House ballroom construction for now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
21:01:50 UTC
06:01:50 KST

The US Supreme Court has allowed construction of a massive White House ballroom to continue for now, giving President Donald Trump a temporary victory for one of his pet renovation projects.
Chief Justice John Roberts temporarily lifted a lower court ruling that had demanded a halt to the building of the controversial ballroom by midnight on Friday.
Roberts's one-sentence order means that work on the ballroom, which has been challenged by historical preservation groups, may proceed while litigation plays out in the lower courts.
Trump, in a post on Truth Social, said he was "grateful" for the Supreme Court decision.
"The Military/Ballroom Complex being built on the hallowed grounds of the White House, which is so vital for National Security, will be the greatest of its kind!" he said. "Construction is under budget and ahead of schedule."
The Trump administration asked the conservative-dominated Supreme Court last week to allow it to finish building the ballroom and an underground bunker at the White House, saying the project was essential for national security.
Trump ordered the demolition of the entire historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for his long-desired ballroom, but the project was quickly challenged in court.
A district court ordered a halt to work on the aboveground ballroom while allowing construction of the underground military bunker to proceed, but that order was stayed on appeal.
The appellate court recently upheld the lower court's order, agreeing that such a sweeping White House overhaul required the explicit consent of Congress, but gave the administration time to appeal to the Supreme Court.
'Not a tenant'
Solicitor General John Sauer, in the appeal to the Supreme Court, also stressed the project's security aspects and argued that the president has the authority to make changes to the White House.
"The President of the United States of America is not a tenant, but rather the sole, elected head of the Executive Branch, and Congress has authorised him to renovate, secure, and protect the White House and its grounds, as other Presidents have been allowed to do, without exception," Sauer said.
The project is already 65 percent complete, he said, and halting it "will stall this vital construction, making this president, the subject of recurrent assassination attempts, much less safe, and risking future presidents' safety."
Work on the ballroom began last year with the sudden demolition of the East Wing, which had housed the First Lady's offices.
The ballroom is just one of Trump's moves to leave his mark on Washington by the time his second term ends in January 2029.
They include renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a White House helipad, work on public parks and plans to construct a gigantic downtown arch.
Several of the projects have similarly faced legal challenges, but the ballroom project is the first to reach the Supreme Court.

Pentagon Fires Editor and Publisher of U.S. Military Newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:56:34 UTC
05:56:34 KST

The Pentagon has fired the editor-in-chief and publisher of the U.S. military newspaper Stars and Stripes.
On Friday, the Pentagon provided separation notices to editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and publisher Max Lederer, CBS News reported. The notices said that the two had five days to appeal the decision, according to CBS.
Slavin told The Associated Press that he was dismissed for insubordination “for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line.” In July, CBS published a story featuring an interview with Slavin, in which he stressed the importance of the newspaper’s independence.
“We need to be able to provide independent news to service members,” he told CBS. “If we can’t do that, if we were turned into something other than that, if we were public relations? Yeah, that's the foxhole.”
While Stars and Stripes receives part of its funding from the Pentagon, it has a years-long history of being editorially independent. In January, though, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said that the Department of Defense “is returning Stars & Stripes to its original mission” and is “bringing Stars & Stripes into the 21st century.”
“We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members,” he said in a post on X in January.
In March, more details about the department’s “modernization” overhaul for Stars and Stripes were revealed by an internal memo, which included a provision that content published by the newspaper must be aligned with “good order and discipline,” a phrase that is in the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
News of the firings also comes after Lederer announced on Tuesday that he plans to retire, effective Sept. 30. Lederer, who has been publisher of the newspaper for nearly two decades, said that he came to the decision after he realized that his “understanding of the value and mission of Stars and Stripes” diverged in “fundamental ways” from the Pentagon’s plans for the newspaper. He said he disagreed with parts of the modernization plan revealed in March, including the Pentagon’s desire to transition all print products to digital; Lederer said he worried that the move would affect the accessibility of Stars and Stripes for some service members.
“I think the right step is for me to step down, get out of the way, and let different leadership step in and continue to make this, the great organization that it is, even better,” Lederer told Stars and Stripes.
In April, the Department of Defense fired the newspaper’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith. As ombudsman, Smith was tasked with ensuring the organization’s editorial independence. Smith told her colleagues in a message at the time, which was seen by The Washington Post, that the Pentagon didn’t provide a reason for her firing, but that she believed the decision came down because she criticized the agency’s moves to overhaul the newspaper.
“I knew it was risky to speak out, but my responsibility to Stripes and the First Amendment was paramount,” she wrote in her message to her colleagues, according to the Post.
In June, Smith filed a lawsuit in federal court against the Department of Defense, in which she alleged that her firing was retaliatory and a violation of her First Amendment rights.

Russian groups keep trying—and failing—to reach Lyman, gateway to Donbas’ fortress belt, officer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:54:56 UTC
05:54:56 KST

Logistical problems are stopping Russian small infantry groups from reaching Lyman, a 53rd Brigade officer told Army TV on 21 August, ArmyInform reported.
Russia is trying to capture Lyman and use it as a launchpad for an advance toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Its forces have repeatedly tried to push into the city. They have reached its eastern edge but have not secured a foothold inside, according to Ukraine’s Joint Forces.
Junior Lieutenant Volodymyr Hirniak, a communications officer with Ukraine’s 53rd Separate Mechanized Brigade, said the situation in the unit’s sector remained tense but had “not changed too radically.”
Russian forces continued to use drones, including fiber-optic models, Hirniak said. On the ground, they were sending small infantry groups to slip through Ukrainian lines and create confusion inside the brigade’s defensive positions.
The tactic was neither new nor confined to the 53rd Brigade’s sector, he added. Russia’s immediate aim was to reach Lyman and “open a gate” for further advances.
However, logistical problems were preventing the groups from achieving that aim, according to Hirniak. Ukrainian troops later detected and neutralized the infiltrating teams, he said.
ArmyInform did not report how many groups had attempted to advance, where within the brigade’s sector the incidents occurred, or over what period. Hirniak’s account could not be independently verified.
Why Russia keeps pushing toward Lyman
Lyman is a frontline city in northern Donetsk Oblast that blocks Russia’s northern route toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, part of Ukraine’s fortified Donbas “fortress belt.” Russia occupied the city for about four months in 2022 before Ukrainian forces liberated it on 1 October.
Joint Forces spokesman Viktor Trehubov said on 4 August that Russia needed to capture Lyman and establish a base there before advancing south toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Russia has pressed towards Lyman for more than a year. In July 2025, another Ukrainian officer said Russian gains near the city remained slow and costly despite repeated attempts to exploit gaps in Ukrainian lines.

Trump loyalist Ed Martin is leaving the Justice Department to focus on election ‘legal battles’
WASHINGTON (AP) — Ed Martin, a loyal White House ally who held multiple Justice Department posts despite unconventional tactics that sometimes rankled his superiors, is leaving President Donald Trump’s administration, the Republican president said Friday.
Trump said in a social media post that Martin is leaving his role as the Justice Department’s pardon attorney to “fight Legal Battles” surrounding this year’s midterm elections and the 2028 presidential election.
“I know he will do an outstanding job, ensure Free, Fair, and Honest Elections, and strongly advance our Constitutional Rights,” Trump wrote.
Martin has been a controversial Trump administration figure since his appointment last year as interim U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, where he oversaw the dismissal of Jan. 6 cases after Trump’s sweeping pardons. Trump later pulled Martin’s nomination for the job over bipartisan concerns about his lack of prosecutorial experience and support for rioters who violently attacked the Capitol.
He then moved to Justice Department headquarters as pardon attorney and director of a group tasked with scrutinizing actions by President Joe Biden’s administration that Republicans say unfairly targeted conservatives. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi also named him a special attorney to help conduct mortgage fraud investigations into Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff and New York Attorney General Letitia James.
He often raised eyebrows during his tenure. In one instance, while conducting his mortgage fraud investigation into James, he sent her a letter urging her to resign from office “as an act of good faith.” He also posed for photos outside her Brooklyn home.
The Justice Department’s case against James was dismissed after the judge found that another prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed.
Martin was later sidelined amid clashes with Justice Department leadership and was removed as head of the “Weaponization Working Group,” though he kept his title as pardon attorney.
In a social media post Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche called Martin a “patriot who loves this nation.” Martin didn’t immediately respond to a message Friday, but on his X account he reposted Trump’s announcement with the message: “Proud to serve. Fight Fight Fight.”
Before his nomination as D.C. U.S. attorney, Martin was a leader of Trump’s “Stop the Steal” movement. He spoke at a rally in Washington on the eve of the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol and later served on the board of a nonprofit that raised money to support Capitol riot defendants and their families.
Trump’s post is the latest sign of his obsession with voting in the upcoming midterm elections, which will determine control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his presidency.
His administration has fixated on messaging around noncitizen voting, a rare problem that Trump falsely insists is a widespread source of fraud. His Department of Justice has been trying to gather detailed state voter data to hunt for noncitizens, and he has been pushing Congress to pass a bill that would require documentary proof of citizenship to vote in time for the November elections.
The FBI has obtained voting records or election equipment from the most populous counties in the battleground states of Arizona, Georgia and Michigan without saying what it was searching for. Trump also has issued two executive orders seeking to take control of certain election operations, even though the Constitution grants states and Congress the authority to determine election rules.
Democratic state officials have been raising alarms about the possibility of the administration deploying federal immigration agents to polling places or ordering the military to voting locations or election offices, although administration officials have said they have no such plans.

US Court allows White House ballroom construction for now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:45:39 UTC
05:45:39 KST

Breadcrumb
US Supreme Court allows White House ballroom construction for now
The US Supreme Court on Friday allowed construction of a massive White House ballroom to continue for now, giving President Donald Trump a temporary victory for one of his pet renovation projects.
Chief Justice John Roberts temporarily lifted a lower court ruling that had demanded a halt to the building of the controversial ballroom by midnight on Friday.
Roberts's one-sentence order means that work on the ballroom, which historical preservation groups have challenged, may proceed while litigation plays out in the lower courts.
The Trump administration asked the conservative-dominated Supreme Court last week to allow it to complete construction of the ballroom and an underground bunker at the White House, saying the project was essential for national security.
Trump ordered the demolition of the entire historic East Wing of the White House last year, without input from Congress, to make way for his long-desired ballroom, but the project was quickly challenged in court.
A district court ordered a halt to work on the aboveground ballroom while allowing construction of the underground military bunker to proceed, but the order was stayed while on appeal.
The appellate court recently upheld the lower court's order, agreeing that such a sweeping White House overhaul required Congress's explicit consent, but gave the administration time to appeal to the Supreme Court.
Trump initially touted the construction of the ballroom as being necessary to host galas and state dinners, but has since repeatedly emphasised the addition of a sophisticated underground military bunker and other security features.
'Not a tenant'
Solicitor General John Sauer, in the appeal to the Supreme Court, also stressed the project's security aspects and argued that the president has the authority to make changes to the White House.
"The President of the United States of America is not a tenant, but rather the sole, elected head of the Executive Branch, and Congress has authorised the President to renovate, secure, and protect the White House and its grounds, as other Presidents have been allowed to do, without exception," Sauer said.
He said the project is already 65 percent complete and halting it "will stall this vital construction, making this president, the subject of recurrent assassination attempts, much less safe, and risking future presidents' safety."
Work on the ballroom began last year with the sudden demolition of the East Wing, which used to house the offices of the First Lady.
Trump has insisted that the ballroom will be privately financed, but according to media reports, significant taxpayer funds are going to the project, which could cost as much as $600 million.
The ballroom is just one of Trump's moves to leave his mark on Washington by the time his second term ends in January 2029. They include renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, work on public parks and plans to construct a gigantic arch.
Several of the projects have similarly faced legal challenges, but the ballroom project is the first to reach the Supreme Court.

With Ukraine’s corruption, one thing is certain: You haven’t seen the worst yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:43:02 UTC
05:43:02 KST

With Ukraine’s corruption, one thing is certain: You haven’t seen the worst yet
The politics of Vladimir Zelensky’s Ukraine remain a smelly swamp, producing a ceaseless seepage of scandals occasionally percolating to the surface in big, toxic bubbles that pop with a noxious stink. Recently, for instance, the returning ambassador to the US – no less – has become the subject of a corruption case bad enough to require bail equivalent to $130,000.
The very latest Zelensky regime stink bubble to burst, however, is centered on a former double minister. Before ending up at the center of yet another big pile of dirt, compliments of Zelensky and cronies, Herman Galushchenko had served as minister of energy and then of justice. And if you know Kiev’s political culture – for want of better terms – you won’t be surprised to hear that, in the end, he ended up arrested under suspicion of very large-scale corruption.
To be precise, Galushchenko is one of the main suspects in the massive scandal featuring the Energoatom, aka Mindich-Gate after Timur Mindich, an intimate friend of Zelensky who, clearly tipped off about his impending arrest, has long fled to Israel. Galushchenko, too, tried to run, but was not fast enough, or more likely, lacked the same level of premium protection, namely from the president himself, and got caught at the border.
Yet if the story had ended there, this would not be Ukraine. Now we are into the sequel, and it’s at least as bad as the first part. Because in essence, Galushchenko in a cell was a thought that Zelensky and his crew could not tolerate. Surely out of sheer mafia-like camaraderie! Perish the thought – they were afraid of any deals the former minister might strike and names he might name. But getting Galushchenko out was expensive: Here as well the court had set bail, and as Mindich-Gate was a $100-million case, the bail wasn’t cheap.
Hence, this time the scandal is not about the embezzling, extorting, or stealing of humungous amounts of money, Ukrainian-establishment style. But that’s only because the stealing had been done already and phase two had started: laundering the loot. In legalese, the official case is about an attempt to “legalize criminally acquired property.” In practice, this meant weaving up a web of criminal deception to pay Galushchenko’s bail, well above $3 million – we are in the big league now – with dirty money made to look clean.
Central to this operation and the highest-ranking official to have lost her position at this point is Irina Mudraya, the deputy head of Zelensky’s very own office, as well as a former deputy minister of justice. But the circle of suspects is much wider, as always in Ukraine where corruption is the passionate national sport of those running and ruining the country, while its ordinary citizens are hunted by military press gangs in broad daylight.
Also officially under suspicion and investigation are Maksim Mikitas, a former parliamentary deputy; Vadim Stolar, a currently serving parliamentary deputy; Viktor Dubovik, another high official from Zelensky’s presidential office; Elena Ferens, a deputy minister of justice; Nikolay Gladishchenko, Oleg Stupak, Liudmila Snygur, all three high up in the management of state-owned Sens Bank, which served as the financial vehicle for the launder-and-pay-for-Galushchenko scheme.
Then we also have “businessman,” a “person linked to Mikitas,” the director of the Metrostroy company, a driver who also happens to run Montazh Servis (a construction company by the name of it – good for concrete foundations to bury the talkative), and a bodyguard who doubles as the director of a firm calling itself The Philosophy of Development.
These, in sum, are typical pillars of the Ukrainian establishment as it really is. Suffice it to say that, in 2018, high-flyer Irina Mudraya, trained at Lviv University, received a ‘Best Legal Adviser in Banking and Financial Law’ award (sure, just be honest next time and call it ‘Best Consigliere in Mafia Ukraine’). In 2021, she won ‘Women Leaders who have Influenced the Development of the Legal Community’ (and unfortunately, she probably has). And just two years ago, Business Woman magazine honored her achievements in “Politics and Diplomacy.”
In short, if the Cohen Brothers were to make a very dark, caustic comedy about corruption in Ukraine, this would be their cast. Not all of it, of course, because rest assured, many accomplices and even leaders have not been caught and won’t ever be caught, including the man everyone is always thinking about but can’t ever name when the latest stink bubble pops – the president himself.
Yet one man who may be looking at an uncertain near-future in conjunction with ‘Operation Forrest Gump’ – the code name for this investigation – is the current head of Zelensky’s administration, Kirill Budanov. Formerly mostly busy with black ops, lies, and terrorism, Budanov has taken his office as Zelensky’s top manager only recently. His predecessor Andrey Yermak, another very close, intimate friend of Zelensky, had been forced out because of his deep involvement in Mindich-Gate. Or probably, really due to both his own crimes and those of Zelensky himself that needed a fall guy.
As caught by eavesdropping, Mudraya reminded an accomplice that “he says that corruption needs to be organized and controlled; we must not fight it.” According to Ukrainska Pravda, the mysterious “he,” the real author of that arrogantly direct and brashly cynical statement, was her boss Budanov.
It is intriguing, as another Ukrainian publication has pointed out that it is precisely Ukrainska Pravda that has dared name Budanov. For the outlet is among the supporters of Mikhail Fedorov, the tech whizz kid and former minister of defense, who has turned from a Zelensky regime insider into a challenger by calling for presidential elections even during wartime. That is, in reality, for calling for an end to the Zelensky regime, because the incumbent, polls show, can be beaten.
Let’s set aside that Fedorov has demolished, in passing, a favorite propaganda lie shared by official Kiev and the West, namely that the Ukrainian constitution does not allow for such elections during wartime. In reality, the constitution does no such thing. Politically, the key fact is that Fedorov has thrown his hat in the ring. And in that coming fight, it is very likely that one of his main rivals will be Budanov.
The swamp that is Ukrainian politics keeps festering. The greed and cynicism of Kiev’s ‘elite’ knows no limits. At the same time what may be even more tragic for Ukraine is that any attempt to reign in the rampant corruption by finally holding everyone accountable, no matter how high up, is not only unlikely to succeed but dishonest too.
Naming Budanov? Yes, but not because he should face scrutiny and accountability but because he needs to be weakened so that another ambitious establishment representative has a better chance at beating him at coming elections. In Kiev, stories of messianic redeemers are popular again and again. Zelensky was once the most enthusiastically endorsed of them all. And yet it is his regime that has become the very worst. Why would Fedorov be any different? Or for that matter, anyone else. Ukraine does not need personnel change; it needs a massive reset.

Fauci's lawyers set up legal defense fund as US probes multiply
Unknown

Fauci's lawyers set up legal defense fund as US probes multiply
WASHINGTON, Aug 21 - Lawyers for Anthony Fauci have launched a legal defense fund for the former top U.S. infectious disease expert, saying that the need to respond to a growing number of state and federal investigations related to his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic will require substantial resources.
In January 2025, then-President Joe Biden issued a preemptive pardon to Fauci, amid accusations from Republican lawmakers that he played a role in research that contributed to the pandemic and later sought to cover up its origins, claims that have not been independently substantiated.
Fauci, who led the U.S. response to COVID-19, has denied the allegations.
U.S. Republican Senator Rand Paul has asked the Department of Justice to prosecute Fauci after he refused to answer questions about the pandemic at a congressional hearing last month. Three state attorneys general have since launched their own probes against him.
The defense fund underscores how Fauci, once the public face of the U.S. response to COVID-19, has become a central target of Republican efforts to revisit the origins of the pandemic and scrutinise government decision-making during the health crisis. His lawyers say the mounting investigations could result in lengthy and costly legal proceedings despite Biden's pardon.
"Dr. Fauci is facing an unprecedented legal barrage for a retired civil servant, and he deserves a robust defense against these unfounded and frivolous actions," David Schertler, counsel to Fauci, said in a statement to Reuters. "Dr. Fauci has not done anything wrong, and we are prepared to fight back against this shameful harassment of an honorable man who dedicated his career to saving lives."
The launch of a legal defense fund has not been previously reported.
Fauci, 85, led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) for nearly 40 years and advised seven U.S. presidents. He retired in 2022.
During the pandemic, he was a leading proponent of lockdown measures, mask requirements and vaccine development that ultimately helped the United States and other countries emerge from COVID. Such recommendations against a novel virus were endorsed by many global health officials and governments worldwide. Scientists and intelligence agencies remain divided over whether COVID was caused by a leak from laboratory experiments in China, or from transmission from animals to humans.
TORRENT OF ATTACKS
Yet Fauci has faced a torrent of attacks over the U.S. response to COVID, largely from Republicans, both during President Donald Trump's first term and then Biden's. Paul has repeatedly called for Fauci to be jailed and blamed him for the U.S. death toll from the pandemic, which exceeded 1 million.
Fauci invoked his constitutional right against self-incrimination and refused to answer questions during the July hearing in Congress, citing Paul's "unhinged" campaign to see him imprisoned.
Allegations about Fauci's role in the pandemic have proliferated among Republican lawmakers. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. wrote a book about Fauci and has helped Paul's inquiries.
Kennedy said health department staff spent eight months locating Fauci's private diary on multiple government servers and gave the records to Paul, who publicly released them. Paul and Republican Senator Ron Johnson have also begun to release private text messages from a copy of Fauci's government cell phone.
David Morens, a former adviser to Fauci, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to conspiring to evade public records laws and conceal government documents related to grant research funding and the COVID pandemic. Paul has referred to that case multiple times this week, asking whether it could implicate Fauci.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier issued a subpoena to Fauci and said he would investigate whether the infectious disease expert "personally profited off the COVID 'guidance' he issued." West Virginia and Louisiana said they would support Uthmeier's effort. Fauci will have to secure legal assistance in at least those three states, his lawyers said, in part for document review and production in response to the subpoena.
Fauci will not receive any payment or other form of distribution from the legal defense fund, his lawyers said. It is set up as a trust with an independent corporate trustee, according to Fauci's legal team.
Neither Fauci nor his lawyers have control over how the money will be distributed or how the fund will be managed, his lawyers said. Invoices submitted by Fauci's attorneys will be reviewed by an independent expert adviser, they said.
Once all of Fauci's litigation concludes, any remaining funds will be distributed to charity, his lawyers said. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Interview: Cinema helps bridge China-Egypt cultural exchange: Egyptian actor
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
04:41:47 CST
05:41:47 KST

CAIRO, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- Egyptian actor Sherif Sobhy said his experience acting in the Chinese film "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" showed how cinema can serve as a bridge fostering closer Egypt-China cultural exchange.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Sobhy said he went through about three rounds of auditions before being selected for the role of Zayd, a character he said immediately attracted him.
"He is a very human, flesh-and-blood character," Sobhy said, recalling that he cried while reading the script of the Chinese anti-war film, which has been drawing attention for telling a Middle Eastern war story through the eyes of a Chinese chef.
In the movie, Zayd begins as a quiet restaurant owner, loving husband and devoted father. But after an explosion kills his wife and daughter, grief and a thirst for vengeance consume him, driving him into the ranks of a terrorist group.
Sobhy said he did not view Zayd as an inherently violent person. "He was not raised in a terrorist group, nor was he originally violent. He was actually compassionate," he said.
The challenge, therefore, was to portray the painful transformation of an ordinary person whose grief gradually overwhelms his former self. To prepare for the role, Sobhy imagined himself as a father suddenly robbed of his family.
"After his family's death, he began to live and behave almost like a robot, without emotions," Sobhy said, adding that many of Zayd's feelings were conveyed through his eyes.
The Egyptian actor said working with the Chinese team was another memorable part of the experience.
He noticed differences between Chinese and Egyptian filmmaking styles, saying Chinese crews could spend many hours perfecting a single scene, with the director paying close attention to every shot, angle and performance.
During one take, the director played the film's soundtrack before the scene to help him immerse himself in Zayd's grief, Sobhy told Xinhua. "As an actor, I really appreciate clear direction and instructions."
What affected Sobhy most, however, came after the film reached Chinese cinemas.
"I could never have imagined the tremendous response from the Chinese audience," he said.
He was touched by messages from Chinese viewers who sympathized with Zayd and understood the difference between the man he was and the person he became.
"They understood that this was not the real Zayd. The death of his wife and daughter changed him," Sobhy said.
For him, such reactions showed that audiences from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds can connect through universal human emotions.
Sobhy also sees symbolic meaning in the film's restaurant setting. Initially, Zayd tells the Chinese chef that the rice is salty, partly to assert his authority as the restaurant owner. Yet as the story develops, he comes to understand people share the same bitter taste of war, even when they are of different cultural backgrounds and eating habits.
"It became a symbol of different cultures coming together and of harmony among people from different countries," he said.
The film's message also resonated with Sobhy as an Egyptian actor from a region that has experienced prolonged conflicts.
"For anyone living in the Arab world, where we are surrounded by many conflicts, the dream is very simple: everyone wants to live in peace and not lose the people they love," he said.
"Regardless of our different cultures or nationalities, we all share the same desire to live in peace," he added. ■

UN Security Council holds 2nd straw poll on secretary-general candidates

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
04:41:24 CST
05:41:24 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Security Council on Friday held its second straw poll on the candidates for the next UN secretary-general.
"The second round of straw polls has taken place," said Christina Markus Lassen, the UN ambassador of Denmark, whose country holds the rotating presidency of the Security Council for the month of August.
After the conclusion of the secret vote, Lassen told reporters that the candidates will be informed of the results through the respective permanent representatives of the member states that nominated them. The president of the UN General Assembly will also be informed that the straw poll has been concluded, she said.
Through straw polls, the Security Council selects a candidate to recommend to the General Assembly for appointment as the next UN secretary-general.
Security Council straw polls on secretary-general candidates are informal closed-door ballots used to gauge support for the candidates. Their results are not officially released.
Article 97 of the UN Charter states that the secretary-general shall be appointed by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council.
Lassen did not provide any details of Friday's vote. However, it is believed that all eight candidates were on the ballot.
The eight candidates currently in the race are: Ivonne A-Baki, former Ecuadorian minister and diplomat; Michelle Bachelet, former Chilean president and former UN high commissioner for human rights; Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former UN General Assembly president and former foreign minister and defense minister of Ecuador; Rafael Grossi of Argentina, current director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency; Rebeca Grynspan, former vice president of Costa Rica and current secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development; Olara Otunnu of Uganda, former UN under-secretary-general; Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Guyana's permanent representative to the United Nations; and Macky Sall, former president of Senegal.
Security Council members were believed to have received one ballot per candidate, containing the candidate's name followed by three options: "encouraged," "discouraged," and "no opinion expressed," according to What's in Blue, which provides insights into evolving Security Council actions.
The term of current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will end on December 31. ■

Mexican governor, indicted by U.S. on charges of collaboration with drug cartel, is back in office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:41:22 UTC
05:41:22 KST

Mexican governor, indicted by U.S. on charges of collaboration with drug cartel, is back in office
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Rubén Rocha Moya, governor of Sinaloa state, has been accused by U.S. authorities of collaborating with the notorious Sinaloa cartel.
- Rocha Moya said in May he would take a leave from office to fight the U.S. indictment. It’s unclear what prompted his return to work now.
- Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has refused a U.S. demand to extradite the governor.
MEXICO CITY — A Mexican state governor — wanted by U.S. authorities on charges of collaborating with the notorious Sinaloa cartel — returned to office Friday, more than three months after going on leave following his stunning federal indictment in New York.
Rubén Rocha Moya, governor of the northwestern state of Sinaloa, resumed his duties as he denounced the “false allegations” against him as “driven by political and interventionist motivations from the national and foreign ultra-right.”
On May 1, Rocha Moya announced that he was taking a leave of absence to defend himself against “false and malicious” allegations. On Friday, he declared on X: “Today I return to the exercise of my responsibility as governor of Sinaloa with the strength of truth on our side.”
It’s unclear what prompted his return. Rocha Moya, 77, is a longtime stalwart of Mexico’s ruling Morena party and confidant of ex-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, the leftist who founded Morena.
The case against Rocha Moya and his alleged confederates sent shock waves through the country’s political and law enforcement establishments.
The U.S. indictment of Rocha Moya — which essentially paints an entire Mexican state as being under cartel control — is also the highest-profile manifestation of the Trump administration’s very public vow to crack down on corrupt Mexican lawmakers allegedly in cahoots with organized crime.
U.S. brings drug charges against Rúben Rocha Moya, governor of Mexico’s Sinaloa state, and other members of President Sheinbaum’s ruling Morena party.
Mexican cartels, experts say, thrive in large part due to collaboration with police and politicians, from street cops to mayors to governors. Mexican gangs employ violence and payoffs to ensure officials do not disrupt their many illicit enterprises, which extend beyond drug trafficking to extortion, fuel smuggling and other lucrative rackets.
Following Rocha Moya’s indictment, Washington demanded that Mexico arrest the governor and extradite him to the United States. But President Claudia Sheinbaum refused to comply, asserting that U.S. authorities did not provide sufficient proof of his alleged crimes.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum accused the U.S. of meddling in Mexico’s internal affairs after a report about two Mexican governors who had their U.S. visas revoked amid probes into possible links to organized crime.
Now, Rocha Moya will return to running a state that is ground zero for the smuggling of fentanyl, methamphetamine and other illicit drugs to the United States.
There was no immediate public comment from U.S. officials.
The case presented Sheinbaum with a dilemma: Either hand over the governor to U.S. prosecutors, thus alienating a core support base in the Morena party and undermining her frequent pledges to resist U.S. intervention, or keep hands off the governor, risking ire from the White House.
While U.S. authorities have bought charges against ex-Mexican governors and other former high-ranking officials, the case against Rocha Moya marked the first time that a sitting Mexican governor has been indicted.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum launched a high-profile campaign against extortion, calling it a nationwide problem.
In April, the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed the indictment charging Rocha Moya and nine other current and former Sinaloa officials with drug trafficking and collaborating with the Sinaloa cartel, among other allegations.
Prosecutors alleged that a cartel faction known as “Los Chapitos” — run by sons of Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, the imprisoned kingpin — provided financial and other support to help Rocha Moya win the 2021 gubernatorial election.
Likely providing U.S. prosecutors with information to implicate Rocha Moya, experts say, were Mexican capos already in U.S. custody, including two jailed sons of El Chapo.
Rocha Moya’s term as governor is slated to end Oct. 21, 2027.
Special correspondent Cecilia Sánchez Vidal contributed to this report.

The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) said the U.S. ride-hailing company had violated the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which restricts decisions made solely through automated processing when they have significant effects on individuals.
Uber drivers suspected of fraud or receiving customer ratings deemed too low could have their accounts automatically suspended, while persistently low ratings could lead to permanent deactivation, the AP said.
"Uber committed serious violations. Drivers were deactivated without warning," AP Deputy Chair Monique Verdier said. "A computer should not make decisions on its own that have major consequences for you. These decisions should first have been reviewed by a human."
The investigation followed complaints from 171 French drivers and examined Uber's practices between 2018 and 2022. The Dutch regulator handled the case because Uber's European headquarters are in the Netherlands.
The penalty marks the fourth fine imposed on Uber by the AP. Uber said it would appeal the decision. ■

Senegal’s former president Macky Sall followed with six votes in favor, Olara Otunnu with five and Maria Fernanda Espinosa Garces with four. Former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet received two votes in favor, while Ivonne A-Baki received none.

minqa atelier steps charred timber refuge down a steep slope in ecuador’s chocó forest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:35:52 UTC
05:35:52 KST

In Ecuador’s Chocó forest, Minqa Atelier places a 53-square-meter residential refuge on a steep site in Pedro Vicente Maldonado, where heavy rain and difficult access shaped how the house could touch the ground. Chocó Pambil Refuge descends with the terrain as a sequence of raised wooden platforms, keeping the slope visible beneath the floor instead of cutting a flat pad into the hillside. From the forest, its dark timber walls sit behind a lighter teak frame, while glazing opens the interior toward the vegetation.
The plan uses those changes in level as its internal organization. Sleeping and shared spaces occupy separate platforms, yet they remain visually connected under the same roof. Because the floor keeps dropping, each zone meets the forest at a slightly different height. A bed sits almost level with the tree trunks outside, while the lower living spaces look through tall panes toward the slope.
The refuge meets the hillside with gabions filled with river stone, reducing the amount of excavation needed across the uneven ground. Above them, local teak forms an exposed structural frame whose dimensions organize the rooms and roof. Limited access to the site also influenced the construction system, so the components were designed as coordinated pieces that could be transported in and assembled on site.
Along the more exposed exterior surfaces, the team at Minqa Atelier uses charred wood suited to the damp setting. The dark cladding gives the house a dense outer skin, while the teak structure stays readable along the glazed elevations and through the interior. Bolted joints remain visible overhead, and rectangular rooflights slot between the beams, making the construction itself much of the visual language.
Chocó Pambil Refuge descends a steep forest slope in Pedro Vicente Maldonado
the forest enters at several heights
Large openings keep views moving laterally through the refuge, while rooflights bring daylight into the deeper parts of the plan. Natural ventilation passes through the open interior, and the surrounding vegetation appears almost wall-like behind the glass. The changing floor heights keep the forest shifting in relation to the body, sometimes below eye level and sometimes filling the full elevation.
At only 53 square meters, the house gets much of its spatial range from the changing section and few internal divisions. The original terrain stays legible beneath the raised platforms, so the construction reads as something assembled over the slope instead of imposed across it.

Former Guyana minister leads in second straw poll for UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:32:13 UTC
05:32:13 KST

Former Guyana minister leads in second straw poll for UN chief
- Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana led the second UN chief straw poll, ahead of Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan and Argentina's Rafael Grossi.
- The Security Council's informal voting process continues amid potential new candidates and veto threats from permanent members.
- A candidate must gain nine votes and avoid vetoes before the General Assembly confirms the new UN secretary-general, with regional rotation expected this time.
AI generated
UNITED NATIONS, United States - Guyanese ex-foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett narrowly led the second round of the informal process to pick the next UN chief, a diplomatic source and specialist media said on Aug 21.
Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan was the front-runner in July when the 15-member Security Council held a first informal vote, behind closed doors and by secret ballot.
She dipped slightly to second place, while Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, the current head of the UN nuclear watchdog, came in third, according to the diplomatic source and specialist publication Pass Blue.
Other candidates include fourth-placed Macky Sall of Senegal, Chile’s Michelle Bachelet, Ecuador’s Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu.
Ecuador’s Ivonne A-Baki has also thrown her hat into the race since the first straw poll.
The outgoing secretary-general, Antonio Guterres of Portugal, ends his second five-year term on Dec 31, 2026.
Denmark’s UN ambassador Christina Lassen, whose country holds the Council’s rotating presidency, said the body was considering the timing of the next straw poll.
“It’s too early to have a consensus,” said council-member Democratic Republic of Congo’s ambassador Zenon Ngay Mukongo after the vote.
International Crisis Group’s Daniel Forti said earlier that the veto-wielding nations – Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States – might wait until later to express their preferences, while new contenders could emerge.
Russia’s ambassador to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, said on Aug 20 he could not rule out that possibility.
“If, for example – I’m speculating now – if there is a deadlock on any of the candidates we are seeing today, if nobody... flies, then I think that we may see other candidates as well,” Nebenzia said.
‘End of the road’?
Even if a candidate earns the required nine votes from the 15 available in the Security Council, they must also avoid a veto by the five major powers, which are deeply divided.
Once a candidate clears those bars, their name will go to the General Assembly of all UN members for confirmation.
The Security Council straw poll was devised in the early 1980s in an attempt to break a deadlock between two candidates shut down by vetoes.
The informal mechanism has persisted, in various forms, despite criticism from countries opposed to the opaque process.
“There is a good chance that some nominees realise after (the Aug 21) vote that their campaigns have reached the end of the road,” Forti added.
Each member state must anonymously assign each candidate one of three labels: “encourage,” “discourage,” or “no opinion.”
Rodrigues received eight votes of encouragement, three of discouragement, and four of no opinion, according to the diplomatic source.
That would give those with no support – such as A-Baki, who received no encouragement straws – the opportunity to withdraw, though they are not obliged.
In the first rounds of the process, which is expected to take several weeks, all ballots are the same colour.
But after an unspecified number of votes, the ballots of the Council’s five permanent members will have a different colour, making it possible to identify potential vetoes, without knowing which country blackballed any given candidate.
It is tradition that the UN’s top job should rotate between different regions.
Under that premise, the role should go to a candidate from Latin America this time. There are many candidates from the region, though Sall and Otunnu hail from Africa. AFP

Ukrainian conscripts fleeing from training camps in Germany – Die Zeit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:30:01 UTC
05:30:01 KST

Ukrainian conscripts fleeing from training camps in Germany – Die Zeit
Dozens of Ukrainian soldiers have deserted while undergoing military training in Germany, Die Zeit has reported, citing interviews with ten men who fled their units.
Kiev has increasingly relied on forced mobilization as it struggles to replenish battlefield losses. Videos regularly circulate online showing recruitment officers detaining men in public places and forcing them into vehicles, sometimes after violent confrontations. The practice has become widely known in Ukraine as “busification.”
Die Zeit reported on Wednesday that during the early years of the conflict, Ukrainian troops sent to Germany for training were generally experienced and highly motivated. More recently, however, many of those arriving have been newly mobilized recruits.
In Saxony-Anhalt alone, the regional Interior Ministry has recorded around 80 cases of Ukrainian soldiers deserting, while the nationwide total is believed to run into the hundreds, according to the weekly.
Among those interviewed was Vladimir Shulgin, a 39-year-old former pianist from Dnepr. He told Die Zeit that after Ukraine intensified its mobilization campaign, he largely avoided leaving home while his wife supported the family.
Shulgin said he was detained by recruitment officers after venturing outside in late January and was subsequently sent to Germany’s Altengrabow military training facility.
According to his account, he initially had no intention of deserting. He changed his mind after allegedly being physically abused by Ukrainian superiors and threatened with death upon his return to Ukraine.
After a German military doctor referred him to a hospital in Berlin, Shulgin did not return to the training facility. He has since applied for asylum and is living in a refugee shelter.
Another deserter interviewed by Die Zeit said he had fled because he did not want to kill or be killed.
“I simply don’t want to die, and I don’t want to kill. Not at the front, and nowhere else. Is that enough?” he said.
Their prospects of obtaining asylum are “likely slim,” however, according to the newspaper.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said last month that while Ukrainian men of military age could still apply for asylum, avoiding military service did not in itself constitute grounds for protection.
Similar desertions have occurred during Ukrainian training programs elsewhere in Europe. In late 2024, Ukrainian media reported that around 50 soldiers from the 155th Mechanized Brigade had deserted during training in France.
The Ukrainian authorities have acknowledged tens of thousands of desertion and unauthorized-absence cases since the conflict with Russia escalated in 2022.
Russia has accused the leadership in Kiev and its Western backers of being willing to fight “to the last Ukrainian.”

Israel is seeking international support following the bombing of a base in Syria — which led to a confrontation with Turkey and drew condemnation from the U.S. envoy as well. Doron Spielman, spokesman for the Prime Minister’s Office’s public diplomacy team, released a video Friday evening presenting Israel’s operation in Syria as an effort to thwart a Turkish military buildup and ensure that the threat does not gradually move closer to Israel’s border.
According to Spielman, who was appointed to his position less than two months ago and is intended to be “the face of Israel to the world,” Turkey has established a significant military presence in Syria since the country’s civil war and currently controls, he claimed, about 5% of its territory.
By contrast, he said, Israel holds approximately one-tenth of 1% in southern Syria, “along a border that has threats from Hezbollah and ISIS and other terror organizations. Which means that Turkey, that has no threats, is holding 50 times more Syrian territory than Israel.”
“More than a year ago, Israel and Syria reached an understanding to maintain the security status quo and to keep this border calm,” Spielman said. According to him, Syria breached that understanding after Israeli intelligence identified that Turkish troops were about to deploy at the Abu al-Dahour airbase in northern Syria, less than 200 miles from Israeli towns and communities.
“Prime Minister Netanyahu made Israel’s position very clear,” he said. “We will not allow Turkey to entrench itself in Syria and to be moving steadily south toward Israel’s border.”
According to Spielman, Israel repeatedly warned Syria: “Don’t do it. We know that Syria received those warnings and that it chose to ignore them.” He said that Israel therefore “delivered the message in another way.”
Later in the video, the prime minister’s spokesman addressed the question of why a Turkish presence in Syria should concern Israel.
“Now, some might ask, why should Israel be concerned about Turkish forces in Syria?” he said. “Well, because Turkish President Erdogan has openly called for Israel’s destruction.”
He added that Erdogan has also spoken negatively about the United States, Israel’s closest partner, saying: “A just world is possible, but not with America.”
“Is this the kind of guy you would want on your border?” Spielman asked.
According to Spielman, the events of Oct. 7 demonstrated the danger of ignoring statements made by enemies.
“And Oct. 7 made it clear to everyone,” he said. “When your enemy tells you that he wants to destroy you, you should probably believe him.”
Alongside the harsh statements against Ankara, the spokesman emphasized Prime Minister Netanyahu’s position that Israel does not want an escalation.
“Prime Minister Netanyahu has also made something else very clear. Israel welcomes a return to the previous status quo. We are not looking for escalation,” he said. “But neither Turkey nor any other country is going to threaten the State of Israel.”
The unusual strike prompted an exceptional U.S. condemnation. Tom Barrack, the U.S. envoy to Syria and Turkey, said that such strikes “could increase the Turkish presence in the region in the near future” and said Turkey had not been warned in advance and therefore could have attacked Israel in response.
The deterioration in relations with Turkey came almost immediately. Netanyahu told the Turks, “Don’t.” They announced that they had issued an arrest warrant and a “red notice” against the prime minister, and he called Erdogan an “antisemitic dictator.” On Friday evening, the Turkish presidency said that “the Netanyahu government’s efforts to portray Turkey as a new threat are part of its election strategy.”

Syria and France take this opportunity to emphasise the importance of the role played by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) in uncovering the facts related to the former regime’s chemical weapons programme, identifying and verifying its remaining elements, and working towards their destruction, in cooperation with the Syrian Arab Republic.
