AI's threat to future jobs considered in landmark NSW compensation decision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:43:30 UTC
03:43:30 KST

AI job disruption priced into man's compensation payout in first known case
In short:
The NSW Personal Injury Commission assessed a 34-year-old Aldi and home delivery worker suffered damages of $950,000 after a car crash on his way to work.
Commission member Phillip Carr cited uncertainties including the impact of artificial intelligence on the job market when calculating his future economic loss.
What's next?
The government says it's too soon to draw firm conclusions that AI is causing or will cause future job losses but will keep monitoring the data.
Artificial intelligence's disruptive impact on jobs was priced into an almost $1 million injury claim after a car accident left a NSW man with reduced working capacity.
It's the first known case of a legal body explicitly considering the impact of AI on the workforce when calculating a worker's future earnings.
Earlier this month, the NSW Personal Injury Commission assessed that Andrew Duong suffered damages of $950,000 after he suffered both physical and psychological injuries following a head-on collision on his way to work in 2023.
This included the 34-year-old's $400,000 of future economic loss after finding he could only continue working with restrictions, and the injuries and pain would impact his ability to find future employment if he could no longer work at his current job.
Commission member Philip Carr wrote that Mr Duong had 33 years of working life ahead of him that would be affected by his loss of capacity.
Mr Carr determined that Mr Duong should receive a "significant buffer" for the uncertainty around future loss of earnings, which included the impact of AI.
"[And] with the uncertainty of any occupation in today's workforce, especially with the advent of artificial intelligence and its workplace challenges during his working life, which requires an allowance for his future continuing loss of capacity," he wrote.
The tribunal did not find that AI had cost Mr Duong work, or predict that it would, only that AI may create more job market uncertainty that could disproportionately affect an injured worker with need for greater accommodations.
Before the crash, Mr Duong was working about 70 hours a week in warehouse roles for Aldi and Home Delivery Service.
The crash caused injuries to his right hand and wrist, shoulder, elbow and lower back, as well as a psychological injury. He had two operations on his wrist.
Mr Duong lost his Aldi job after the crash because he was not cleared to return to full-time work, but was still employed by the delivery company on reduced hours.
Mr Carr found Mr Duong could continue in that role with restrictions but said his prospects on the open labour market would be "considerably reduced" if he lost it.
Artificial intelligence was one of multiple considerations mentioned by Mr Carr when assessing Duong's capacity to earn, alongside his injuries, medication and the risk of losing his current role.
How will AI impact future jobs?
Queensland University of Technology's associate professor in economics, Dr Leonora Risse, said there was a lot of uncertainty about how AI would influence the job market.
"There's no one definitive clear result. In some ways it'll be positive, in other aspects, it will be negative," she said.
Dr Rissa said even if certain jobs or industries were not threatened by automation, there would still likely be an impact on the tasks that comprise a job and the skills required.
"Work and tasks are going to look very different," she said, adding that the job market has always been in flux as a result of technological change.
The decision comes after the federal government recently released its first ever analysis of AI's impact on the jobs market, which found no evidence of broad AI-driven disruption in Australia's labour market so far.
Modelling by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations suggested employment in a more AI-exposed occupation was about 2 per cent lower by February than under its pre-ChatGPT trend.
But the department repeatedly cautioned that this was not proof AI had caused job losses. Jobs exposed to the technology had already been growing more slowly before ChatGPT became widely available.
The government said it would continue monitoring the data as more evidence became available.

Employers forced to wait 12 months for overseas nurses, teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:43:30 UTC
03:43:30 KST

Nurses and teachers facing 12-month wait to get to Australia under visa overhaul
In short:
Overseas skilled visa applicants not working in defence or law enforcement have seen their wait times blow out as a result of shift in visa priorities by the government.
Business leaders have said the changes have forced offshore nurses and teachers to the "emergency stopping lane".
What's next?
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke faces pressure to reduce migration and is set to announce a more comprehensive overhaul of the system.
Employers wanting to bring nurses, teachers and other skilled workers to Australia are facing waits of up to 12 months, under a far-reaching directive issued by the Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke to reduce overseas arrivals.
The directive, issued in July, determines the order in which the department processes skilled and employer-sponsored visas, prioritising applications made by migrant workers already in Australia over offshore applicants.
Workers in defence and law enforcement are now at front of the queue for visa processing, or in the first of the five tiers, followed by workers in construction, healthcare and teaching who apply from Australia.
But any migrant applying for a skilled visa from overseas — who is not in defence or law enforcement — has been bumped to the back of the queue, in effect pausing applications, as the government seeks to put its foot on the brake to stop people coming to the country.
Before the new rules were introduced, Home Affairs was working through a 12-month backlog of applications for onshore permanent and temporary skilled visas, according to sources in the sector who note processing times differ depending on the exact visa type.
Jamie Lingham, CEO of Absolute Immigration Group, criticised the directive as a "blunt tool".
"The impact is huge and I don't think everyone has grasped the reality of what's happening," Mr Lingham said.
"Why aren't there priority areas for offshore applications too? It means your marketing manager could get in before your nurse."
Business groups have slammed the delays "being built into the system" which have seen decisions on visas blow out, in some cases, from "a few weeks to close to a year", according to Australian Industry Group CEO Innes Willox.
"The longer the pause goes on the more we risk robbing Peter to pay Paul — appearing to soothe public concern about migration at the cost of our long-term development and maintaining living standards," Mr Willox said.
"We have unfortunately gone from a processing fast lane implemented by the government after COVID to the emergency stopping lane."
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry CEO Andrew McKellar has also expressed alarm at the change, which comes on top of a separate directive which effectively paused the processing of Working Holiday Maker, or backpacker, visas in July.
"You now have the government putting in place a sequence of measures to slow the processing of skilled visas, responding to a short-term political imperative rather than focusing on the proper administration of system and the urgent skills needs of business," Mr McKellar said.
Working rights under cloud
Under pressure to reduce migration, Immigration Minister Tony Burke is working on a more comprehensive overhaul of the system which was due to be announced at the National Press Club a fortnight ago, before the minister was forced to postpone.
Central to the new policy will be a clampdown on temporary visas to reduce Net Overseas Migration (NOM) from the current 300,000 to Labor's target of 225,000 by 2028.
The figure, which represents the number of people coming to live in Australia minus those departing to live overseas, reached a peak of 556,000 when international borders reopened after COVID and has not fallen as fast as forecast.
As revealed by the ABC, the government is considering removing the work rights of visa-holders whose claims for protection have been rejected to crack down on the migrants who stay in Australia for years longer than expected on bridging visas.
When asked if the proposal was on the table, Mr Burke said: "I'm not going to start ruling in and out when we're in the middle of a process."
Backpackers, students targeted
Business leaders, including Mr Willox, have pleaded with the minister to announce the details of the new migration policy, and said, "the quicker the minister can outline future policy and intake settings the better".
"Given that there is a global war for talent, we hope the current settings are in place for a very short time," Mr Willox told ABC, referring to the new directives.
Mr Burke would not give any hints when asked today, but defended the process so far.
"I think the silliest thing is to get into the exact situation where you haven't completed the consultation and you give the speech anyway and that's exactly what Andrew Bragg did," Mr Burke said.
Senator Bragg was counselled by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor for using a speech to suggest the Coalition should bring NOM down to 180,000 a year by cutting both student and backpacker visa numbers.
The comments exposed a rift with the Nationals who want to cut overall migration numbers but are refusing to touch the backpacker visas many farmers and regional communities rely on.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has also vowed to ring fence backpacker visas from any cuts, instead calling for international student numbers to slashed.
More than 528,000 migrants are currently in Australia on student visas, up from 383,910 in 2017, while the number of backpacker visas has risen from 146,340 to 225,650 in the same period.
The number of people on a bridging visa has more than tripled since 2017 from 130,450 to 413,000.

"The FSB is blackmailing me": how Russian secret services tried to recruit a volunteer through his son, and why he decided to go to Moscow to save him

8 Dead as Contractor Plane Crashes near Remote Alaska Radar Site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:42:42 UTC
03:42:42 KST

A small civilian plane carrying eight people and contracted by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers crashed Aug. 20 near a remote Alaskan radar site managed by the Air Force in support of NORAD, killing all aboard.
A spokesperson for the Federal Aviation Administration told Air & Space Forces Magazine the Cessna 441 crashed west of Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site at 12:15 p.m. local time, after taking off from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport, some 450 miles away. A spokesperson for NORAD’s Alaskan Region and the 11th Air Force confirmed in a statement there were no survivors.
A NORAD spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine no personnel from the command were on the flight. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said in a statement that two of its employees were on board. In statements on social media, Sen. Lisa Murkowski and Rep. Nick Begich both indicated the plane belonged to Security Aviation, an air charter company that flies passengers to remote locations across Alaska.
The identities of the passengers and crew will be released 24 hours after their next of kin are notified. The FAA spokesperson said the National Transportation Safety Board and the FAA will investigate the crash.
HH-60W helicopters, an HC-130 personnel recovery plane, and Guardian Angel Airmen from the Alaska Air National Guard all responded to the crash, according to the 11th Air Force statement.
Cape Newenham Air Force Station dates to the 1950s, according to the Air Defense Radar Veterans Association. The base opened in 1954 as one of more than a dozen long-range radar sites that monitored for Russian military activity in the Arctic region. More than 100 personnel were assigned to the 794th Aircraft Control and Warning Squadron there.
By 1983, however, the AN/FPS-117 radar was upgraded to transmit data via satellite and the Air Force deactivated the 794th, leaving only contractors to maintain the site.
Now, Cape Newenham is considered part of the Alaska Radar System, comprised of 15 remote long-range radar sites and three remote radio sites. It is managed by the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center, which tracks aircraft operating in Alaskan airspace.
According to documents from a 2024 solicitation for operation and maintenance of the sites, the Newenham site spans 2,359 acres, with the main buildings split between an upper and lower camp. It has a 3,950-foot gravel runway, a dozen or so buildings, and an AN/FMQ-22 automatic meteorological station. Its estimated to support up to 22 people. The strip serves up to 170 flights annually, a third of which might carry passengers.
Radar sites like Newenham are famed for their isolation and harsh weather, with an average annual temperature of 33 degrees. They play a key role in helping NORAD monitor the Arctic airspace near Russia.
“This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve,” said USAF Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan NORAD Command Region, and 11th Air Force. “These individuals were dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment. Our absolute priority right now is providing unwavering support to their families, friends, and teammates during this devastating time. We are profoundly grateful for the swift and tireless response of our search and recovery professionals.”

Oman, Iran discuss means of restoring navigation through Hormuz Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:39:14 UTC
03:39:14 KST

Abdulsalam Fayez,  Mohammad Sio
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Oman and Iran on Friday discussed developments affecting navigation through the Hormuz Strait, with both sides stressing the need to reach “practical understandings” paving the way for the free flow of maritime traffic.
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi and his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, spoke by phone amid ongoing disruptions to traffic through the strait and persistent tensions between Iran and the United States, the state-run Oman News Agency reported.
According to the news agency, the two top diplomats discussed “ways to create conditions conducive to resuming dialogue, with the aim of narrowing differences and reaching peaceful solutions … while taking the interests of all parties into account.”
They also reportedly stressed the importance of reaching “practical understandings” with a view to restoring smooth navigation through the strategic waterway.
In early August, Tehran announced it had reached an understanding with Muscat on the geographic coordinates of a proposed maritime corridor for commercial vessels transiting the Hormuz Strait.
At the time, Iran’s foreign ministry said the two sides had agreed on the corridor’s geographic criteria, while a joint statement outlining main points of agreement remained to be finalized.
Traffic through the Hormuz Strait remains well below prewar levels amid continued security risks and frequent attacks on commercial vessels traversing regional waters.
On Friday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that traffic through the strait stood about 90 percent below prewar levels.
In mid-August, the UKMTO reported that maritime traffic had reached 17 percent of its prewar average after falling to 4 percent the previous week.
In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding calling for a cessation of hostilities and the restoration of shipping through the strait.
But the deal later fell through amid chronic disputes over the terms of its implementation and the future of navigation through the waterway.
The conflict began in late February with a surprise US-Israeli attack on Iran, to which Tehran has responded by striking targets in Israel and US military bases across the region.

Is lettuce back on the menu? New data suggest cyclosporiasis cases are slowing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:36:49 UTC
03:36:49 KST

This summer the U.S. has been gripped by a parasite-borne illness that causes explosive diarrhea and has basically taken iceberg lettuce off the menu. But new U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention numbers, as well as state data, suggest new infections may be tapering off.
As of August 18, the CDC had received reports of more than 15,000 lab-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases since May. That’s an increase of more than 14,000 cases compared with May 1, 2025, through August 31, 2025. Some 828 people have been hospitalized, and two people died because of the infection, according to the CDC.
There are many more thousands of yet-to-be-confirmed cases, especially considering that some states are tracking the outbreak differently than the CDC does. On Thursday in Michigan, for example, local officials said the state had seen 14,277 cases since June. And the true number nationwide may be higher still because some people who get cyclosporiasis may not have serious symptoms, meaning they are less likely to go to the doctor or get tested for the bug.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The outbreak has been linked to iceberg lettuce, particularly lettuce produced by Taylor Farms de Mexico. The lettuce was sold at stores and at Taco Bell restaurants across the U.S. before it was recalled. Cyclosporiasis is caused by a parasite that spreads through food and water contaminated with infected human feces. The Food and Drug Administration, which oversees food safety, has said it is “confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce related to this specific Cyclospora outbreak is off the market.”
The number of new cases seems to be lessening. The CDC’s tracking data show a spike in case reports in early and mid-July, with a significant drop in new infections since then. Michigan, one of the hardest hit states, has also seen a similar tapering off of new infections in the past week or so—but they are still showing up.
It is possible that most new infections just aren’t reflected in the data yet. Cyclosporiasis symptoms can take two weeks or more to appear, and new cases are reflected in CDC data after about six weeks.
Those symptoms can include explosive, watery diarrhea, as well as fatigue and nausea. These can last anywhere from a few days to a month or longer without treatment.
To prevent an infection, the CDC recommends washing your hands and any fresh produce under running water before eating, preparing or cooking it. Cyclospora, the parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, is trickier to get rid of, though, so you need to cook any food to at least 158 degrees Fahrenheit (70 degrees Celsius) to kill the parasite. Michigan state officials said on August 6 that people can probably go back to prepping and eating salad the normal way, however.
“The broad, precautionary recommendation to avoid bagged salad mixes during the Cyclospora outbreak is no longer in effect,” the Michigan officials wrote in the August 6 announcement. “Residents may resume their usual food handling practices and make choices based on their individual risk tolerance.”

Abbas seeks Erdogan's help as US moves to block UN trip again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:33:31 UTC
03:33:31 KST

The Trump administration intends to again prevent Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas from traveling to New York to address the U.N. General Assembly next month, U.S. officials told ynet. It would be the second consecutive year that the United States has barred Abbas from entering the country to attend the General Assembly.
Abbas appealed to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and asked him to intervene and persuade President Donald Trump to reverse the decision. Erdogan, whom Trump has frequently called a "good friend," spoke with him on Friday, but the administration does not intend to change its position. Abbas is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Sept. 24 and if he is not granted permission to enter the United States, he may be forced, as he was last year, to deliver his speech by video.
In response to a query from ynet, the State Department said, "The Trump administration protects the country and its citizens by maintaining the highest standards of national security and public safety in the visa process." It added that the United States had provided all U.N. member states with guidance and recommended timelines for submitting visa applications and that it "takes its obligations under the U.N. Headquarters Agreement seriously." However, U.S. law allows the secretary of state to impose restrictions or conditions on the movement in the United States of members of foreign delegations.
Meanwhile, a second round of voting was held on Friday as part of the process to select a new U.N. secretary-general to replace Antonio Guterres. Eight candidates are competing for the post: Rebecca Grynspan of Costa Rica, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana, Rafael Grossi of Argentina, Michelle Bachelet of Chile, María Fernanda Espinosa of Ecuador, Makie Sall of Senegal, Olara Otunnu of Uganda and Ivonne Baki of Ecuador.
This was not a vote to elect the secretary-general, but rather a round designed to gauge the positions of the Security Council's 15 members toward the candidates. Each country is asked to indicate for each candidate whether it encourages their candidacy, opposes it or has no position. This allows the balance of support and opposition to be mapped and tracked as the race progresses.
In the previous round, held July 31, differences among the candidates had already emerged. Grynspan, who is Jewish, led with 10 votes in support and one against her candidacy, followed by Rodrigues-Birkett with nine in support and one against and Grossi with seven in support and one against.
This time, Grynspan lost ground, receiving seven votes in support and four against, while Rodrigues-Birkett, whom officials in Israel are seen as preferring not to be elected, rose to first place with eight votes in support and three against.
Grossi, Otunnu and Espinosa received more votes in support than opposition, while Bachelet — who during her tenure as U.N. high commissioner for human rights led a series of harsh criticisms of Israel — fell to the bottom with two votes in support and six against. Aki-Sawyerr, the latest candidate to enter the race, received no support from any country, compared with eight opposing her.
Israel's U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon said, "The selection of the next secretary-general is a test of the U.N.'s future. After years of bias, failure and loss of trust, the organization needs leadership that is willing to change the system rather than become absorbed by it. Israel will assess the candidates based on their record and their willingness to stand up to terrorism, antisemitism and hypocrisy. The next secretary-general must restore the credibility the U.N. has lost, not continue the failures that brought it to this point."

From Hedwig to Bowie, John Cameron Mitchell on art fighting fascism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Hedwig and the Angry Inch creator John Cameron Mitchell on Bowie, punk and fighting fascism
When John Cameron Mitchell first hit the stage in a Farah Fawcett wig at a New York punk rock drag club in the 90s, little did he know he'd be birthing an iconic, transgressive character that would endure more than a quarter-century later.
Hedwig And The Angry Inch began as an off-Broadway musical in 1998, co-written with Stephen Trask and starring Mitchell in the titular role: a genderqueer rock singer from segregated Berlin touring the American Midwest after a botched operation left them with the nominal "angry inch" between their legs.
A 2001 movie written, starring and directed by Mitchell compounded Hedwig's cult status as a lasting "freak flag for the misfit, the outsider", he said.
"That can be anybody, right? … If you didn't feel like you fit in, you understand Hedwig's journey."
The film's 25th anniversary brings the 63-year-old to Melbourne International Film Festival for a 4K screening with a "stoned or drunk director's commentary", he deadpans.
"Have a nice little edible or a Côtes du Rhône wine," then entertain with insider anecdotes but respectfully not "mess it up" for first-time viewers.
"I'm not interfering with the emotional parts, obviously."
Both the film's subversive humour and nuanced portrayal of love and fluid identity continue to reach and resonate with all kinds of communities: drag, trans, non-binary, film buffs, theatre nerds — you name it.
Not bad for what was initially a box office flop.
Enduring legacy and controversy
After sparking a bidding war among Danny DeVito, Tim Burton and Forest Whitaker, Hedwig's film rights landed with New Line Cinema founder Bob Shaye, who gave Mitchell a $US6 million budget and full creative freedom.
"It couldn't really be mainstreamed," says Mitchell. "It kept it pure. It also meant we didn't make much money because marketing is based on comparing it to something that did make money."
Despite its financial shortcomings, Mitchell says Shaye was "more proud of it in some ways" than New Line's blockbuster Lord of the Rings.
Widely screened for free in the wake of the September 11 attacks, Hedwig found new life in the DVD and video market as a word-of-mouth litmus test between friends.
"It was passed around as: 'I think you're gonna like this' or 'If you don't, I may not date you'," explains Mitchell. "I heard that one a lot. And I meet a lot of people with Hedwig tattoos.
"I don't see any Argo tattoos or Gladiator tattoos or whoever else won Best Picture."
He credits part of Hedwig's lasting effect on the fact "it doesn't smell like Hollywood. It came directly from the depths; the queer rock and roll swamp that was New York in the '90s".
Beneath the glam rock theatre, the film trades in androgynous concepts of "undoing the binarchy", as Mitchell puts it, and timeless storytelling.
"It comes out of Plato. It comes from the Gnostic Christian Gospels. Its origins and its themes are deep, classical, and really useful for people of all genders, of all sexualities, races, ages.
"The audience is never one thing, which is why I always say, anyone can play Hedwig too."
Some have strongly disagreed.
The Queer Artist Alliance protested a 2020 Sydney Festival staging of Hedwig over the "casting of cis-gender actor Hugh Sheridan", calling it "offensive and damaging to the trans community" in an online letter.
"Not my favourite department of protest, the internet," Mitchell remarks sourly.
"These young, non-binary, internet petition activists decided this is a trans role and must be played by trans actors. And really, they just wanted to play the role."
"And to me, that goes against everything that it stands for."
The production was cancelled and Sheridan "tried to kill himself", alleges Mitchell, aggravated at the misunderstanding of a character whose most famous non-trans portrayal, besides himself, is Neil Patrick Harris's Tony Award-winning turn.
Complicating matters was the fact that, privately, Sheridan was "on his own gender journey," says Mitchell. "Who are you to interrupt that?"
In 2021, the Packed To The Rafters actor identified as non-binary and bisexual. In 2024, Sheridan said he was "straight for now" in an interview on The Kyle and Jackie O Show.
For Mitchell, he refuses to have his creation dictated or policed by identity politics.
"It's really about someone recovering from the trauma of people telling them what they are, which is exactly what these petitioners were doing."
"The best communities don't force you into identities. They don't say 'You can't do this because you're gay' or 'You can't write a character that's trans if you're not'.
"I reject that. Fiction is a hallowed institution where we imagine ourselves as people that we are not … If you really want to follow that line of don't tell any story that's not your own, then you might as well cancel all fiction and only have autobiography."
The gospel of Bowie
Punk and rock music has a long history with gender fluidity, "and Hedwig is just one little gemstone on that necklace".
The most influential jewel? David Bowie, a lifelong idol of Mitchell's and an early champion who helped finance a Los Angeles production of Hedwig out of his own pocket.
"He loved [Hedwig]. He told me, 'John, you got it right.' It's the best compliment…"
"But it also implies a certain authority … In other words, he gets to decide. But if you're going to give that authority, you might as well give it to Bowie."
Discussing Bowie produces several fascinating detours.
He shades Lady Gaga as a bad Bowie analogue ("she's just cycling through fashion"). How Australian cabaret artist Meow Meow taught him to crowd-surf in a seated venue (slowly and carefully). Or how his New Orleans artist space features a stained-glass window of Bowie crafted by an Australian living in Canada (shout out Haydn Butler).
Burnt out on Hedwig, one of Mitchell's big regrets was turning down Bowie's offer to adapt Ziggy Stardust for the stage.
"It would have been cool. It was stupid of me to ignore it at the time."
He's made up for it since, staging Bowie-themed productions Queen Bitch, Black Star Symphony and now, I'm Afraid of Americans: A Bowie Song Cycle.
Playing Sydney and Melbourne in September, the show sees Mitchell performing Bowie's "most apocalyptic and fascist-facing songs", which became a salve to him after Donald Trump's re-election.
"Let's not even mention the Orange Man," he sighs. "But there's a slow boiling kind of fascism [in America]. People only reading the news they want, which is part of the fascist playbook: You degrade fact and give the facts you want."
He found catharsis in the darker, subversive corners of Bowie's catalogue. "Bowie's never been reassuring. Even his most romantic songs are tense and have fear in them.
"He's not a pure pessimist. He's a realistic romantic in many ways. There is love in there, too. Otherwise, I wouldn't be interested."
Practising punk and what comes next
Mitchell's jam-packed Australian visit also includes presenting a masterclass on punk at the Festival of Dangerous Ideas.
It's an extension of his New York Times opinion piece and 2025 college tour where he instructed younger generations to "stop cancelling each other, find out about punk, and get laid while you're at it".
He believes gen Z should reacquaint themselves with rebellion because their prudish attitudes and politically correct policing, afraid of risks and "internet drunk" on short-form content, have had nasty side effects.
"There would be no fascism in the US without the smartphone, I truly believe that."
"Because if you're only watching the news you care about, and can't get past 10 seconds of something: Oh look! There's a fascist in charge!"
His Dangerous Ideas presentation will include examples of artists who used art to fight totalitarianism.
Namely, French surrealist Claude Cahun, who fought Nazi-occupied Jersey "in a kind of graffiti, Banksy type way."
Mitchell discovered her "gender-bending art of the 1920s and 30s" in an early 2000s exhibition organised by — you guessed it — Bowie.
He's writing a new play about Cahun and developing two film biopics on figures who "dealt with their own kinds of fascism."
The first concerns beat poet Alan Ginsberg in 1968, at the height of the Vietnam War and president Richard Nixon's reign.
The other is based upon the "applied punk" of AIDS activist Peter Staley, whose ACT UP coalition successfully pressured big pharma to reduce the astronomic costs of HIV drug AZT. And it sounds like it already has a pivotal scene.
In 1991, Staley had a giant condom placed over the home of senator Jesse Helms in protest of his vehement opposition to funding AIDS research and safe sex practises.
"This horrible, homophobic senator couldn't get out of this big, inflatable condom," Mitchell gushes.
From Hedwig to prophylactic protest, Mitchell is a life-long creator whose work is always interested in interrogating otherness.
"I want things to be not topical, but useful to the moment."
John Cameron Mitchell Presents: Hedwig and the Angry Inch 25th anniversary screens at MIFF on Friday 21 August
Mitchell then appears at Sydney's Festival of Dangerous Ideas on Sunday 23 August.
I'm Afraid Of Americans: A Bowie Song Cycle plays on Sunday 6 September at Sydney's Enmore Theatre and Wednesday 9 September at Melbourne Recital Centre

From failures to flirtations, Miles Franklin's not-so-brilliant career
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

If My Brilliant Career is all you know of Miles Franklin's life, you're missing out
With the release of Netflix's new TV adaptation of My Brilliant Career last week and the announcement of the winner of this year's Miles Franklin Literary Award earlier this month, August feels like the month of Miles.
Hey, maybe it's the year of Miles, with a recent musical and novel about the writer the latest additions to the growing Miles Franklin canon.
Yet so much of what most people know about the woman who gives her name to not one, but two, of Australia's most prestigious literary awards (the other being the Stella Prize) is limited to what we can draw from her partly biographical debut novel, My Brilliant Career.
That's just her early life and Franklin always insisted the book was less autobiographical than it seemed.
Beyond her gutsy resistance to marriage in favour of her writing career (like her heroine Sybylla), the author's life was filled with failures, flirtations and even a stint under cover.
The 'bush girl' becomes a literary superstar
Stella Maria Sarah Miles Franklin was born in Talbingo, NSW, in 1879, into the squattocracy, and spent the first decade of her life at her family's farm, Brindabella Station.
A depression and drought saw the family (Franklin was the eldest of six siblings) move to shabbier living situations, as did so many farming families at the time.
Despite the family's increasingly dire circumstances, Franklin accessed other worlds through books and writing.
By 16, she was writing articles for the local newspaper and working on her first novel, a London-set drama about lords and ladies.
Historian Alecia Simmonds, co-host of ABC podcast The Dead Can't Sue, says: "Literature and writing are the one form of artistic, intellectual, creative expression that women are given [in this period].
"And it is a form of power; it allows them to understand the world, to imagine a new world, and to influence the world — all of which Miles goes on to do."
Franklin was expected to marry and dedicate herself to housework and children, but instead, Simmonds says, "She really wrote her way out of that destiny".
After being encouraged by the local newspaper editor to write what she knew, 19-year-old Franklin began work on My Brilliant Career. She wrote it over a six-month period, at night, after her farm chores and sibling minding were done.
In 1899, Franklin wrote to one of the country's biggest publishers, modern-day booksellers Angus & Robertson.
She asked them to kindly read her manuscript and to "state whether or not it is fit for publication". They deemed her manuscript unworthy (a decision George Robertson would later regret).
Undeterred, Franklin wrote to her literary hero, the bush poet Henry Lawson. With his help, My Brilliant Career was published by British publishers in 1901. Lawson's preface revealed that despite the male pen-name, the author is "just a little bush girl".
It became an international sensation.
"She offers readers a pure bush ideal at a moment of extraordinary turmoil in Australia," Simmonds says. "This is the beginning of Australia's national literary culture."
Miles goes under cover
The success of her debut novel gave Franklin access to the Sydney intelligentsia, and she was befriended by the famous suffragist Rose Scott. Franklin charmed everyone she met, including many men.
"Miles says no to marriage … but she really loves flirting," Simmonds says.
Between 1899 and 1902, she had a flirtation with the other pre-eminent bush poet of her time, Banjo Paterson (of Waltzing Matilda fame). She later said he was "the most sophisticated man that ever attempted to woo me sexually".
Franklin seemed to be on the cusp of a glittering literary career, but her next few books were rejected by publishers.
Perhaps that's because the success of her first book hadn't rescued her from poverty, leaving her with little time to work on her craft.
At this point she could've chosen to become a nurse, governess or teacher, but instead, inspired by "girl stunt reporters", she decided to "go under cover" as a maid and servant for wealthy families, taking the name Sarah Frankling, in an effort to investigate the conditions and complaints of the servant class.
"If you are a domestic servant, your day starts at dawn, and this is what Miles writes about," Simmonds says. "They are horrific conditions. You're paid a pittance."
While she was unable to publish her manuscript about her servant experiences over defamation concerns, she began writing for The Sydney Morning Herald.
A broad abroad
With introductions to American feminists facilitated by Scott and Vida Goldstein, and with the hope of getting one in her mounting pile of manuscripts published, Franklin moved to the US in 1906, at 26 years old.
The move led her sister Linda to write to her: "You bad girl, to leave such a lot of broken hearts behind."
By 1907, Franklin was living in Chicago, a bustling city of extreme luxury and poverty, where immigrants toiled in slaughterhouses and sweatshops.
There she worked with social reformer Alice Henry at the National Women's Trade Union League of America.
"Miles is turning up to picket lines," Simmonds explains. "She's there in the rallies. She's running around, collecting strikers' stories and she's witnessing police brutality. She is absolutely in the thick of it."
But it's also in Chicago that Franklin's insomnia and anxiety culminate in a nervous breakdown.
"There is a bush girl in her that just constantly yearns to go home," Simmonds says.
Throughout all this, Franklin continued writing and flirting. She became embroiled with two (yes, two) millionaire brothers, one of whom was already married.
"She's politically opposed to marriage, as are many women at this time but … she is open to the idea of marrying [the younger divorced brother]," Simmonds says.
Franklin's biographer Jill Roe alleges the affair ended in 1914 because of an attempted abduction and rape.
After World War I breaks out, Franklin, who was anti-war, moved to England to help on the home front and write about the war effort. She also worked as a cook and orderly at the Scottish Women's Hospital for Serbian soldiers in Macedonia.
Franklin comes home
By 1925, five of Franklin's siblings had died, and she moved back to Australia in 1927.
A year later, Franklin published a pastoral saga under the name Brent of Bin Bin, the first book in a trilogy and her first hit since My Brilliant Career.
In 1931, her father died and her money ran low. But it's also around this time that she returned to her original pen-name, publishing All that Swagger, the novel that restored her reputation in Australia, in 1936.
Franklin began devoting herself towards the very idea of Australian literature itself, championing her peers and local literary journals. She mentored younger writers and used her influence to campaign against censorship.
In 1941, after World War II broke out, Franklin attended a few meetings of the Australia First Movement. The movement was against the war, prioritising Australia over a European conflict, but this ultranationalism slipped into fascist and Nazi territory.
Franklin's friend and publisher Percy Stephensen was one of the movement's leaders.
"But [her biographer Roe contends] that she clearly opposed the views of the movement around Nazism," Simmonds explains. "And she claimed to have not seen the antisemitism until a friend from overseas points it out."
Simmonds suggests it's not straightforward; Franklin attended more than one Australia First meeting and continued to subscribe to the movement's magazine.
"Miles also writes to a friend and says, 'This movement is very much needed,'" Simmonds says.
Franklin, like many 20th century feminists and thinkers, held eugenicist ideas.
The Dead Can't Sue's Leigh Boucher suggests Franklin "is a complicated, complex thinker in a period of intense political and ideological contest and contradiction".
Mother Miles?
In 1946, Franklin finally published the sequel to My Brilliant Career: My Career Goes Bung.
By this stage, she was celebrated as a founding matriarch of Australia's national literary tradition.
But Simmonds says that obscures the legacy of other Australian women writers of her time, including Ada Cambridge, Rosa Praed, Barbara Baynton and Mary Fortune.
"There's no one mother … she's part of this groundswell of women writers."
Franklin died in 1954, at age 74. She had published somewhere between 14 and 19 books (depending on whether you count edited collections) under all her various pen-names, but none ever reached the fame of her first.
The Miles Franklin Literary Award, Australia's most prestigious literary prize, exists today because she left her estate, valued at £8,922 (just over $200,000 in today's terms), to establish an award for Australian literature. Nobody knew she'd been squirrelling that money away by living frugally.
Simmonds says, beyond her writing, she'd like Franklin to be remembered as "a social justice activist, feminist, nationalist and an internationalist and this great big, fabulous flirt".
This article is based on research by Alecia Simmonds

Australia has a soft spot for the amazing flannel flower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Flannel flower rises from fire to win Australia's heart
With soft woolly (and sometimes feathery) star-shaped flowers and grey-green foliage, the flannel flower is a well-known wildflower.
But this beautiful flower has a few superpowers up its floral sleeve.
Out of a group of 10 incredible native flowering plants, the flannel flower has been crowned Australia's most amazing wildflower for National Science Week 2026.
The flannel flower might look a daisy but it's actually in the Apiaceae family, which includes carrots, celery, parsley, fennel, coriander and cumin. It even has a carroty smell when it is cut.
While most of us are familiar with the beautiful east coast flannel flower Actinotus helianthi — you'll find it in florists and nurseries — there are actually 14 species found in Australia, and one in New Zealand.
The two most common species in Western Australia are Actinotus leucocephalus with creamy white flower heads; and Actinotus superbus, known for its prominent, showy white flowers.
In the NT, Actinotus schwarzii, is found only on the cliffs of Standley Chasm, says Cathy Offord, head of Australian PlantBank research at the Australian Botanic Gardens.
Tasmania has the tiny crimson flannel flower (Actinotus suffocatus).
Hope from the ashes
After the devastating 2020 Black Summer bushfires, pink flannel flower (Actinotus forsythii) bloomed across eastern NSW in places they hadn't been seen in decades.
The flowers literally rose from the ashes in their billions in a symbol of hope and resilience.
Dr Offord says the flowers will last for between three to 15 years.
"Mass flowering events produce billions of plants and then over the next couple of years they just fade away."
Several other flannel flower species, including two from Western Australia, are known to bloom en masse within a year or two of bushfire.
"One to two years after fire you'll just see a carpet of these flowers," says Dani Hamilton of Kings Park and Botanic Gardens in Perth.
"It's quite breathtaking,"
Seeds have the power of dormancy
Flannel flower seeds can survive for decades in the soil in a dormant state, a trick that explains the plant's ability to suddenly pop up in places it hasn't been seen for decades.
Seed dormancy is found in all flannel flower species.
"They all have this weird dormancy mechanism that responds to a variety of cues," Dr Offord says.
For flannel flowers that bloom after bushfire, the cues are typically smoke from fire awakening the seeds, and then rain.
But what "awakens" the sleeping flannel flower seeds can vary between locations and species.
"There's no one thing that will break that dormancy, no one thing that you can say, 'Oh, you do this,'" Dr Offord says.
"There's rain, smoke, wetting and drying cycles through the years, possibly heat. Also the length of time the seed has been in the soil.
"So there's no straightforward story around that, other than they do have this dormancy, which helps them to survive in sometimes hostile environments.'
Talara'tingi a significant D'harawal flower
For the D'harawal people, the flannel flower, known as Talara'tingi, is linked to one of their most significant places, says Gawaian Bodkin-Andrews, a D'harawal scholar at Western Sydney University.
"The story is that there was a time where children had not ever seen the Sun. A young girl, named Tiana travelled to a significant place and realised that the people had not been taking care of the country."
The story holds two important lessons: to remember the laws, protocols and need to look after country to ensure it is healthy, and to listen to the youth, who can also bring wisdom.
Hope and health was brought back to country and Tiana was gifted with the springing of the flannel flowers, shaped like a star and with leaves covered in a very fine type of fur that looks like frost.
Hence the name Talara'tingi, which means star of frost.
"The flowering of the flannel flower in the story indicated the ending of a long winter or maybe an ice age. Which gives an indication of how old this story truly is, and how long it's survived," Professor Bodkin-Andrews says.
You can grow them yourself (or buy a bunch)
Many years ago, Dr Offord worked with the cut flower industry to develop varieties of Actinotus helianthi suitable for cultivation.
"At one stage, they were only being harvested from the wild," she says.
"Now there are a few growers who cultivate flannel flowers and they have a much superior vase life and look beautiful."
While it's illegal to collect flannel flower plants or seeds without a permit, you can still grow them at home. Many nurseries sell the plants or seeds.
"They're quite self-sufficient," Dr Offord says.
"We generally suggest to grow them in pots. It's much easier to control their growth than in soil, because they do prefer to live in a somewhat light sandy soil.
"And they don't need a lot of fertiliser."
Where to see them in the wild
The flannel flower's sleeping seeds make it hard to predict where, or when, it might bloom.
"They can be quite ephemeral," Dr Offord says.
"You can have them growing somewhere and people will say, 'Oh, they're growing in a great abundance here.' You go back a few years later and they've gone."
Yet, at some point, probably after a bushfire, the flowers will rise from the ashes like a floral phoenix, bringing hope and joy to those who see them whether in the wild or through media viewed across the world.
Definitely amazing!

Operations "Forrest Gump" and "Themis": three suspects remanded in custody
Kyiv • UNN
The court arrested three suspects in the criminal organization case. Bail amounts are UAH 30 million, UAH 20 million, and UAH 7 million.
The High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) imposed preventive measures on three suspects in a case concerning the activities of a criminal organization that, according to investigators, included members of parliament, officials of the Office of the President, and other individuals. The Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office reported this, UNN reports.
The court remanded all three in custody, but they may be released from the pretrial detention center after bail is posted.
Who was remanded in custody
The court ordered former Member of Parliament Maksym Mykytas to be held in custody with the possibility of posting bail of UAH 30 million.
Valentyn Yelizarov, director of Metrobud (which, according to the investigation, was effectively controlled by the former MP), was granted bail of UAH 20 million. Law enforcement officials call him former parliamentarian Mykytas's "right-hand man."
Another suspect is the Director General for Legal Affairs of the Office of the President. He was also remanded in custody, and bail was set at UAH 7 million.
If the suspects or other individuals post the amounts set by the court, they will be able to leave custody, but will remain subject to the procedural obligations imposed by the court.
Will the decision be appealed?
The SAPO reported that it would decide whether to appeal the amount of bail for the suspects after receiving and studying the full texts of the court decisions.
What you should know about the case
According to investigators, the case concerns a criminal organization that operated for several years. Law enforcement officials claim that it may have included current and former Members of Parliament of Ukraine, senior officials of the Office of the President, and other individuals.
Law enforcement officials are investigating certain episodes of this case as part of the "Forrest Gump" and "Themis" operations.
Context
Mykytas is one of the figures in the case being investigated by NABU and SAPO as part of the special operation "Forrest Gump." According to investigators, he may have been involved, together with other individuals, in the activities of a criminal organization engaged in corporate raiding and the legalization of funds.
One episode of the proceedings concerns UAH 150 million which, according to investigators, was to be legalized through controlled companies and used to post bail for one of the figures in another anti-corruption investigation—the "Midas" operation.
The investigative materials state that in June 2026, members of the alleged criminal organization received UAH 150 million in cash, which they planned to channel through a number of companies to make it appear to be funds of legal origin. The money was subsequently to be used as bail. According to anti-corruption organizations, this concerned bail for former Minister of Energy and Justice Herman Halushchenko.
In addition, NABU and SAPO link the group's activities to the alleged corporate raiding of two enterprises in autumn 2025. Law enforcement officials estimate the value of their assets at approximately UAH 248 million. Investigators are also examining an attempt to seize other real estate in Kyiv worth more than UAH 200 million.
According to NABU, forged court decisions and documents, interference with the electronic accounts of state registrars, and the registration of corporate rights in the names of nominal owners may have been used in carrying out the schemes.
Mykytas's defense denies the criminal nature of the actions attributed to him. The lawyers claimed that the actions concerning certain enterprises were aimed at restoring the businessman's property rights, which, in their version, had previously been violated.
The pretrial investigation is ongoing.

Defence spending supports 12,200 jobs in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:24:13 BST
03:24:13 KST

Ministry of Defence spending with industry in Scotland supported 12,200 direct jobs in 2024/25, an increase of 800 on the previous year, according to official statistics published on Friday.
The department spent £2.16 billion with Scottish industry over the period, equivalent to £390 per person, directly supporting 560 jobs for every 100,000 people in full time employment, up from 520 in the preceding twelve months.
Counting civilian and military posts alongside industry roles, the figures record 26,300 jobs in Scotland supported by MOD expenditure, comprising 12,200 direct industry jobs, 4,050 civilian staff and 10,010 service personnel.
Shipbuilding and submarines dominate the industrial figure at 7,900 jobs, up from 6,700 a year earlier, a rise of nearly 18 per cent. Other construction accounts for 800, with weapons and ammunition at 200 and aircraft and spacecraft also at 200.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “Scotland’s defence sector is a powerhouse of innovation and expertise and, as these figures clearly show, it is also a key driver for economic growth in Scotland, with the Ministry of Defence spending £2.16 billion a year here directly supporting 12,200 jobs.
“Through historic levels of funding, the UK Government is delivering a real defence dividend for Scotland. From investing in naval shipbuilding expertise on the Clyde and at Rosyth, to our nuclear deterrent and submarine support at Faslane, to our world-leading strengths in cyber, space, advanced radar and electronic warfare, we are supporting thousands of jobs and opening exciting career pathways for young Scots.”
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “These figures show that a rising defence budget is creating more good jobs across the UK. Defence is an engine for growth and our investments are driving reindustrialisation. As we increase our military readiness and capabilities we are generating good well-paid jobs nationwide.”
Across the United Kingdom, MOD expenditure with industry totalled £31.9 billion in 2024/25, supporting 274,000 jobs.
The department points to several commitments underpinning the Scottish figures. The Defence Investment Plan confirmed £26 billion for naval base infrastructure including £15.1 billion to regenerate HM Naval Base Clyde, while the £10 billion Type 26 deal with Norway is expected to sustain over 2,000 jobs and support more than 100 Scottish businesses, over 50 of them small and medium-sized enterprises.
The statistics measure jobs supported by MOD expenditure within Scotland, a different measure from the population-based allocation of defence spending used in the Government Expenditure and Revenue Scotland figures published last week.

"There are missing people who are not responding to calls," the mayor added.

In the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, three people were injured when a drone exploded near a taxi, the regional head said.

Tesla recalls nearly 3M vehicles in China over door handle safety risks
HONG KONG (AP) — Tesla and other Chinese carmakers are making a major recall of more than 4 million vehicles over safety concerns mostly related to their door handles, according to Chinese authorities on Friday.
The U.S. carmaker is recalling about 2.98 million China-made and imported EVs including Model 3, Model Y, Model X and Model S over door handle safety risks, according to China’s State Administration for Market Regulation.
The recall, the largest this year according to Chinese media, comes a few months after Chinese authorities said in February that starting next year, it would be banning hidden car door handles that are commonly seen on Tesla electric vehicles and many Chinese EV models.
China has stepped up scrutiny recently on hidden, or flush, car door handles following EV accidents in the country and elsewhere, in which cars’ hidden electronic doors failed and trapped people inside.
In a notice on the Chinese regulator’s website, it cited safety risk. In extreme situations, such as a severe collision that causes an electrical system failure, the car handles could hinder car users from quickly opening the doors to escape, or prevent rescuers outside the car from gaining access, the notice said.
Tesla will perform software updates on the vehicles to mitigate risks, the notice added. Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
Xiaomi, the Beijing-based Chinese technology giant, is recalling more than 390,000 vehicles. Hangzhou-based Leapmotor is recalling over 370,000 cars. Other Chinese carmakers, including Geely and XPENG are also recalling some vehicles.
The reasons given in each case were similar, mostly relating to issues with their car door handles.
A report published by the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of China’s ruling Communist Party, said the large-scale recall “serves as a unified safety upgrade” for existing vehicle models ahead of the 2027 implementation of the ban on hidden car door handles.
“For the rapidly evolving NEV (new energy vehicle) industry, competition should be defined not only by the pace of technological innovation but also by the high standards set for safety,” the newspaper said.

Supreme Court chief justice allows work on Trump’s $400M White House ballroom to continue for now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Supreme Court’s chief justice allows work on Trump’s $400M White House ballroom to continue for now
WASHINGTON (AP) — Chief Justice John Roberts on Friday allowed the White House to continue construction on President Donald Trump’s $400 million ballroom project for now, as the Supreme Court considers the Trump administration’s emergency request to intervene in lawsuits over the project.
The temporary order came hours before lower-court rulings would have forced a halt to aboveground construction of the project because Trump didn’t get congressional approval.
It will remain in place until the Supreme Court issues a more durable decision, though the one-page document does not detail Roberts’ reasoning or indicate when another ruling will be handed down. Roberts signed the order because he oversees emergency appeals of cases filed in the capital.
Ballroom case tests the limits of presidential power
The case is coming before the nation’s highest court as Trump, a Republican, exercises unparalleled assertions of presidential power and increasingly seeks to mold the capital in his own image.
The administration has argued that the president has total authority to renovate the White House and other federal buildings as he sees fit and that the ballroom project must be completed due to national security concerns.
When Trump first announced the plans for a new ballroom, he did not emphasize national security. He said the project would be funded by private donations, including from himself.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation argues that Trump has no unilateral authority to undertake the work, which has included demolishing the East Wing. Lawyers for the preservation group accused the White House of trying to “outrun the courts” by accelerating construction.
A spokesperson for the trust said Friday that the order from Roberts is not a final decision and the group is awaiting further action. The full Supreme Court will likely weigh in next on whether construction can continue for the potentially long duration of the lawsuit.
Trump said his administration is grateful for Friday’s decision, writing in a social media post that the project is “under budget and ahead of schedule.”
While litigation plays out, the ballroom is going up quickly
The Trump administration says 65% of the work has already been completed on the planned 90,000-square-foot (8,400-square-meter) ballroom, where the East Wing stood before the president ordered its demolition.
Crews are working 20 hours a day, seven days a week, on the project, where about $200 million in private donations has been spent or committed, according to court documents filed by the Justice Department.
The work has proceeded against the backdrop of the litigation winding through the courts.
In April, a district court judge ordered a stop to the aboveground construction of the planned ballroom. That ruling was briefly suspended, then upheld by an appeals court panel. U.S. District Judge Richard Leon in Washington allowed work to continue only belowground on bunkers and military installations. Leon was nominated by President George W. Bush, a Republican.
Leon’s decision was upheld by an appeals court panel, as two judges appointed by Democratic presidents found the project was for Congress to decide and “not a matter for Executive self-help.” A third judge, appointed by Trump, found that the preservationist group challenging the project had no legal standing to sue.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer picked up on that argument, calling the decision halting the work “extraordinary and unlawful.” He said the completion of the project was “vitally required by national security.”
The Trump administration has scored a series of victories on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket, though the justices have ruled against some of the president’s signature policies after fuller review.

Cambodia-US operation uncovers money laundering link to Sinaloa Cartel
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Cambodian and U.S. anti-drug agencies have uncovered a network that authorities say uses cryptocurrency to launder money for Mexico’s notorious Sinaloa Cartel, officials from both countries said Friday.
Meas Vyrith, secretary-general of Cambodia’s National Authority for Combating Drugs, told The Associated Press that his office had confiscated about $7 million in cryptocurrency linked to the Sinaloa Cartel, a powerful criminal conglomerate designated a “foreign terrorist organization” by the Trump administration.
He said Cambodian anti-drug police working with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration also made several arrests and seized assets, drug laboratories and storage facilities. Authorities also confiscated over 200 kilograms (440 pounds) of illegal drugs and more than one metric ton (2,200 pounds) of precursor chemicals used to produce them.
Law enforcement agents raided four locations in the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, and neighboring Kandal province from Aug. 1 to 5, he said.
“Collaborative efforts involving DEA offices in Phnom Penh and New Jersey successfully uncovered a local network laundering cryptocurrency on behalf of the Sinaloa Cartel,” the U.S. Embassy said in a statement Thursday.
The Sinaloa Cartel has become a major producer of the synthetic opioid fentanyl, blamed for tens of thousands of overdose deaths each year in the U.S. The group has obtained precursor chemicals, including from China, to produce fentanyl in Mexico and smuggle it into the U.S.
Cambodia serves largely as a transit area for drugs such as methamphetamine that originate in the Golden Triangle, the region where the borders of Thailand, Myanmar and Laos meet.
But in recent years, it has also been a stronghold for Chinese-led organized crime groups, best known for running scam centers that have bilked people around the world out of billions of dollars while employing many thousands of foreigners in slave-like conditions.
Over the past year, Cambodia has intensified a crackdown on such operations, shutting down scam centers and arresting several alleged kingpins, including some who had established legal financial institutions.
A report issued in July by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime said several transnational organized crime groups from outside Southeast Asia are important criminal actors in the region, primarily involved in trafficking large quantities of methamphetamine and cocaine.
It said Latin American cartels’ engagement with Southeast Asia “appears to extend beyond drug and precursor chemical supply, and the region now functions as a supply, financial management, and logistics hub for multiple Latin American criminal organizations.”
In 2024, U.S. federal prosecutors said the Sinaloa Cartel worked with Chinese underground banking groups in the United States to launder more than $50 million from the sale of fentanyl, cocaine and other drugs.

Associated Press writer Grant Peck in Bangkok contributed to this report.

Karmelo Anthony dropped plans to testify over track stabbing, lawyer says as teen seeks retrial
McKINNEY, Texas (AP) — Karmelo Anthony had planned to testify during his Texas murder trial over a track meet stabbing but backed out amid sudden concerns that prosecutors would raise potentially damaging evidence about the teenager’s past, one of his lawyers said Friday.
Anthony, 19, is asking for a new trial after a jury in June sentenced him to 35 years in prison for killing 17-year-old Austin Metcalf, who attended a rival school and was stabbed during a confrontation at a track competition last year. Since then, the case has stirred tensions over race and led to both families becoming targets of harassment.
During the second day of a hearing near Dallas, defense attorney Toby Shook said the teenager’s plans to testify unraveled over worries that prosecutors would renege on agreements to not present evidence that might further inflame an already highly charged case.
“It was essential that the jury hear Karmelo and hear his explanation,” Shook said.
It was not clear when state District Judge Michael Chitty would issue a ruling on whether to grant a new trial.
Prosecutor Bill Wirskye has defended the trial as fair and said the possibility of Anthony testifying wasn’t part of the original agreement with the defense. Anthony’s attorneys say it should have been obvious the teenager would want to explain to jurors himself how he acted in self-defense.
Anthony is Black; Metcalf was white. Among the details that jurors never heard because of the agreement, according to attorneys on both sides, were that Anthony once sent a text message fantasizing about stabbing someone and Metcalf had a history of fighting and using racist language.
During the trial, lawyers on both sides told jurors the tragedy had nothing to do with race, but social media posts amplified the killing nationwide in racial terms.
In an interview with NewsNation, Metcalf’s father, Jeff Metcalf, said he supported the original agreement between prosecutors and defense attorneys. He said information about his son’s juvenile history does not change what happened the day his son was killed.
“We all want our children to be the best they can be, and obviously, we all fall short,” Jeff Metcalf told NewsNation. “It still doesn’t change the facts of the case.”
Metcalf’s parents and Anthony’s parents have attended both days of the hearing.
Anthony’s attorneys have also told the judge he should get a new trial because of errors that limited access to the proceedings. They have argued that the case’s original judge allowed a “shadow docket” that shielded character information about both sides.
The trial in June took place amid heightened court security. Wirskye said there had been threats against a judge who granted Anthony bond, fake autopsy reports circulating online and attempts to intimidate witnesses. Parents of some witnesses also filed protective orders for their children because of threats, according to Wirskye.
Anthony secured one legal victory this week when the judge who presided over his trial was removed from the case. Chitty was then assigned to consider the motion for a retrial.
Anthony’s attorneys had asked for state District Judge John Roach to be removed in part because of a TV interview in which Roach said jurors “got it right” when they delivered a guilty verdict.

Kurt Busch shares emotional last moments with late brother Kyle Busch in ‘Today’ interview
NEW YORK (AP) — NASCAR Hall of Famer Kurt Busch wiped tears from his eyes in recalling the final day he spent at his younger brother’s hospital bedside in his first public comments about Kyle Busch’s death.
“I was at the hospital. I was there all day, hoping, praying, hoping for a turnaround,” Busch said in an interview on NBC’s “Today” show on Friday.
“I said, ‘I got you man. Come on, I got you. I got you. Come on, be strong,’” an emotional Busch added, before a brief pause. “It just wasn’t fair.”
The interview marked Busch’s first comments since Kyle Busch died on May 21 after severe pneumonia progressed into sepsis, resulting in rapid and overwhelming complications. Busch’s death at the age of 41 devastated the racing community and one of NASCAR’s most accomplished families. The borthers were born in Las Vegas.
Kyle Busch won Cup Series championships in 2015 and 2019 for Joe Gibbs Racing, and holds the record in winning 234 combined races across NASCAR’s top three national series. His older brother was a Cup champion in 2004 and inducted this year into the Hall of Fame.
In the interview, Busch outlined how his brother became increasingly ill while practicing in a simulator on May 20. Asked by his crew chief whether he was OK, Busch responded no and he was taken to a hospital by ambulance.
Kyle Busch initially believed he was dealing with a sinus cold while racing at Watkins Glen, New York, on May 10. He continued competing, including winning a Truck Series race at Dover, Delaware, less than a week before he died. Kurt Busch said their father, Tom Busch, chose not to be at the hospital in order to “remember him the way he wanted to remember him.”
“There is no book, there is no outline on what we’re supposed to do right now,” Kurt Busch said, before recalling the on-track chemistry he had with his brother.
“Him and I were carbon copies of each other. We could speak on track without saying a word,” he said. “I miss the words we never spoke to each other, and the vibe that we had on track.”
Busch said he’s now mentoring his nephew, Kyle’s 11-year-old son Brexton, who has taken up racing.
“He’s a prodigy,” Busch said. “He can be a big start in the world of motorsports. He’s 11, but he’s already racing like an 18-year-old.”
As for his brother’s legacy, Busch said the achievements speak for themselves.
“It’s already there. Winningest driver in NASCAR history in all the series,” Busch said.
“The tenacity that he had. It was every day, 24-7, to help people in the latter part of his career, to be a great father like he was,” he added. “It will all shine as time puts different things in spotlights.”

Flock cameras destroyed as anti-surveillance protests spread (VIDEOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:22:30 UTC
03:22:30 KST

Flock cameras destroyed as anti-surveillance protests spread (VIDEOS)
As more US police departments deploy Flock cameras to monitor traffic and track criminals, public backlash has grown. In San Diego, a protester dressed as Darth Vader showed up to a city council meeting to portray Flock as a tool for tracking “rebel scum.”
There are now more than 130,000 Flock cameras dotting the US, with law enforcement departments in at least 4,000 cities erecting the AI-powered surveillance devices on intersections, parking lots, and public land. Flock Technologies says the cameras have helped police stop burglaries, carjackings, and homicides, but opponents say they encroach on civil liberties.
At a meeting of the San Diego City Council on Wednesday, a man dressed as Star Wars villain Darth Vader shared his opinion on the technology, approaching the podium with his character’s signature mechanical breathing.
“The Emperor is a fan of Flock, and we must continue utilising Flock technologies so that we can surveil the rebel scum,” he declared. “As they move from playground to playground, from playground to pool, from pool to gymnasium, because we all know that the Flock cameras are not only following the license plate readers, they are following children.”
Darth Vader comes out in favor of Flock cameras pic.twitter.com/YL3jaiwIEx
— Orwell Day (@OrwellDay) August 20, 2026
Flock is best known for its Falcon ALPR (Automated License Plate Recognition) cameras, which capture still images of passing vehicles. However, the company’s Condor PTZ video cameras can be used by police departments to track the movement of individuals across multiple cameras with AI, and search for people via description.
Flock’s Falcon ALPR cameras have already been used by more than 50 police officers to stalk women – including ex-wives and partners – without their consent, the Washington Post reported earlier this month. Vulnerabilities in Flock’s software have also left images of children, recorded with the company’s video cameras, exposed online.
“I need this so I can stalk my ex-girlfriend,” ‘Darth Vader’ told the city council meeting. “This technology will help us find Luke Skywalker as he traverses the universe in his X-Wing.”
The rollout of Flock cameras began at scale in 2020, but the process has not been smooth. Flock cameras have been shot, spray-painted, cut down, and obstructed across the country. According to FlockStats, a website that counts confirmed incidents of vandalism against the devices, at least 162 have been destroyed nationwide.
As the cameras have proliferated, so have their detractors. Republican Representative Thomas Massie is among the highest-profile opponents of the technology, introducing a bill last month that would withhold federal funding from police departments deploying the cameras. Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont, a Democrat, has also ordered cities to pause the installation of Flock cameras until the state develops new privacy legislation.

US supreme court lets Trump continue work on White House ballroom for now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:21:43 UTC
03:21:43 KST

The US supreme court has allowed Donald Trump to continue construction of his controversial White House ballroom for now, temporarily pausing a lower court order that would halt much of the project.
Supreme court chief justice John Roberts signed a temporary order on Friday, permitting work to continue on the planned White House addition – a top priority of the president – while the court considers an emergency appeal from Trump’s administration.
Democrats accused the supreme court, which is controlled by a conservative super-majority, of “rubber stamping Trump’s vanity-driven, gilded corruption”. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said: “As costs skyrocket, the administration is wasting money on an endless and illegal war, corporate giveaways and Trump’s pet projects.”
The president swiftly welcomed the order, which puts the Friday deadline from the appeals court on pause. That court had ordered construction to stop while a legal challenge proceeded, after concluding earlier this month that the ballroom project probably requires congressional approval before work can continue.
The Trump administration then turned to the supreme court, arguing that construction of the structure was critical to national security and the safety of the US president.
On Tuesday, the National Trust for Historic Preservation had urged the supreme court to suspend the ballroom project following an earlier lawsuit seeking to block construction.
The massive 90,000sq-ft (8,400 sq meters) ballroom project part of the president’s sprawling plans to reshape the nation’s capital, has already involved the demolition of the White House East Wing. Construction also includes an underground military facility that the administration says is needed to protect the president.
The underground military bunker would be a five-story complex that will include shelters, a hospital and other features designed to protect the president and senior officials during an emergency.
The total cost of the project is expected to exceed $400m.
“It is something that Presidents have wanted for 150 years, and that the Military has been seeking for the last 100 years,” Trump claimed in a social media post on Friday. “Their wish will soon be fulfilled! Construction is under budget and ahead of schedule.”
Administration officials say the ballroom itself will be reinforced with missile-resistant columns and a drone-proof roof, allowing the structure to serve as a shield for both the underground military complex and the wider White House.
Construction on the ballroom has been under way for 10 months with the administration saying the project is now approximately 65% complete.
The administration has argued that authority over White House renovations is held by the president, not Congress or the courts. The justice department also argued that leaving the site in its current condition, effectively an open construction zone, makes protecting the White House more difficult.
