South Korea’s push for defense autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:59 UTC
01:42:59 KST

The unusual convergence between Seoul and Washington toward greater South Korean defense autonomy could reshape the purpose of the US military presence on the Korean Peninsula. The implications of this convergence could strengthen or complicate US-led allied deterrence in the event of a Taiwan contingency.
For Taipei, the key question is whether Seoul and Washington agree on what US forces on the peninsula are for and whether they should be available for contingencies beyond South Korea. Even if US forces there did not directly participate in a Taiwan contingency, their role within the broader US logistical and support architecture across the Western Pacific makes it impossible to divorce the peninsula from such a conflict.
Despite the very different political outlooks of US President Donald Trump and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, last week’s decision announcement reducing the annual joint US-Republic of Korea (ROK) Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise coincides with a longstanding push by some in Seoul to transfer wartime operational control (OPCON) within the US-ROK Combined Forces Command (CFC) from a US Army four-star general to an ROK Army counterpart.
For some South Koreans, especially in Lee’s progressive coalition, OPCON transfer represents more than a technical reorganization of the CFC. It raises the broader question of how Seoul and Washington should divide responsibility for defending the peninsula.
Yet, greater ROK responsibility for deterring North Korea raises an uncomfortable question that directly affects Taipei and regional allies: If Seoul assumes greater responsibility for its own defense, what purpose should the 28,500 US troops stationed on the peninsula serve? Washington’s emerging answer is greater strategic flexibility for US forces on the peninsula.
The diminished emphasis on North Korea as a direct threat to the US homeland in the recent US National Security and National Defense Strategies, alongside the growing use of US forces on the peninsula for unilateral and third-country exercises, reflects the push for greater “strategic flexibility” that CFC commander General Xavier Brunson has repeatedly emphasized.
US Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby reinforced this logic in Manila last week, arguing that stronger allies should assume greater responsibility for their own defense as Washington builds a more resilient regional deterrence architecture.
However, Seoul has its own interests. Greater South Korean defense autonomy does not necessarily imply greater willingness to allow US forces stationed on the peninsula to be employed against China in a regional contingency.
The US military presence on the peninsula remains rooted in the unfinished Korean War and the alliance’s mission of deterring North Korean aggression. Washington’s push for greater “strategic flexibility” must therefore contend with the political constraints governing how those forces can be employed beyond Korea, a reality that directly affects Taiwan’s security.
Paradoxically, the harder Washington pushes Seoul to assume greater responsibility for its defense to increase US strategic flexibility, the more it could strengthen South Korean demands for autonomy that constrain Washington’s ability to employ peninsula-based forces in regional contingencies.
OPCON transfer also carries questions of sovereignty and strategic agency alongside warfighting effectiveness. Wariness of strategic flexibility in the alliance was reflected in the 2006 joint US-ROK statement that launched the Strategic Consultation for Allied Partnership. The statement, issued at the height of the Global War on Terror, recognized the need for flexibility for peninsula-based US forces while affirming that South Korea should not be drawn into a regional conflict “against the will of the Korean people.”
OPCON transfer was also a priority for Lee’s predecessor, Moon Jae-in. Still, it remained incomplete when he left office, as COVID-era reductions in combined exercises delayed crucial capability assessments. Ironically, reducing the UFS exercise could once again complicate the capability assessments necessary to advance Lee’s push for OPCON transfer.
A Taiwan contingency could bring this paradox to a head. Washington would likely seek greater flexibility from its South Korea-based forces precisely when Seoul, fearing North Korean opportunism amid a wider regional conflict, wants more US capabilities focused on the peninsula.
Taipei therefore has an enormous stake in how Seoul’s pursuit of greater defense autonomy reshapes the US-ROK alliance. OPCON transfer could make South Korea more capable while simultaneously opening a new political argument over what South Korea-based US forces are actually for.
For Taiwan, the larger lesson extends beyond the peninsula. Assessing the US’ ability to respond to a Taiwan contingency requires more than counting US forces in the Indo-Pacific region. Taipei must also understand the alliance politics governing how those forces can be used. Developments in Seoul — and in other allied capitals — could ultimately shape what Washington is politically and militarily able to do in a crisis.
Bryce C. Barros is a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Studies. He served as a US Senate National Security Advisor from 2023 to 2024. The views expressed here do not reflect those of the US government or other affiliations.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Exhibition showcases heat adaptation technologies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

The Ministry of Environment has set up an exhibition of heat adaptation products in front of its building to showcase the industry’s development and encourage public participation.
The ministry on Thursday held a news conference to unveil the exhibition demonstrating the cooling technologies of a “high-transparency, heat-insulating balloon canopy” and “nano-mineral diffused light net.”
Temperatures of 40°C or higher are expected to become the new normal in Taiwan within the next 10 years due to global warming and the urban heat island effect, Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Environment
The ministry has therefore been promoting interagency efforts to plant more trees to increase green shade coverage, he said.
While it is difficult to plant trees in some places and seedlings need time to grow big enough to provide shade, locally developed innovative cooling technologies can be applied to protect pedestrians against heat injuries, Peng said.
Using lightweight shading structures to provide “immediate coverage” can help reduce solar heat load, said Lin Tzu-ping (林子平), a member of the Executive Yuan’s National Urban Forest Promotion Committee.
Such measures are a key strategy for preserving people’s thermal comfort and protecting health in urban areas where planting trees might be unsuitable or where trees have yet to grow big enough, said Lin, a professor of architecture at National Cheng Kung University.
The two shading technologies demonstrated in the exhibition area are capable of blocking shortwave solar radiation by 30 to 40 percent, Lin added.
Lin Yi-chun (林怡君), who invented the nano-mineral diffused light net, said the net incorporates mica minerals produced locally in Taiwan into recycled PET polyester fibers.
It transforms harsh direct sunlight into soft, diffused light, while the nano-minerals allow the fibers to absorb moisture from the air, she said.
When the net is exposed to sunlight, the moisture evaporates and lowers temperatures, she said.
Huang Yi-xing (黃翌星), the inventor of the balloon canopy, said the balloons can lower temperatures by up to 6°C, depending on how cloudy it is.
The balloons feature a dual-layer structure and a cesium tungsten oxide nanoparticle film, making them capable of blocking 86 percent of infrared radiation and more than 99 percent of ultraviolet radiation from the sun, he said.
The exhibition, scheduled to run for 100 days, was set up to showcase how heat adaptation technoliges can be integrated into people’s lives, the ministry said.
Aided by investments from industry, more comprehensive heat adaptation strategies can be developed for outdoor workers, vulnerable groups and the general public, it said.

UN holds second informal poll for body’s next leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:57 UTC
01:42:57 KST

The UN’s most powerful body, the Security Council, met yesterday to hold another straw poll to gauge the popularity of a growing field of contenders to lead the embattled organization.
UN Conference on Trade and Development Secretary-General and former Costa Rican vice president Rebeca Grynspan was the front-runner after last month’s first informal vote, in which the council’s 15 members, including the five with veto power, pass judgement in secret on the candidates.
Argentine diplomat and International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi is also a candidate along with former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet, former Ecuadorian minister of foreign affairs Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Guyanese minister of foreign affairs Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, former Ugandan minister of foreign affairs Olara Otunnu and former Senegalese president Macky Sall.
Photo: EPA
After the first round concluded, former Ecuadorian minister of industries and productivity Ivonne A-Baki threw her hat into the race to succeed Antonio Guterres, who would complete his second five-year term on Dec. 31.
“While the first straw poll set the scene for the Secretary-General race, the second may give us some direction about where it is headed,” UN International Crisis Group head Daniel Forti said. “Diplomats expect fluctuations in the vote distribution compared to the July poll. Most will be watching to see whether the early front-runners consolidate their support or slip in the standings.”
“It is unlikely that any candidate will emerge from [yesterday’s] poll with a decisive lead,” he said.
The veto-wielding nations — the UK, China, France, Russia and the US — might wait until later to express their preferences, while new contenders could emerge, he added.
Even if a candidate earns the required nine votes from the 15 available in the Security Council, they must also avoid a veto by the five major powers, which are deeply divided. Once a candidate clears those bars, their name would go to the General Assembly of all UN members for confirmation.
The Security Council straw poll was devised in the early 1980s in an attempt to break a deadlock between two candidates shut down by vetoes.
The informal mechanism has persisted, in various forms, despite criticism from countries opposed to the opaque process.
Each member state must anonymously assign each candidate one of three labels: “encourage,” “discourage” or “no opinion.” That would give those with no support the opportunity to withdraw — although they are not obliged.
In the first rounds of the process expected to take several weeks, all ballots are the same color.
However, after an unspecified number of votes, the ballots of the five permanent members would become a different color from those of the elected members, making it possible to identify potential vetoes, without knowing which country blackballed any given candidate.
It is tradition that the UN’s top job should rotate between different regions.
Under that premise, the role should go to a candidate from Latin America this time. There are many candidates from the region, although Sall and Otunnu hail from Africa.

16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

The Coast Guard administration (CGA) yesterday said it had warned off and shadowed a Chinese research ship sailing in sensitive waters to the nation’s west, the third time the vessel has been spotted since May.
Taiwan has complained of regular appearances by Chinese ships, including China’s coast guard, in waters near Taiwan as part of “gray zone” harassment designed to pressure Taipei and give an impression of Chinese jurisdiction.
The CGA said that the ship, the Tongji (同濟號), which was commissioned only last year, appeared late on Thursday 24.9 nautical miles (46km) northwest of Penghu County, which lies in the Taiwan Strait and is home to major military bases.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan ADIZ
The ship was not observed deploying or towing any instruments and the CGA said it sent one of its patrol boats to sail alongside the Tongji and broadcast “strong” warnings for it to leave.
As of yesterday morning, the ship was 28 nautical miles west-southwest of Siaoliouciou (小琉球), a popular tourist destination at the bottom of the Strait, continuing to sail southeast, the CGA said in a statement.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The CGA said it would deploy its ships to respond to Chinese vessels, “firmly defending national sovereignty and ensuring the safety of our nation’s waters.”
China’s military also operates around Taiwan on an almost daily basis.
The boat was first spotted in waters near Taiwan in May, the CGA said, adding that at least on one occasion it was observed lowering ropes into the water, suspected to be the deployment of scientific instruments for “illegal” survey operations.
Chinese state media say the Tongji has all-weather operational capability and can carry remotely operated vehicles, laboratories and uncrewed systems.

Group protests anime’s removal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:54 UTC
01:42:54 KST

The removal of the anime Chainsmoker Cat (尼古喵喵) from streaming platforms due to complaints about tobacco product placement contravenes the principle of proportionality and stifles creative expression, an advocacy group said on Thursday, after the Health Promotion Administration launched an investigation that could result in platform operators facing fines of up to NT$1 million (US$31,399).
Bahamut Animation Crazy, an animation streaming platform, confirmed that the show is no longer available in Taiwan, after anti-smoking groups on Thursday called on authorities to investigate and called for its removal for allegedly promoting smoking.
Other streaming platforms also confirmed that they had removed the show.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Alliance for Tobacco Control
Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) yesterday said that he had watched the show and found that it contained multiple close-up shots of cigarette brands, which should have been obscured or blurred.
Smoking scenes should also have carried on-screen warnings stating that smoking is harmful to health, Shih said.
The Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act (菸害防制法) prohibits the promotion or advertising of tobacco products through film, television and radio, he said.
The government in 2010 also established production guidelines that include avoiding content aimed at minors, keeping such content out of time slots commonly viewed by children, limiting frequent close-ups of smoking and discouraging smoking by main characters, he said.
Chainsmoker Cat failed to comply with the guidelines, he said, adding that even Japanese anime broadcast in Taiwan must follow domestic regulations.
In a Facebook post on Thursday, the ACGN Creative Rights Association said that demanding the platform remove the series contravenes the principle of proportionality and could have a chilling effect on creative expression.
Authorities had yet to release a complete investigation report, provide a detailed legal analysis or issue a formal removal order, yet the work has already disappeared under the pressure of potential penalties, the association said.
The situation reflects a pattern that bypasses due process and shifts the burden of administrative judgements onto platforms, distributors, creators and audiences, the association said.
The original manga’s target audience was adult men and the anime was broadcast in a late-night time slot in Japan, it said.
The series was classified as PG-15, meaning it should not be regarded as content aimed at children simply because it is animated, it said.
The series uses nicotine addiction and the disorder it causes in daily life as the core of its character development and comedy, making smoking scenes integral to the narrative, it said.
The show already includes disclaimers stating that it does not encourage smoking and warning that excessive smoking and drinking are harmful to health, it added.
Opposing the harmful effects of tobacco does not mean opposing artistic portrayals of those effects, and protecting minors does not mean depriving adults of access to lawful creative works, the association said.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:51 UTC
01:42:51 KST

The High Court yesterday acquitted a lawmaker, a former lawmaker and two associates in a bribery case involving efforts to help former Pacific Distribution Investment Co chairman Lee Heng-lung (李恆隆) regain control of Pacific SOGO, while upholding prison sentences for two former legislators.
The court upheld a 10-year sentence for former independent legislator Su Chen-ching (蘇震清) and an eight-and-a-half-year sentence for former Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) legislator Sufin Siluko (廖國棟), while acquitting former New Power Party legislator Hsu Yung-ming (徐永明) and KMT Legislator Chen Chao-ming (陳超明).
Former independent legislator Chao Cheng-yu (趙正宇) was sentenced to six months and fined NT$60,000 (US$1,883.95) for tax evasion.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Also acquitted were Hsu’s assistant, Wu Shih-chang (吳世昌), and Chen’s office director, Liang Wen-yi (梁文一), who had received six-and-a-half-year and five-year sentences respectively in the first ruling.
In July 2022, the Taipei District Court handed prison sentences to five lawmakers in the case, ranging from six months to 10 years.
Hsu was previously sentenced to seven years and four months in prison for accepting a bribe without violating his official duties, while Chen was handed a jail term of seven years and eight months and ordered to forfeit NT$1 million.
Prosecutors accused Lee of bribing lawmakers including Su, Sufin, Chen and Hsu in exchange for their help in pressuring Ministry of Economic Affairs officials over the company’s ownership dispute, including through amendments to the Company Act (公司法), public hearings and other legislative actions.
Lee was sentenced to one year and two months in prison, suspended for five years, and ordered to pay NT$10 million to the public treasury.
He sought to regain control of Pacific Distribution Investment and Pacific SOGO after failing to resolve the ownership dispute through legal channels, the court said.
Lee sought lawmakers’ help to pressure the ministry through legislative oversight, questioning government agencies and proposed amendments to laws, the ruling said.
Su met Lee in 2012 and used his legislative powers to assist him in handling the Pacific Distribution Investment case, it said.
The court found Su guilty of receiving NT$25.8 million in bribes over more than five years, and frequently holding coordination meetings and questioning ministry officials.
Sufin and his office director, Ting Fu-hua (丁復華), also assisted Lee through coordination meetings, questioning officials and legislative proposals, with Sufin receiving NT$6.2 million in bribes, the ruling said.
Chen and Liang were found to have been bribed to pressure ministry officials to attend a public hearing at Soochow University, it said.
Hsu was accused of accepting NT$2 million in bribes disguised as political donations.
Lee sought Hsu’s help to organize a public hearing at the university, with Hsu arranging to borrow a Legislative Yuan meeting room and issuing notices inviting ministry officials to attend, the ruling said.

The ruling can be appealed.
Chao’s six-month tax-evasion sentence is final, as neither side appealed that portion of the case.

Report outlines AI’s workplace effects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:50 UTC
01:42:50 KST

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping workplaces rather than simply eliminating jobs, with companies across the Asia-Pacific region expecting their workforces to grow even as they struggle to find skilled workers needed to drive AI adoption, Jones Lang LaSalle said in a report.
About 61 percent of senior executives in the region expect employee numbers to continue rising, despite concerns that AI would trigger widespread job losses, the property consultancy said.
Companies at the forefront of the technology shift are instead increasing investment in physical workplaces to support higher-value work, collaboration and productivity, Jones Lang LaSalle Taiwan managing director Kevin Hou (侯文信) said.
Photo: Bloomberg
“AI will not necessarily reduce demand for physical office space,” Hou said. “Companies leading the AI transition are upgrading workplaces as technology shifts employees toward tasks requiring deeper thinking, concentration and interaction.”
The findings are from Jones Lang LaSalle’s global survey on workplace trends, which polled more than 2,200 senior executives and corporate real-estate leaders across 21 countries.
About 78 percent of respondents expected AI to significantly change their corporate real-estate strategies, but only 31 percent have begun planning workplaces designed for human-machine collaboration, the survey showed.
Just 15 percent have reached an advanced stage of AI adoption, it showed.
The gap between expectations and implementation is emerging as a key challenge as companies balance technology investment against talent shortages, budgets and organizational change, Jones Lang LaSalle said.
For the first time in the survey’s history, talent and skills shortages have overtaken budget constraints as the biggest obstacle to AI transformation.
Globally, 36 percent of respondents cited a lack of skills in AI, data analytics and emerging technologies as a major barrier, the survey said.
The problem is more acute in the Asia-Pacific region, where 42 percent identified AI skills shortages as their biggest constraint, the highest share among regions, it said.
Almost half of companies in the region expect AI-driven demand for employee retraining to further worsen talent shortages over the next three to five years, it said.
The skills crunch is particularly significant as firms in the Asia-Pacific area lead globally in applying AI to corporate real-estate strategy, property-portfolio optimization and technology management, Jones Lang LaSalle said.
AI is also creating new challenges for office managers. As companies increase technology investment to boost productivity, 46 percent of respondents now rank employee productivity as their most important corporate real-estate performance measure, ahead of traditional cost control, the survey said.
Technology-related risks are mounting. Information security and data governance were cited by 47 percent of respondents as a major risk, followed by disruption from AI and emerging technologies at 41 percent, and uncertainty over future office-space demand at 40 percent, it said.
In the Asia-Pacific region, 44 percent viewed technology and AI as a major risk, the highest share globally.
Rather than trying to predict exactly how AI will change headcounts and office demand, companies are being pushed to build flexibility into real-estate strategies through flexible leases, multiple locations and adaptable workspaces, it said.
The shift suggests the office is not disappearing in the AI era, it said.
Instead, its role is evolving as companies seek environments where employees can work more effectively alongside increasingly capable machines, it added.

New cancer treatment saves python named Jodie Foster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

A UK zoo yesterday hailed curing a cancer-stricken python named after Hollywood star Jodie Foster, who became the first snake to receive an innovative treatment combining surgery and electrochemotherapy (ECT).
Chester Zoo, in northwest England, said the 4.5m reticulated python had fully recovered after first undergoing surgery and then receiving ECT following the return of a cancerous tumor in her jawbone.
Animals are increasingly being treated for cancers with drugs and therapies once only used on humans.
Other creatures — including a turtle and lizard — have had ECT treatment previously, case reports posted on medical science databases showed.
However, Chester Zoo’s veterinary team, who worked alongside University of Liverpool cancer specialists to adapt the pioneering treatment, believe it is a first for a snake.
“We were facing the possibility of losing her as the tumor made it more and more difficult for her to eat,” Chester Zoo vet Ian Ashpole said. “So we worked with cancer specialists to see whether we could adapt electrochemotherapy for a snake. As far as we’re aware, this is the first time it’s ever been used in one.”
Zookeepers first became concerned when 23-year-old Jodie began eating less and spending more time inactive in her habitat.
Tests confirmed a malignant tumor in her jaw, which was removed through surgery, but it returned, prompting another surgical procedure when ECT was also deployed to target any remaining cancerous cells.
ECT combines the use of cancer drug bleomycin with a series of electrical pulses directly on the tumor site which temporarily make cancer cells more permeable, allowing the drug to enter more effectively.
“She is so big we had to put two operating tables together, effectively making one the size of a double bed,” said Ashpole, who carried out the procedure.
It included removing part of the python’s jawbone.
“We used heated blankets and warmed air to keep her body temperature stable throughout the operation. After 90 minutes of surgery, she recovered remarkably quickly.”
Following a check-up this week, the zoo said Jodie is “cancer-free, eating normally and back to her usual ‘bright and feisty’ self.”

Donovan’s Deep Dives: The TPP-KMT marriage is under strain — but the ball is in the KMT’s court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:47 UTC
01:42:47 KST

The Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is facing some difficulties, and there are some tensions in their alliance with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT). However, though these problems are real, the local press is blowing them out of proportion and hyping too much out of context.
Take, for example, a poll released by Z.media on Wednesday of 1,070 adults with a sampling error of ±3 percentage points. It showed support for the TPP dropping to 6.3 percent, an all-time low on their historical chart and 4.2 percent lower than their May poll and 11 percent from a year earlier. This led to speculation that the party is disintegrating (paomohua 泡沫化, a delightfully evocative term that means “foaming”).
When asked about this poll, TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) claimed he was not worried at all by the poll, as the pollster “frequently works with the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) for manipulation.” He provided no proof of that allegation.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
On one level, he is right. In my 2024 weighted poll of polls, Z.media was not so bad as to be excluded, but I ranked them as “underweight,” meaning low reliability.
Additionally, the latest Formosa poll released on Aug. 4 showed the TPP’s “favorability” rising 5.4 percent to 29.1 percent from the month prior and an all-time high for this year. Of course, asking if one views a party favorably and if one identifies as a supporter of the party are very different questions, but that one rose and the other fell paints a blurrier picture than the Z.media poll alone. Also, consider that smaller parties have much smaller sample bases, making them more prone to volatility.
Huang is right to dismiss a single poll, but he should still be concerned. Looking across all polling, the party is significantly less popular than at their previous peaks in past years. Looking across multiple polls, I would estimate their support is down by roughly a third, but it does not indicate the party is disintegrating.
Photo courtesy of Chiu Chen-yuan’s campaign team
At least, not yet. The TPP is seven years old, by which many of Taiwan’s previous third parties had already begun to lose momentum. Whether the TPP follows that pattern remains to be seen.
CAUCUS SPLITS
There are also tensions, disagreements and problems in their alliance with the KMT.
Photo: Wang Chun-chi, Taipei Times
The two parties’ legislative caucuses split on several referendum proposals. This was unusual; typically they negotiate behind the scenes to agree on the details of legislation before it goes to a vote.
Of the six referendum proposals by the two parties, three passed. One, a TPP proposal concerning absentee voting, did not receive KMT backing and was not placed on the legislative agenda. Similarly, a KMT proposal on rejecting the abolition of the death penalty was also not on the agenda.
The KMT abstained on the TPP’s euthanasia proposal, killing it. The TPP abstained on the KMT’s caning proposal, though the KMT still had enough votes to get that passed. The two parties were united in passing the proposals on traffic-fine spending and ending the “nuclear-free homeland” policy.
TPP founder Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) downplayed any split in their alliance, saying the two parties are cooperating, but have not merged. He also said the TPP and the KMT will cooperate when possible but compete when necessary, and that it is not possible for the two sides to agree all the time.
Does this indicate a breakdown in their legislative alliance? Not necessarily. It could indicate that the current legislative caucus wants more independence than when it was led by Huang. It could also indicate that the party wants to carve out a more independent image ahead of November’s elections.
In other words, it could mean a split is coming, but it is far too early to say. It could simply mean the TPP caucus will be a more publicly assertive partner within the alliance rather than breaking from it entirely.
ELECTION TENSIONS
There are also tensions in their electoral alliance.
Most notably, neither party appears to be willing to back away from running their respective candidates in Jhubei City (竹北), Hsinchu County. This threatens the two parties’ agreement to coordinate behind a single candidate, with the TPP insisting that an earlier understanding reserved Jhubei for its nominee. Time is running out; candidate registration closes on Sept. 4.
Huang, appearing on an online talk show on Aug. 12, reiterated that he believes KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) and KMT Hsinchu County commissioner candidate Hsu Hsin-ying (徐欣瑩) will “do what they say” and honor an agreement to back the TPP candidate in Jhubei.
He also bluntly warned that if this leads to a so-called “breach” in their alliance, it would be detrimental to future cooperation.
“It would also be difficult for me to go back and persuade my fellow party members: If the other side can go back on its word, why should we keep ours?” he said.
Meanwhile, in Taipei, the KMT party chapter decided that incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) will not appear at campaign events for individual TPP candidates, only joint unity rallies.
On a BCC News talk show on Wednesday, Huang said he “really respected” the Taipei chapter’s decision, but he said that they had always understood that the TPP ultimately had to rely on itself. He then underscored how much tighter the relationship is with the KMT in New Taipei City and Taichung.
On the relationship more broadly, Huang said that from the outset, he had advocated a coalition government and joint governance, and that from signing a party cooperation agreement with the KMT to agreeing on shared policy positions, he could say with a clear conscience that “when I, Huang Kuo-chang, promise something, I will definitely keep my word. I won’t tell you one thing to your face and do another behind your back. I don’t play that game. Because if that’s how we’re going to operate, then we shouldn’t cooperate at all.”
On Jhubei, he again admonished the KMT: “I’ll say it again: I hope Legislator Hsu Hsin-ying will do what she says. We’re giving you time and space.”
Asked whether there had been any new developments, Huang said bluntly, “I really don’t want to say anything unpleasant right now, but I guarantee you that they understand every single thing I say.”
R-E-S-P-E-C-T
Watching the talk show, Huang delivered those lines with relaxed confidence, not anger or hostility.
In the broad scheme of things, the alliance remains functional despite these increasingly visible points of friction.
Huang’s message is essentially that the honeymoon period is over; now we need to do the hard work to make the relationship last, not that he is giving up on it. “Why must it always be us who yields?” he asked.
He is asking for some respect and making some requests of his partner to make the relationship work better. In other words, asking for some help with the dishes and taking out the garbage, not saying the relationship is necessarily fundamentally flawed.
If the KMT yields in Jhubei and shows more respect in the legislature for the TPP’s positions, this will likely blow over.
In Taipei, the KMT can hold firm on the campaigning issue, as Huang indicated, even if he is not happy about it. City and county councils are elected in multi-member districts, which complicates the math and not only pits a party’s candidates against the opposition, but also against candidates within their own party. The KMT’s Taipei chapter wants to win an outright majority of seats, and TPP candidates ultimately threaten that goal.
The ball is in the KMT’s court. For now, the TPP’s requests are not large and easily met.
However, if the KMT does not show flexibility and respect, these problems will accumulate and fester into a broader frustration with the nature of the relationship itself.
That is how divorces happen.
Donovan’s Deep Dives is a regular column by Courtney Donovan Smith (石東文) who writes in-depth analysis on everything about Taiwan’s political scene and geopolitics. Donovan is also the central Taiwan correspondent at ICRT FM100 Radio News, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, co-founder Taiwan Report (report.tw) and former chair of the Taichung American Chamber of Commerce. Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.

Indigenous groups unequally affected by energy poverty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:44 UTC
01:42:44 KST

A National Taiwan University study found that energy poverty affects 52.2 percent of disadvantaged households in Taiwan’s designated indigenous areas, higher than 42.9 percent of indigenous households in Han-majority areas.
The university’s Risk Society and Policy Research Center conducted the survey from January to March, using questionnaires to poll 578 disadvantaged indigenous households, the research team told a news conference on Thursday.
The study was a partnership with World Vision Taiwan, which assists the households surveyed.
Photo: Wu Po-hsuan, Taipei Times
Shih Yi-jen (施奕任), a post-doctoral fellow at the institute, said that the EU defines energy poverty as using more than 10 percent of all income on electricity.
The study revealed significant structural inequality facing disadvantaged rural residents and ethnic minorities in Taiwan, he said.
It showed that the median monthly household energy costs surged to NT$2,492, up from NT$1,960 in off-season months, marking a 27.1 percent increase, Shih said.
The steep rise in the cost of energy resulted from seasonal electricity price hikes and high temperatures, with a stark increase in the number of households spending more than NT$2,501 a month on energy, he said.
About 57.3 percent of families polled have been in arrears on power bills at least once, and 2.9 percent had their power cut off due to non-payment, Shih said.
It suggested that 32.4 percent of households that have air-conditioning reported barely managing or struggling to pay for their use, and a large share of the households were using old, inefficient systems, he said.
According to the study, 37 percent of the families reported not being able to afford repairing their home air-conditioning system, he said.
Government subsidies for replacing obsolete, power-wasting appliances have limited effect, as 42 percent of households surveyed reported not knowing about the program, he said.
Another 10.2 percent said they knew of the program, but could not afford to replace their air-conditioner even with the subsidy, he said.
This traps impoverished families in a spiral of having to pay more for less, Shih said.
The survey found that 65.1 percent were opposed to the proposed policy of raising electricity costs to facilitate energy transition, and that 29.6 percent reported being willing to support the policy if the price increase is marginal, he said.
Lin Chia-nan (林嘉男), associate professor in National Taitung University’s Department of Public and Cultural Affairs, said the government has long neglected the needs of indigenous people.
The distribution of the nation’s energy infrastructure reflects the structural inequality that diverted resources away from indigenous people, who have little say in energy policy, he said.
The energy poverty of indigenous Taiwanese communities exposed a “green energy colonialism” that forced ethnic minorities to absorb the costs of the energy transformation, he said.
The government is urged to pay more attention to the needs of indigenous communities when deciding on energy policy, he said.

US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent on Thursday said that he might further increase the US government’s repurchases of Treasuries, attempting to jawbone a government debt market that was beginning to balk after the previous day’s surprise plan to double buybacks.
Bessent, a former hedge fund manager with extensive experience in sovereign debt and currency markets, said the recent upswing in long-dated Treasury yields to near two-decade highs was unwarranted against the vibrancy of the US economy.
He also pointed to the plans of US President Donald Trump’s administration to curtail government spending that has driven the collective US IOU to the world north of US$40 trillion.
Photo: Bloomberg
In the latest of Bessent’s maneuvers, the Treasury on Wednesday announced that it would double the size of buybacks on longer-dated securities over the next quarter to at least US$4 billion per operation, a move that for one day at least brought the administration some relief from the high bond yields that are rapidly driving up federal debt service costs.
“We’re going to increase the size of the buyback,” Bessent said in a CNBC interview. “I would note that it could be more than the [US]$4 billion per issue.”
The 30-year yield dropped on Wednesday by the most in a day since October last year after Bessent’s tactic caught the market by surprise amid thin late-summer trading and liquidity conditions.
However, by Thursday half of that move was retraced and a brief lurch lower in yields on his comments to CNBC held only for a few moments.
The 30-year yield last traded at 5.24 percent, only about 10 basis points from its high point on Tuesday, when it struck the highest since June 2007.
Bessent, who earlier this month executed the first joint intervention in the Japanese yen in 15 years, told CNBC that his objective was to support liquidity in an area of the market that is thinly traded, especially in August, while having to compete with a large volume of corporate issuance at higher yields, including for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
“Part of it is signaling here, and to show that we believe that the yields don’t reflect the underlying fundamentals. This Iran conflict, we will get on the other side of this, we don’t know when,” Bessent said.
A day after total US public debt outstanding crossed the symbolic US$40 trillion threshold, Bessent said that he and White House budget director Russell Vought would be embarking on a new fiscal consolidation effort directed by Trump, and that combined with efforts to cut waste, fraud and abuse, savings of several hundred billion dollars could be found.
There was “nothing magic about the [US]$40 trillion figure” and the US would grow its way out of the debt, he said.
The deficit this year has been pushed up by refunds of Trump’s tariffs, which were declared illegal by the US Supreme Court — a phenomenon that would not be repeated next year, as new tariffs are being implemented under other trade laws that have withstood court challenges, he said.
Tariff revenues this year are expected to match those of last year, he said, without specifying whether he was referring to calendar or fiscal years.

Nuclear referendum a political ploy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:42 UTC
01:42:42 KST

The opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan on Friday last week approved three referendum proposals. One of the questions is: “Do you agree that the government should abolish its ‘nuclear-free homeland’ energy policy to ensure public health, stabilize power supply, lower electricity prices, enhance national defense resilience and support the development of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry?” To prevent this biased and politically coercive referendum from interfering with the nine-in-one elections in November, the Central Election Commission should reject this wasteful exercise.
For one, the referendum lacks objectivity and neutrality. Article 9 of the Referendum Act (公民投票法) states that the main text of a referendum proposal must be “concise, clear and objectively neutral.” No consensus has been achieved in policy discussions on whether nuclear power could serve as a means of stimulating economic growth, yet its proponents — Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) lawmakers — have deliberately linked the two by equating the use of nuclear power with the development of the AI industry. This is absolutely misleading rhetoric and completely lacks objectivity.
Second, this referendum is a clear attempt to undermine a previous referendum. As Article 32 of the Referendum Act stipulates: “No proposal on the same matter may be resubmitted within two years of the date on which the competent authority announces the results of the referendum.” Although last year’s vote on restarting the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant was defeated, President William Lai (賴清德) — out of respect for public opinion — instructed Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) to conduct independent safety inspections and assessments of the plant’s units. Taipower complied with the policy directive and on March 27 submitted its “Third Nuclear Power Plant Reactivation Plan.” Taiwan’s return to nuclear power is already under way — the question is whether the plan to restart the Ma-anshan plant would pass its review. Is it legal for the KMT and the TPP to put forward another referendum on the same matter within such a short period?
Third, this referendum is being maliciously abused. The Referendum Act also stipulates that referendums may be held on matters such as laws, initiatives on legislative principles and initiatives on major policies. It also empowers the legislature to propose referendums on the initiation of major policies. As laws and legislative principles already fall within the legislature’s purview, the law limits its direct power to initiate referendums to matters concerning legislative principles. In other words, the legislature should not use a referendum to circumvent the ordinary legislative process.
The KMT and the TPP’s joint referendum proposal to abolish the government’s “nuclear-free homeland” policy is a position that they have advocated since early last year. They know well that removing the “nuclear-free homeland” provisions from the Basic Environment Act (環境基本法) and the Climate Change Adaptation Act (氣候變遷因應法) would be a straightforward matter. Yet, for the sake of political mobilization, they have deliberately slipped the policy’s abolition — a matter that falls under the category of “initiatives on legislative principles” — into the referendum process to achieve their political objectives, abusing a system designed to allow for the direct exercise of civil rights.
Shieh Jyh-cherng is a retired National Taiwan University professor.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

====================================================================================================

Ebola is back — and the IMF’s relief fund is empty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:39 UTC
01:42:39 KST

Almost every major global health emergency has exposed the same flaw in the international financial system. When disaster strikes, the institutions built to support affected countries must scramble to raise money for relief funds.
Twelve years ago, when the Ebola virus was ravaging Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, the world discovered that the IMF — the global economy’s firefighter — had no instrument to provide debt relief during a public-health catastrophe. The IMF did have a related mechanism for crisis response: the Post-Catastrophe Debt Relief (PCDR) Trust Fund, created in the wake of Haiti’s devastating 2010 earthquake to provide debt relief to countries struck by natural disasters. However, a fast-moving epidemic proved to be a different kind of emergency entirely, and the PCDR Trust had no mandate to respond.
However, the international community adapted with unusual speed. In November 2014, then-US Secretary of the Treasury Jack Lew called on the IMF to cancel approximately US$100 million in debt owed by the three Ebola-stricken countries, and then-Managing Director Christine Lagarde proposed an additional financing package to the G20 heads of state. Within three months, the PCDR Trust was transformed. A new public-health window was added to its mandate, and existing resources were combined with leftover funds from the earlier Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative, resulting in the Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust (CCRT), a dedicated mechanism allowing the poorest countries to redirect fiscal resources from debt repayment to protecting lives.
Illustration: kevin sheu
Yet, the global fiscal strain of the COVID-19 pandemic nearly exhausted the CCRT’s resources, leaving the trust running dry just as another Ebola crisis has erupted. As of this week, more than 2,000 deaths have been confirmed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Beyond deaths, the UN Development Program estimates that the outbreak could push almost 1 million people into poverty.
The DRC was among the countries that borrowed heavily from the IMF during the COVID-19 pandemic to support its economy. It now carries more than US$3 billion in outstanding IMF debt. While the country has not yet maxed out its borrowing capacity at the Fund, it would likely require additional financing as it confronts a combination of oil-price shocks, slowing growth and now Ebola. It would need not just liquidity, but also relief from existing obligations.
The CCRT exists precisely for this purpose, but its available resources total only US$120 million, whereas the DRC alone must pay the IMF almost US$300 million in debt service next year. The Fund’s primary instrument for disaster relief does not have sufficient funds to cover even one country facing a disaster, let alone the 30 others that could potentially apply for assistance.
Donor countries have previously shown a willingness to fund debt relief. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the IMF received US$800 million in contributions, with the UK pledging US$185 million and Japan US$100 million within days of the pandemic being declared. However, successive rounds of donor pledges, although welcome, address symptoms, not causes. Every time a major health crisis erupts, the IMF must again ask its shareholders to replenish an instrument specifically designed to respond to recurring shocks, causing political delays in delivering what should be an automatic, rapid stabilizer.
There is a better way. The IMF holds about 90.5 million troy ounces of gold, a legacy from the Bretton Woods era when member countries paid their quotas in bullion. This gold sits on the books at a historical cost of US$45 per ounce. At today’s market price of about US$4,000 per ounce, it represents an unrealized profit of about US$357.9 billion.
The IMF’s gold generates no income, but if a small fraction were sold — incrementally, to avoid disrupting markets — the proceeds could seed a permanent endowment capable of funding the IMF’s subsidy accounts indefinitely.
The proposal is straightforward: Sell a small portion of IMF gold, say 10 percent, and place the proceeds in a permanent endowment account. At a modest 3 percent annual return, consistent with the yield assumptions underpinning other IMF instruments, a US$35.8 billion endowment would generate more than US$1 billion per year in perpetuity. That would be sufficient not only to fund the CCRT fully, but also to subsidize the IMF’s entire concessional lending architecture — the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, the Resilience and Sustainability Trust and any successor instruments — without ever again requiring the institution to solicit donor contributions.
Selling gold to support concessional lending is not a new idea. The IMF sold 12.94 million ounces in 1999 and 12.97 million ounces in 2009 — almost three times this proposal. In the past year, calls for another gold sale have come from many groups, including the V20, the G-24, the Jubilee Commission and 165 civil-society organizations.
The case is straightforward: A gold sale costs taxpayers nothing, creates no loss for the IMF and simply converts an idle, illiquid, non-interest-bearing asset into one that generates a permanent income stream for the world’s most vulnerable countries. And with gold prices at near-record levels, there might never be a better time to make that conversion.
Critics would argue that the IMF’s Articles of Agreement require an 85 percent supermajority for gold sales, making US congressional support essential — and thus uncertain. However, this is precisely an opportunity for the US to show leadership. Ebola is no longer solely an emergency in African countries. The US government’s recent actions to respond to Ebola demonstrate policymakers’ recognition that the virus is a threat everywhere, and that a stronger DRC response would protect everyone.
To achieve that, the DRC should receive relief from upcoming IMF payments, giving it fiscal space to focus its efforts where they matter most: combating the epidemic and expanding the social safety net. Moreover, an immediate donor-replenishment campaign should be initiated to replenish the CCRT. In parallel, serious negotiations on a gold endowment should begin to render the question of CCRT funding permanently moot.
The CCRT was born because US leadership decided that the machinery of international finance should not stand idle in the face of a humanitarian catastrophe. That was correct in 2014, and it should inspire action again now.
Marina Zucker-Marques is senior academic researcher at the Boston University Global Development Policy Center.
Copyright: Project Syndicate
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

China’s foreign and defense ministers yesterday met their Indonesian counterparts in Jakarta for talks seeking greater political and military cooperation days after a joint navy drill Taiwan blasted as a “provocation.”
The talks marked “an important milestone in our bilateral relations,” Indonesian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sugiono, who goes by one name, said as he welcomed his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi (王毅).
“It serves as a forward-looking strategic platform, guiding our bilateral partnership across all five pillars — political, economic, maritime, people-to-people, and security,” he said.
Photo: Reuters
Indonesia maintains a neutral foreign policy, what it calls “free and active” — walking a diplomatic tightrope between Beijing and Washington.
Jakarta and Beijing raised the ire of Taipei earlier this month with a joint navy drill off the nation’s east coast.
The two countries said it was a “passing exercise” with an Indonesian frigate passing through on its return home from the Russian port city of Vladivostok.
Taiwan called it a “military provocation” from the Chinese Communist Party.
Wang said it was crucial for Beijing and Jakarta to “increase strategic communication, to deepen strategic coordination” as important representatives of the Global South.
“Today’s world is fluid and turbulent,” he said. “We are seeing unilateralism and hegemonism. They have dealt a heavy blow to this world as well as to the global development agenda.”
The ministers headed the inaugural meeting of what is being called a “China-Indonesia Comprehensive Strategic Dialogue Mechanism.”
Its purpose is to boost “the alignment of development strategies,” Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Lin Jian (林劍) said ahead of Wang’s visit.
Wang was later joined by Chinese Minister of National Defense Dong Jun (董軍) in talks with Indonesian counterparts on “political security and defence cooperation and international and regional situations,” Beijing said.
Indonesian Minister of Defense Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin said the countries would “cooperate in missiles, rockets and so on.”
“They [China] will help and they will transfer their technology so that we can build factories together in Indonesia,” he said.
The two countries would also hold another military exercise this year under Heping Garuda, a recurring joint drill focused on humanitarian assistance, disaster relief and military-to-military cooperation, Sjafrie said.

Japan protests Russian missile tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

Japan yesterday said it had protested against Russia’s notification that Moscow would conduct missile tests off disputed islands visited by Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this month.
“We lodged a protest in response to the notification about the plan to conduct a missile test” off the Kuril Islands, known as the Northern Territories by Japan, a Japanese government spokesman said.
Kyodo quoted Russia’s Pacific Fleet as saying that it had already conducted the missile test, although it was unclear when it took place.
Photo: Bloomberg
A unit equipped with the Bastion surface-to-ship missile system conducted the test, Kyodo quoted the Russian naval fleet as saying.
The guided missile cruiser Varyag, the flagship of the Pacific Fleet, also took part in the test, along with the Omsk nuclear-powered submarine, it added.
The exercise simulated an attack on enemy vessels and succeeded in hitting all the intended targets at a range of at least 300km, the fleet said
“We believe Russia’s military buildup in the Northern Territories including these missile drills runs counter to Japan’s position regarding the Northern Territories, and is unacceptable,” Japanese Minister of Foreign Affairs Toshimitsu Motegi said.
Putin made his first official visit to the islands, administered by Russia since 1945, on Thursday last week, prompting Japan to summon Russia’s ambassador — a move then reciprocated by Moscow.
Putin went there after visiting the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where Russia’s navy was conducting drills.
His visit was the first trip to the islands by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.
After Putin’s stop, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the islands “are an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law.”
Ties between Japan and Russia have worsened since the full-scale conflict in Ukraine began in 2022.
Japan has joined other G7 countries in sanctioning Moscow and aiding Kyiv.
Ukraine, like the US, recognizes Japanese sovereignty over the disputed islands.
Analysts said Putin’s visit to the Kurils could have been aimed at warning Japan against deepening its support for Ukraine — potentially including the direct supply of Patriot missiles — and closer cooperation with NATO.
Japan provides only non-lethal defense aid to Ukraine.
While Japan has eased restrictions on defense exports over the past few years, it is still barred from supplying lethal military equipment directly to a country at war.

Having your cake and eating it too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

With the November nine-in-one elections drawing closer, the collaboration between the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is once again drawing public attention. The KMT Taipei chapter has reportedly decided to focus on winning an outright majority in the council. As such, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) will not appear in individual campaign events for TPP councilor candidates, and instead only attend joint campaign rallies.
The question is whether this blue-white “alliance” can hold, with the TPP not having a mayoral candidate and both parties pursuing their own interests in the council races. Despite their professions of cooperation, the KMT’s priority is to win a majority amid concern that the TPP could hurt its candidates’ electoral prospects. If they cannot even lend one another a hand on the campaign trail, what kind of alliance is this?
If Chiang hopes to win the support of TPP voters in the mayoral race, he cannot simply enjoy the electoral benefits of the blue-white alliance while refusing to bear any political cost. Asking voters in the white camp to support him while keeping his distance from TPP councilor candidates creates the impression that he wants a boost from the TPP, but is unwilling to offer anything in return.
Political cooperation is not one-sided. For the KMT to ask the TPP for support while imposing restrictions of its own would only erode mutual trust. Political parties can negotiate and coordinate, but they cannot force voters to cast their ballots according to the parties’ calculations. If the two parties cooperate on one hand while trying to block each other on the other, it would reduce the alliance to nothing more than an empty slogan.
The KMT and the TPP are, after all, distinct parties whose principles and interests do not always align, making genuine cooperation all the more dependent on sincerity. As much as Chiang would like to have his cake and eat it too, he should not merely expect votes from the white camp; he should also demonstrate commitment to cooperation through his actions. Otherwise, what kind of alliance does he claim to run?
Tsai Jr-keng is a retired elementary-school principal.

A source in South Korea’s diplomatic corps said that two lawmakers were asked by the Chinese embassy in Seoul to be removed from the delegation that was to visit China on Wednesday, allegedly over a prior visit to Taiwan, the Korean-language Chosun Daily reported yesterday.
The embassy had, at the beginning of the month, told the South Korean National Assembly that it wished that Kim Gi-hyeon of the People Power Party and Kwak Sang-eon of the Democratic Party of Korea be removed from the delegation list, the source said.
The National Assembly Committee on Climate, Energy, Environment and Labor had chosen a 15-member delegation to embark on a four-day, three-night trip to China, with the itinerary including a visit to the World Robot Conference and meetings with Chinese officials.
Photo: EPA
The delegation, traveling on official passports, would in principle not need to apply for visas, but the South Korean National Assembly was still expected to talk with their Chinese counterparts regarding the itinerary, the source said.
Ultimately, the trip was canceled due to overlapping issues with flight arrangements.
The source said that the Chinese side had not given an exact reason, only stating that “it would be difficult” for Kim and Kwak to visit China.
Kim and Kwak had earlier this year visited Taiwan, with Kim visiting as head of the Asia Human Rights Parliamentary Alliance and meeting with Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍).
Kwak visited Taiwan in June and met with Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Francois Wu (吳志中), expressing support for strengthened exchanges between South Korea and Taiwan, Chosun reported.
The report, citing an anonymous source, said that the move was Beijing’s attempt to intimidate lawmakers from other countries into not interacting with Taiwan.
Asked for comment by Chosun Daily, Kim said that he did not visit Taiwan in a personal capacity and that the Chinese government is intervening and preventing his visit to China on National Assembly business.
Kwak told the paper that “the Chinese government is attempting to evaluate and interfere in the parliamentary activities of South Korean lawmakers.”
Kwak said he had also issued a formal letter of complaint with the Chinese embassy, but had yet to receive a response, the report said.
The embassy told the paper it had no comment on the issue.
The incident was not the first time China had refused entry or delayed visa issuance to South Korean National Assembly members over Taiwan or human rights issues, the report said.
In one 2004 incident, opposition members faced delays in visa applications when attempting to enter China to inspect ruins from the Goguryo period, allegedly because they had attended the inauguration of then-president Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁).
In 2012, Park Sun-young was refused a visa from China due to her criticism of Beijing repatriating people fleeing North Korea to Pyongyang.

The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) yesterday called for the immediate release of two Hong Kong pro-democracy activists after Hong Kong’s Court of First Instance convicted them and the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China of subversion.
The MAC expressed “deep regret and sorrow” over the convictions, and urged the Chinese and Hong Kong governments to stop what it described as political persecution.
Hong Kong media outlet Sing Tao Daily said the convicted defendants are former alliance chairman Lee Cheuk-yan (李卓人) and former vice chairwoman Chow Hang-tung (鄒幸彤).
Photo: Reuters
Another former vice chairman, Albert Ho (何俊仁), pleaded guilty before the trial began.
The alliance, which was dissolved in 2021, had for decades organized peaceful events commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown, and advocated for democracy and freedom in China, the MAC said.
The defendants were charged under Hong Kong’s National Security Law with inciting others to organize, plan or participate in acts aimed at subverting state power between July 1, 2020, and Sept. 8, 2021, Sing Tao Daily reported.
The MAC said the case took nearly five years to work its way through the courts, during which the defendants spent a prolonged period in detention, raising international concerns about the deterioration of human rights and the rule of law in Hong Kong.
The rule of law, freedom of speech and thought, and respect for human rights are essential to maintaining Hong Kong’s status as an international financial center, as well as its prosperity and stability, the MAC said.
It urged Beijing and the Hong Kong government to stop using national security laws to suppress dissent and release those detained in the case.

Rough animated film becomes a surprise Chinese cinemas hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:29 UTC
01:42:29 KST

A low-budget Chinese animated film that was widely mocked for its crude visuals became a viral hit, with people packing cinemas to see just how bad it is.
Niu Lai, which translates to “Here Comes the Cow,” earned about 7,000 yuan (US$1,041.60) in its opening week from Aug. 5, before surging to 33.06 million yuan at the Chinese box office, according to ticketing platform Maoyan.
The film, made by a mother and son, follows the journey of a calf named Niu Lai and was crafted frame by frame over five years, local media reported, with the duo also composing original scores for the end credits.
Photo: AFP
Caelan Moriarty, a US musician working in China, said the film is “so bad that it’s so good.”
“I appreciate how bad it is, but there’s some heart [put] into it, so you can’t hate that,” Moriarty said.
Artificial intelligence (AI) could make the movie in “like ten seconds or even faster,” but “the fact that they didn’t use AI, they took time” was impressive, he said.
“It’s not perfect. But because it’s not perfect, it’s good, it shows how human it is... and I think that’s why this is trending,” he added.
With its stiff 3D characters and awkward dialogue, the movie traces Niu Lai’s relationship with his mother. The film’s unpolished style quickly went viral on social media, with fans embracing its imperfections as part of its charm.
Student Stella Xing, who watched the film in Beijing after seeing memes online, said: “Even though it’s pretty rough around the edges, there are so many funny details — like the way [Niu Lai] walks, for instance.”
“It’s hilarious and really makes people want to come see it,” she added.
At cinemas in Beijing, hand-drawn banners of human-like cows with eyebrows stood in stark contrast to the glossy posters promoting filmmaker Christopher Nolan’s latest movie The Odyssey.
Barely any conventional marketing had been done to promote the film.
As Niu Lai took China’s Internet by storm, online retailers on platforms such as Taobao rushed to produce merchandise featuring the yellow cow, including T-shirts, figurines and even boxer shorts.
The film offers “something different from the polished, sophisticated productions we are used to,” University of New South Wales associate professor Pan Wang said.
“It is a bit like eating refined grains every day and then suddenly having some coarse grains for a change — the contrast itself feels refreshing,” Wang said. “Its roughness, absurdity and imperfection become part of its appeal.”
Animated films have proven highly popular in the world’s second-largest economy.

The Legislative Yuan yesterday passed an amendment to the Income Tax Act (所得稅法) raising the tax exemption threshold for dependent minor children and expanding itemized deductions for social insurance premiums.
The amendment, which cleared its third reading, increases the tax exemption for dependent minor children by 50 percent to NT$151,500 (US$4,757).
It also removes the NT$24,000 annual limit on itemized deductions for insurance premiums for labor insurance, farmers’ health insurance, National Pension Insurance, and insurance for military personnel, civil servants and public-school teachers.
Photo: Tyrone Siu, Reuters
The new rules are to take effect retroactively from Jan. 1, meaning taxpayers would be able to apply the increased exemptions and expanded deductions when filing their income tax returns in May next year.
The Executive Yuan proposed the amendment on June 25 to alleviate financial pressure on families raising children and create a more family-friendly tax environment.
The 50 percent increase for minor children is modeled after the tax code, which already grants a 50 percent exemption increase for dependents over the age of 70.
During an initial review, Minister of Finance Chuang Tsui-yun (莊翠雲) said that the increased exemption for minor children would result in a tax revenue loss of about NT$8 billion, but would directly benefit an estimated 2.37 million households.
Under the previous regulations, only National Health Insurance premiums were exempt from the NT$24,000 annual itemized deduction cap.
The amendment expands this exemption to include the other forms of social insurance.
In addition, lawmakers passed a bipartisan attached resolution requiring the Ministry of Finance to study the feasibility of amending Article 17 of the act to alleviate the tax burden on wage earners.
The resolution aims to ensure that the original intent of special deductions for salary income is not eroded by regular wage growth.
The ministry is required to submit a report on its findings by the end of this year.

The Mecca Agreement is no ‘Sunni NATO’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

It might be hard to imagine that the Middle East is looking beyond Washington at the precise moment it is being massively disrupted by a US-led war. Yet that is exactly what is happening — most recently through this month’s signing of the Mecca Agreement, a mutual defense pact between Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey and Shehbaz Sharif of Pakistan.
This pact is simultaneously less and more than it seems. On the one hand, the agreement insists that “an attack on one is an attack on all,” deliberately echoing NATO’s Article 5. It binds together major regional powers, each of which brings significant strengths to the table: bottomless funds, in the Saudis’ case; a muscular defense-industrial complex, in Turkey’s; and, in Pakistan’s, ample trained manpower and a nuclear deterrent.
However, regardless of what the paperwork says, this is no Sunni NATO. True alliances are more than treaties. Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed one on mutual defense last year, but it did not seem to be triggered when Iran started firing missiles across the Gulf, nor did it appear to deter Tehran from escalation.
In this case, it is hard to understand exactly where and when these countries would come to one another’s aid. Would it happen if the Houthis violated Saudi borders? Or if India and Pakistan had another confrontation? Alliances require countries to be willing to fight for each other — and the sad truth is that, in the past few decades, only the US has been willing to run that risk.
These three countries have relied on that US backstop for decades. Turkey remains in NATO, although the bilateral relationship is fraught; Riyadh has always viewed Washington as its primary security guarantor; and the US’ on-again, off-again embrace of Pakistan has shaped that country’s worldview, rarely for the better.
As Washington makes it clear that it is willing to disrupt the Middle East rather than stabilize it, the Mecca Agreement is best seen as a formal admission that all three capitals are going to have to find new partners and alignments.
This is not easy. They do not have that many stability-loving friends to draw upon, partly because of their own poor choices. Turkey has its hands in multiple messes across the Caucasus and Mediterranean, Pakistan is far too comfortable thinking of terrorists as ideological fellow travelers and Saudi money has long supported religious extremists around the world, even though it has tried to dial that down in the past few years. These are revisionist powers, ill-at-ease heirs to an order that they never really loved.
Yet the purpose of this pact is not to upend the regional order. Instead, it is conservative in intent, an attempt to freeze or reverse the current turmoil. None of these three is interested in accelerating the chaos, the way Iran might be. Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan might resent the regional arrangements they have inherited, but they also know that a permanently ungovernable Middle East does not benefit them.
Powers unhappy with their status quo would meddle in each other’s affairs, bully their neighbors, and pursue imperial or revanchist dreams — but most of them would stop viewing such provocations as useful the moment they threaten trade routes, energy access or their own domestic legitimacy. At that point, even restless leaders begin to look for someone willing to share the burden of stabilizing their neighborhood.
For decades, that has been the US. Washington’s retreat from that role would inevitably produce this kind of faux alliance: a middle-power attempt to recreate the US’ role piecemeal, with every partner throwing something into the pot in the vague hope that whatever emerges is lasting and effective.
So questions about what the Mecca Agreement would look like in practice, however sensible, tend to miss the larger point. With no secretariat, no unified command and insufficient trust, it might survive only as a platform to talk shop, but even an obligation that Riyadh, Islamabad and Ankara consult one another in a crisis is not nothing. Over time, such self-interested improvisation might create a new geometry of restraint in one of the world’s most troubled regions.
However, I am not that hopeful. The problem with middle powers is that they all want to be great powers. Pakistan’s self-image, as the only Muslim-majority nuclear power, is elevated enough. Meanwhile, the Saudis and Turkey have long assumed that they, and they alone, deserve to lead the Sunni world. The House of Saud believes that its role in Mecca and Medina gives it certain privileges, but Istanbul remembers the four centuries when it was the seat of the caliphate.
The reason they have been complaisant allies in the past is that each was willing, regardless of these supposed claims to prominence, to accept the US as a senior partner. However, that does not mean they would accept each other as equals. If they ever do, then the Mecca Agreement stands a chance of success.
Mihir Sharma is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist. A senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi, he is author of Restart: The Last Chance for the Indian Economy. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.
