MOSCOW, August 21. /TASS/. Russian authorities have set a goal to optimize maintenance schedules of oil refineries to minimize the risk of supply shortages in the fuel market, the cabinet reported following a meeting chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak.
TASS has compiled the key takeaways from the meeting.
Optimization of refineries’ maintenance schedules
Russian authorities have set a goal to optimize the schedules for planned maintenance at oil refineries, according to a statement by the cabinet of ministers.
This is necessary "to minimize the risks of a reduction in market supply."
Availability of information on fuel class
The meeting addressed the mechanism for distributing fuels of environmental classes K2, K3, and K4, as well as quality control, pricing, and labeling for such fuels, the government said.
Information regarding the fuel’s environmental class must be displayed "on the fuel dispenser’s information panel, in the consumer information area, and on the cash register receipt."
The cabinet has already said that the information must be presented in an accessible format.
The Russian government previously authorized the production, import, and release into circulation of gasoline meeting environmental classes K2, K3, and K4 (Euro 2, Euro 3, Euro 4) until July 1, 2027.
Meeting
Participants of the meeting discussed the implementation of measures "aimed at saturating the domestic fuel market, maintaining fair prices, and increasing the transparency of fuel sales in both the wholesale and retail segments."
Monitoring of the fuel market also continues in cooperation with the Agriculture Ministry regarding supplies to agricultural producers, and with the Ministry for the Development of the Russian Far East regarding the northern delivery program, the report said.
The Energy Ministry reported on the implementation by oil companies of recommendations to increase supplies of motor gasoline and diesel fuel to the domestic market, including by boosting imports and releasing fuel of environmental classes K2, K3, and K4 into circulation.

'World looking at India as bright spot of growth & hope': PM Modi at Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 21, 2026, 21:20 IST

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday said the world is looking at India as a "bright spot of growth and hope", stressing that the country's reform journey has shifted from a "punishment model" under the earlier licence raj governments to an incentive-based approach.Addressing the Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026, PM Modi said the world had witnessed several ups and downs in recent years and that the future of all nations was interconnected."The world has witnessed many ups and downs over the past few years, and these experiences have made one thing abundantly clear: whether one likes it or not, the futures of all nations are interconnected. Nothing is possible in isolation," the Prime Minister said."'One Earth, One Family, One Future' was India's guiding mantra during its G20 presidency. This spirit of a shared future, along with the accompanying sense of responsibility, offers solutions to many of the challenges facing the 21st-century world. There are various concerns regarding global growth. The world has witnessed a grim scenario recently; resources are being weaponized, and an atmosphere of mistrust is giving rise to numerous new challenges.
Yet, even in such times, the world views India as a bright spot of growth and hope," he added.
From 'production-linked punishment' to PLI
PM Modi criticised the earlier licence raj governments, saying they followed a "Production Linked Punishment" (PLP) model that penalised companies for increasing production.“Today’s younger generation will be surprised to hear that there was a time in our country when if a company produced more than the prescribed limit, it was punished. This was the PLP, or Production Linked Punishment, model of the earlier licence raj governments,” he said.“Those who make fun of the Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat campaigns today are rooted in the same thinking of the past — PLP, or Production Linked Punishment,” he said.
'Prohibited unless permitted' to 'permitted unless prohibited'
PM Modi also said the government is changing the country's regulatory philosophy by moving away from the earlier approach of requiring permission for activities unless explicitly allowed.“Earlier, the approach to regulations was ‘prohibited unless permitted’ — meaning you could not do something unless the government gave you permission. We are changing this approach to ‘permitted unless prohibited’. That means, for anything that is not explicitly prohibited by law, there should be no need to seek permission at every step.”He said the shift was intended to recast the relationship between the state, citizens and businesses around trust rather than suspicion.“The relationship between the government and citizens should be based not on suspicion, but on trust,” PM Modi added.The Prime Minister also highlighted legislative work undertaken during the Monsoon Session of Parliament."In the Monsoon Session of Parliament, we have passed the Bankers’ Books Evidence Bill, even as the Opposition has continued to create disruptions in Parliament. We did not allow the work of serving the country to stop," he said."We are not just changing regulations, we are changing entire policy of regulations," PM Modi said at the ET Global Leaders' Forum.Speaking ahead of PM Modi's keynote address at the summit, Times Internet chairman Satyan Gajwani said Modi had emerged as a source of stability in a world "lurching from one crisis to the next."
Gajwani said the global landscape was being reshaped by multiple, overlapping disruptions - two ongoing wars, an energy crisis, disrupted shipping routes, trade wars and the rapid AI revolution - creating unprecedented uncertainty for governments, businesses and economies.He said India's political and economic stability, coupled with its growth and reform trajectory, had positioned the country as a reliable force amid growing geopolitical uncertainty.Gajwani said PM Modi's leadership and policy continuity had helped provide businesses and investors with greater predictability, while giving India an opportunity to play a larger role in the evolving global order.

Ukraine warns Russia could exploit upcoming Independence Day for attacks and sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:47:31 UTC
00:47:31 KST

Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) urged Ukrainians to remain particularly vigilant ahead of Independence Day on 24 August, warning of potential Russian attacks and other security threats around the holiday.
Security threats are often heightened around major national holidays in Ukraine during the full-scale war with Russia, when large public gatherings can create opportunities for attacks and Russia has an added incentive to use symbolic dates to spread fear and disruption.
The SBU said Russia could exploit Independence Day gatherings for attacks, provocations, sabotage, cyberattacks, or other crimes.
Russia may recruit Ukrainians for sabotage
The SBU specifically warned about attempts by Russian intelligence services to recruit Ukrainians to carry out attacks inside the country.
According to the agency, Ukrainians could be offered money to set fires, damage property, plant suspicious objects, collect information about military facilities, or carry out other illegal activities.
The SBU urged people not to accept such offers and to immediately report attempts at recruitment.
It also warned that recruiters may disguise requests as ordinary tasks. People could be asked to photograph a particular location, deliver a package, or leave an object somewhere without being told the real purpose of the task.
The SBU said people should be especially cautious about requests from unknown individuals, including those claiming to represent law enforcement.
Russia has repeatedly sought to recruit Ukrainians for sabotage and other activities inside Ukraine during the full-scale war. Ukrainian authorities have previously reported cases in which people were offered money to carry out arson attacks, damage infrastructure, gather intelligence, or perform other tasks on behalf of Russian handlers.
Alleged Russian agent arrested in Dnipro, accused of activating 1,000+ Starlink communications terminals to support Russian forces
Warning over information that could help Russia
The agency also urged Ukrainians to avoid sharing information that could help Russia identify military targets or assess the results of its attacks.
That includes photos and videos showing the locations of Ukrainian troops, critical infrastructure, checkpoints, and air defense systems.
The SBU also told people not to publish information about the consequences of Russian strikes, Ukrainian air defense operations, or the movement of Ukrainian military personnel.
Such information can reveal the location and activity of Ukrainian forces or help Russia assess the effectiveness of its strikes.
Independence Day under wartime threats
Ukraine will mark its 35th Independence Day on 24 August, more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
The holiday comes as Russia continues to use missiles and drones to attack Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, while Ukrainian authorities remain concerned about Russian intelligence activity and sabotage inside the country.
The SBU urged Ukrainians to remain particularly vigilant before and during Independence Day and to report suspected recruitment, preparations for sabotage or terrorism, and other activity that could threaten national security.

At least 3 injured in sword attack at Swedish high school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:47:00 UTC
00:47:00 KST

One person was killed, at least three others were injured after an 18-year-old armed with a sword targeted a high school in central Sweden on Friday before police shot and detained him, authorities said, as reports emerged that the suspect was a former student with a previous assault conviction.
The attack unfolded Friday afternoon at Brinell High School in Fagersta, a town of about 13,000 people. The school had just reopened after the summer break, and for some students, it was their first day back.
Police said at a news conference that officers responding to the school shot and subdued the 18-year-old suspect before taking him into custody on suspicion of murder.
Local police chief Tommy Alriksson said officers entered the school shortly after arriving at the scene.
"The first patrol entered and let us know that the perpetrator was subdued with gunfire," Alriksson said.
Swedish public broadcaster SVT, citing unnamed sources, reported that the attacker was wearing a helmet and carrying a sword. It said he was a former student at the school and had previously been convicted of assault.
Local health authorities said two of those wounded were teenage boys who suffered severe injuries. A third injured person was released from the hospital.
The violence triggered a major emergency response and a five-hour lockdown at the school, which has about 450 students between the ages of 16 and 20. Several other schools and public buildings in Fagersta were also initially placed under lockdown.
One student, Nellie, said the school day had begun normally before she saw an injured person covered in blood and police officers rushing into the building.
Another student, Abdulrahem Salmo, told SVT he saw a victim with a bloody wound to the arm before students fled and contacted police.
Fagersta Mayor Asa-Marta Sjostrom said the attack had shaken the small community and that authorities were focused on supporting students, school employees and others affected by the violence.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson canceled a speech scheduled for Saturday following the attack, according to Swedish news agency TT.
"Our thoughts are with all those affected," Kristersson said on X.
King Carl XVI Gustaf said in a statement released by the royal household that he received news of the attack "with dismay and sadness."
Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson, whose center-left coalition leads opinion polls ahead of next month's parliamentary election, expressed solidarity with the community.
"All of Sweden stands together with Fagersta at this difficult time," she said.
Police were also investigating a TikTok account potentially linked to the attack, according to Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet. The account reportedly posted an image of a sword about 20 minutes before the violence began.
Dagens Nyheter reported that details visible in the background suggested the image may have been taken inside a restroom at the school.
Before the month-old account was removed Friday, it contained videos referring to two previous episodes of mass violence in Sweden as well as Norwegian far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik.
The attack comes amid memories of previous deadly violence at Swedish schools. In February 2025, a gunman killed 10 people at a school in Orebro before killing himself in Sweden's deadliest mass shooting.
In 2015, a masked attacker armed with a sword killed a teaching assistant and two students at a school in Trollhattan in western Sweden before police shot him dead. Authorities later determined that the attack was racially motivated.

peleg design’s crocodile clips keep beach towels from blowing away

Peleg Design brings a little reptilian assistance to windy beach days with Crococlips, a set of crocodile-shaped grips designed to keep towels securely in place. Attached to the corners of a towel, the compact accessories clamp onto the fabric and help prevent it from folding, shifting or taking an unscheduled trip across the sand when the wind picks up.
The idea follows the studio’s familiar formula of combining function with visual humor. Rather than disguising the mechanism, Crococlips turn the gripping action itself into the joke: the crocodile’s open jaws close around the textile, transforming a straightforward fastening device into a characterful beach companion. One on each corner, and the towel suddenly has its own small security team.
the crocodile-shaped clips secure towels in place | images courtesy of Peleg Design
A BITE-SIZED SOLUTION TO WINDY DAYS
Designed for beaches, picnics and other outdoor settings, the clips respond to an everyday inconvenience with an intentionally simple gesture. Their pronounced jaws create a secure hold on the fabric, while the animal silhouette makes their purpose immediately legible. Instead of adding another technical-looking accessory to the beach bag, Peleg Design gives the mechanism a personality of its own.
That approach reflects the broader philosophy of the studio, founded by Shahar Peleg in 2004. Peleg Design develops household and lifestyle objects around three recurring principles — functionality, aesthetics and humor — often using visual twists and playful associations to rethink familiar products. Crococlips continue this strategy at a particularly modest scale: no reinvention of the beach towel required, just something determined enough to hold onto it.
each clip grips onto the edge of the fabric
FUNCTION GETS A SENSE OF HUMOR
The clips also embody Peleg Design’s interest in objects that reveal their idea almost instantly. Their crocodile form is not merely decorative but tied directly to the way the product works, with the metaphorical bite becoming a literal gripping mechanism. This overlap between image and function allows an otherwise ordinary accessory to operate somewhere between practical tool and small visual gag.
For a product designed to solve such a minor problem, Crococlips make a surprisingly visible intervention. They keep fabric anchored while adding a playful detail to the edges of a towel or blanket, turning wind resistance into something a little less serious. The beach may remain unpredictable, but at least the crocodiles are holding on.

The dragon spreads its wings: China is balancing between rival powers to expand its influence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:45:46 UTC
00:45:46 KST

While the U.S. and Russia remain bogged down in their wars of choice, China's formal. neutrality has allowed it to benefit from the situation, hosting Trump, Putin, and various European leaders in Beijing. Balancing between the opposing sides in Ukraine and the Middle East, China is doing everything it can to avoid direct involvement while continuing to provide measured support to its authoritarian partners. While presenting itself as a peacemaker, China is in fact not particularly interested in establishing any peace that would deprive it of its leverage.
As early as 2017, Chinese leader Xi Jinping described the state of affairs in the world as a period of “changes unseen in a century.” Since then, the international order has faced a series of serious challenges, from the war in Ukraine to the protracted conflict in the Middle East and the military confrontation between Iran and the U.S. All of these upheavals have one thing in common: Chinese involvement — not as a direct participant, but as an interested party nevertheless.
The forms of this involvement can vary, from indirect support for one side to mediation efforts in disputes between countries friendly to Beijing. In Western analytical circles, such behavior is often described as opportunistic – aimed at capitalizing on chaos.
Yet viewing all of Beijing’s moves through this lens would be an oversimplification. China’s responses do indeed vary depending on how strongly its key interests are affected, the level of risk involved, and the opportunities that arise. Protecting national interests while maintaining relations with all sides is not a neutral position; it is a deliberate strategy in which the long-term strengthening of China’s position always takes precedence over short-term gains.
What drives Beijing
Until the mid-2010s, China and its position on international conflicts were noticeably more restrained. Before Xi Jinping came to power, the foreign policy of the People’s Republic of China was cautious and even reactive. This approach is often described using the well-known dictum of Deng Xiaoping: “Hide your capabilities and bide your time.” For nearly three decades, Beijing deliberately prioritized economic development over geopolitical ambitions, avoided unnecessary friction with the West, and avoided taking on the role of arbiter in other countries’ disputes.
The shift began after Xi took the helm of the country in 2012–2013. Within the Chinese leadership, there was growing discussion that Beijing's international status no longer corresponded to its dramatically increased economic power.
Foreign policy therefore became more assertive. China launched global initiatives, above all the Belt and Road Initiative, established its first overseas military base in Djibouti, and, most importantly, became more willing to defend its own interests. This meant not only greater involvement in global affairs but also an attempt to gradually reshape the international order.
China’s behavior in international conflicts is determined above all by a hierarchy of interests. These can broadly be divided into two groups. The first consists of core interests. When a conflict touches on them, compromises are effectively off the table, and Beijing’s actions become significantly more assertive. These absolute priorities include the country’s territorial integrity (including the Taiwan issue), economic development, and the stability of the political system.
When secondary interests are at stake, China’s approach can become more pragmatic. If a crisis does not threaten the country’s vital interests, Beijing can use it to strengthen its image as a responsible international player and expand its influence. Moreover, participation in such processes allows China to promote its own vision of international relations and present an alternative to Western approaches to conflict resolution.
When a crisis does not threaten the country’s vital interests, Beijing uses it to strengthen its image as a responsible international player
According to political scientist Rush Doshi, China pursues a long-term strategy in international politics aimed at displacing the United States from the regional and global. Ultimately, Beijing seeks to become the power that shapes the world’s destiny. Similarly, international relations scholar Oriana Skylar Mastro argues that China uses its “agents of chaos” – Iran, Russia, and North Korea – to create problems for the U.S. and its allies. In her view, these actions weaken Washington's power by diverting its attention and resources.
However, China rarely opts for direct confrontation with the West. The logic behind its foreign policy is best described by the Chinese concept of relationality, which contrasts with the emphasis that the Western school of international relations places on the rational calculations of individual states and their national interests. According to relationality proponent Qin Yaqing, China views the world not through the prism of individual countries’ interests but through the relationships that are constantly evolving among the participants in global politics. From the Chinese perspective, relations between states should be maintained despite disagreements. When conflicts arise, they should be contained in order to minimize the damage to those relationships.
Closely linked to relationality is another important concept in Chinese foreign policy: the principle of peaceful coexistence. Formulated by Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai as early as 1954, this principle includes mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, mutual non-aggression, noninterference in internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence.
Beijing invokes these principles when commenting on international conflicts as well. In doing so, China demonstrates its willingness not to intervene directly in other countries’ disputes while at the same time demanding the same treatment for itself. This approach allows it to maintain relations with all sides even in tense situations.
Yet it would be inaccurate to portray Chinese foreign policy exclusively in pacifist terms. Since the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, there have been numerous instances when the principles of respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity, and non-aggression gave way to military force. This was the case, for example, during the invasion of Vietnam in 1979 and the armed clashes with India along the disputed border in 1962. During the Maoist period, Beijing also actively interfered in the internal affairs of other countries, supporting communist insurgencies in the so-called Third World.
After the launch of the reform and opening-up policy in the late 1970s, the Chinese authorities no longer took such overtly adventurous steps, instead favoring gray-zone tactics, economic pressure, and diplomacy. Strategically, if China were to behave the way it alleges the U.S. does, Beijing would lose an important advantage: its image as a restrained and “constructive” player. For this reason, China generally adheres to the fundamental principles of its foreign policy, but it is nevertheless prepared to selectively depart from them when its core interests are threatened.
This combination of factors – the primacy of interests, a focus on relationships, and a desire to play a greater role in global affairs – allows China to take a flexible approach to conflicts. Chinese diplomatic strategy is thus aimed at building the desired type of relations with other countries while strengthening China’s image as a defender of peace. Beijing does not always succeed in this, however, and calls for peace are sometimes replaced by shows of force.
What kind of China are you today?
In responding to different crises, China actively adjusts its role and chooses the strategy it considers most appropriate. These roles can broadly be divided into four types: the coexisting titan, the uncompromising master, the wise judge, and the advocate of “everything good.”
Chinese diplomacy adopts the first role in its relations with the U.S. Although Washington and Beijing are not engaged in an armed conflict, their strategic rivalry is one of the major potential conflicts of the 21st century.
Even under the Biden administration, the U.S. National Security Strategy described China as its main long-term competitor. China, for its part, also acknowledges that its relationship with the United States is the most important in the world and that it needs to be managed carefully to avoid a crisis.
The contentious nature of the relationship stems from the fact that China poses a threat to the U.S. in virtually every key sphere. The rivalry between the two powers encompasses semiconductors, trade, the military sphere, technological development, as well as the struggle for influence around the world.
As a rising great power, China has its own vision of the future world order. In Beijing’s view, the existing international system should not be dismantled but reformed along multipolar lines. In the model of the world order that China openly advocates, it does not seek the emergence of a single hegemon but instead says it wants to create an order based on dialogue. Within this framework, the U.S. still has an important role, but in the long term Beijing hopes to secure Washington’s recognition of a multipolar world, respect for its “red lines,” and fairer competition.
China’s strategy is aimed at preventing open conflict, which is why Xi has consistently advocated building a “new type of great-power relations.” The idea is to acknowledge the differences between the two countries and continue competing while maintaining direct, high-level dialogue in the political and military spheres.
When conflict cannot be avoided, China responds to pressure with symmetrical measures. For example, during the latest tariff war of Donald Trump’s second presidential term, Beijing not only responded to U.S. tariffs with tariffs of its own, but also restricted exports of rare earth minerals. Even amid intense rivalry, the PRC seeks less to gain a decisive advantage than to preserve the status quo by keeping the competition within reasonable limits.
However, when disputes directly affect China’s core interests — territorial integrity, sovereignty, and national security — Beijing’s pragmatism takes a back seat. Geographically, most of these interests are concentrated in East Asia, a region where China expects to become the dominant power.
When it comes to territorial disputes, rhetoric about mutual benefit gives way to assertive and forceful action, as is most clearly evidenced in the case of Taiwan (and the debate over a possible Chinese attempt to forcibly annex the island by 2027). China insists that it does not want an escalation of the conflict over the island, but it is also unwilling to tolerate manifestations of political support for the democratic authorities in Taipei. Rather than openly seeking to alter the status quo in the Taiwan Strait, Beijing actively uses “gray-zone” tactics that include expanding the area of its naval exercises, conducting regular flights by military aircraft, and patrolling the waters around the island. This allows China to deter Taiwan’s allies from becoming involved lest they cross the threshold into direct armed confrontation.
When it comes to territorial disputes, rhetoric about mutual benefit gives way to assertive and forceful action
China responds similarly to other challenges of this kind. For example, Beijing often answers with forceful measures to what it considers unfriendly moves by Japan. In November 2025, when Tokyo's newly appointed Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described a possible attack on Taiwan as an existential threat to Japan itself, China’s reaction was swift. Japan was hit by a barrage of restrictive measures, including the suspension of imports of Japanese seafood and the cancellation of flights. In this way, China demonstrates that any actions it considers to be an infringement on its sovereign interests will be met with the strongest possible response.
China also participates in conflicts as a mediator. This usually occurs in situations where Beijing has significant economic interests, the U.S. has a relatively weak presence, and the risk of being drawn into armed confrontation is minimal. In such circumstances, Beijing seeks to maintain an equidistant position from the conflicting parties while preserving working relations with each side until an agreement is reached.
One notable success of Chinese diplomacy was the normalization of relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023. Thanks to Chinese mediation, on March 10 of that year the two sides signed a joint statement in which they pledged, among other things, to restore diplomatic relations.
It was not by chance that China achieved this success. The PRC buys substantial volumes of oil from both countries and is a particularly important oil export market for Iran. Second, Beijing maintains good relations with both Riyadh and Tehran, whereas the U.S. could not credibly claim the role of a neutral mediator because of its decades-long confrontation with Iran. The combination of these factors enabled China to mediate in a distant conflict while simultaneously strengthening its image as a peace-loving power.
However, the latest escalation of the Middle East conflict – between Iran on one side and the U.S. and Israel on the other – demonstrated the limitations of China’s peacemaking capacity. After the armed conflict in Iran entered a hot phase in late February, China’s Foreign Ministry condemned the actions of the U.S. and Israel and expressed concern over the developments. At the same time, Zhai Jun, the Chinese government’s special envoy for Middle Eastern affairs, engaged in shuttle diplomacy, visiting regional capitals in an attempt to maintain contact with all its partners.
As the conflict dragged on, Beijing again called on the sides to resolve their differences as soon as possible and return to dialogue. The results of China’s 2023 efforts did not go to waste: Iran and Saudi Arabia maintained diplomatic relations despite U.S. strikes against Iran launched from Saudi territory.
In practice, however, this was the extent of China’s role in the conflict. Beijing’s actions demonstrated that Chinese diplomacy can help improve relations only when the parties themselves are willing to do so. In a hot conflict where Beijing lacks coercive tools comparable to those available to Washington, China’s peacemaking efforts prove ineffective.
There is, however, a fourth role China plays in international conflicts, one that has been most clearly manifested in its position on the war in Ukraine. After February 24, 2022, Beijing found itself in a difficult position. On the one hand, its key economic partners in the West expected China to pressure the Kremlin and work to stop the war. On the other hand, there is Russia, which Beijing needs as a counterweight in its strategic confrontation with the West.
To preserve its image as a constructive player, China had to adopt a position that many researchers describe as pro-Russian neutrality. Beijing continued to develop economic ties with Moscow, providing Moscow with dual-use goods and assistance in circumventing some sanctions. Formally, China does not supply Russia with lethal weapons, and in its official statements it continues to emphasize the importance of the principle of respect for territorial integrity – a message aimed at Western audiences. In reality, however, military cooperation with Russia is far broader than officially acknowledged.
At the same time, the war in Ukraine remains fairly remote from China’s vital interests. Although both Russia and Ukraine are important partners for China, it has little reason to intervene directly in the conflict. That is why Beijing’s policy on the issue remains highly abstract. In a peace plan published in February 2023, China called for a ceasefire and the start of negotiations, but offered no concrete measures for ending the war.
This once again shows that Beijing has no desire to act as the world’s policeman, certainly not when it comes to faraway conflicts that have little bearing on its interests. Instead, in such conflicts, China balances between the interests of the various parties, makes peace proposals largely for the sake of appearances, and waits for an opportunity to normalize relations and further develop ties.
China’s involvement in the war between Iran and the U.S. has taken on features broadly similar to its position on the conflict in Ukraine. According to media reports, Beijing is supplying Iran with dual-use goods, intelligence and satellite imagery, and, according to some reports, is also making commercial arms shipments. The Chinese side, however, denies all allegations of any involvement in military operations.
As in the case of Russia, Beijing has no interest in the fall of Iran’s regime – an important oil supplier – and is therefore prepared to support the combat capability of Iranian forces to some extent. However, this assistance is provided in ways that preserve as much room as possible for plausible deniability.
More than just calculation
In practice, Beijing’s involvement in conflicts does not always lead to success. By trying to balance between the opposing sides in the war in Ukraine, China’s close ties with Russia have in one way or another undermined the trust of Western countries. Although China’s peacemaking efforts have produced some successes, they are typically undertaken reluctantly. Meanwhile, attempts to impose its preferred order in the Taiwan Strait or the South China Sea encourage its rivals to strengthen their own military and political coordination with the U.S.
Importantly, China’s strategy in different conflicts is not driven by material gain alone. Whenever fighting breaks out anywhere in the world today, the international community inevitably asks: what will China gain from it? The answer is most often sought in economic or geopolitical terms. However, if Beijing’s main objective truly were to maximize the benefits it derives from other countries’ conflicts, its actions would be far more aggressive.
For example, it would use crises to resolve disputes along its borders by force, or else impose more favorable terms of cooperation on Russia and Iran, both of which are already dependent on China to some extent. Yet this does not happen.
For Beijing, involvement in international conflicts is neither an end in itself nor a means of scoring political points. Moreover, when it comes to conflicts that are distant and have little bearing on its interests, China’s leadership seeks to distance itself by limiting its actions to calls for peace. By playing different roles depending on the situation, China is pursuing broader goals: strengthening its power, pushing for changes to the international order, and turning itself into a recognized center of influence.
China has ambitious goals: to strengthen its power, reshape the international order, and turn itself into a recognized center of power
In the view of China’s ruling elite, the desired global order has several distinctive features. First, there should be no single hegemon in the world, and international relations should be “democratized.” Second, great powers must respect each other’s sovereignty and “red lines,” recognize the legitimacy of different political systems (rather than just liberal democracy), and build relations on the basis of managed competition rather than direct confrontation. Third, in the future world order envisioned by Beijing, greater weight should be given not only to international organizations but also to countries of the Global South.
Judging by the statements and actions of the Chinese leadership, the transition to such an order should take place gradually and relatively smoothly, without immediately undermining the existing system. That is why maximizing the benefits of each individual conflict is not a priority. Instead, China’s strategy continues to put long-term relationships and the protection of its interests first – a foundation whose returns will become evident in the future.

lotus-shaped bamboo roof floats over pablo luna studio’s yoga space in bali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:45:13 UTC
00:45:13 KST

Pablo Luna Studio completes a bamboo pavilion for yoga in Bali whose roof spreads outward to recall a lotus when seen from above. The reference is literal enough to read from the air, while the building feels looser from the ground, where the petal edges extend beyond a circular floor deck and a sparse ring of bamboo supports. Set on a planted slope beside a river, the shala sits slightly above the terrain, with the forest continuing right up to its edge.
The architects began developing Lotus Yoga Shala in 2021 and describes it as one of the first buildings through which the practice explored biomimicry. The broad lotus silhouette was maintained throughout the long development stage, but in its finished form much of the building’s character comes from the dense bamboo work underneath.
Each of Pablo Luna Studio’s ‘lotus petals’ grows from a structural system of petung bamboo that turns the floral outline into the actual construction of the roof. Its primary arches bundle three lengths of petung, while split bamboo forms an interwoven gridshell across them. At the perimeter, loads gather into clusters of three to five bamboo poles. The supports concentrate around these structural junctions, leaving broad openings between them and keeping the edge of the pavilion visually open toward the landscape.
From inside, the roof becomes a dense drawing of crossing bamboo ribs, with woven panels stretched between them to filter daylight. The construction has enough pattern to give the ceiling its own visual weight, even as the floor plate stays simple beneath it. Hoping to preserve the existing contours and limiting contact with the ground, the architects design the raised platform to follow the hillside instead of flattening it.
Pablo Luna Studio shapes a bamboo roof as an array of overlapping lotus petals
the landscape stays inside the room
Conventional walls largely disappear around the practice space, which leaves the roof overhead as its strongest spatial boundary. Views extend toward the river and dense vegetation, while daylight and air move freely through the perimeter. For a pavilion intended for yoga and meditation, that openness gives the building much of its atmosphere before any wellness language enters the picture. The floor and canopy simply frame the surrounding landscape as part of the room.
The lotus gives the shala an easy visual identity, though the more convincing move is how Pablo Luna Studio makes that image structural. The petal outline grows directly from the roof system, and the same curved geometry creates broad shelter with relatively few columns. At 125 square meters, the building remains compact, with most of its presence coming from a canopy that expands far beyond the deck and seems to hover among the vegetation. It is a small pavilion whose roof largely defines its identity.

FIFA has banned three Argentina players, including a 10-match suspension for Leandro Paredes, along with fines against the team and federation for post-final violence and other incidents during the tournament.
FIFA has banned three Argentina players, including a 10-match suspension for midfielder Leandro Paredes, for striking Spain opponents moments after losing the World Cup final.
The ban for Paredes — who grabbed Spain’s Eric Garcia by the throat and pushed Gavi to the ground — ranks alongside the FIFA sanctions for Uruguay forward Luis Suarez in 2014 as among the most severe in World Cup history.
Argentina defender Nahuel Molina was handed a seven-game ban while Thiago Almada was given a one-game suspension. FIFA imposed fines of €76,000 on Paredes and Molina, and €25,000 for Almada.
The ban for Paredes is effectively a one-year expulsion from the Argentina team as the FIFA calendar for national team schedules includes 10 games through June 2027.
All of those games could be friendlies with no competitive games currently scheduled.
Spain’s Gavi also was banned for one game, which is a Nations League match against England at Wembley on 26 September.
Argentina coach Roberto Ayala also got a three-game ban and a €25,000 fine.
The Argentina football federation was fined €94,000 for a range of incidents during the World Cup, including players carrying a political banner about the Falkland Islands after the semifinal win against England, and discriminatory chants by fans.
The federation also was ordered by FIFA to spend €85,500 on anti-racism projects. Argentina received €29 million in World Cup prize money from FIFA.
The Argentina federation can appeal the longer sanctions and fines to FIFA, and likely after at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
In 2014, Suarez was banned from all soccer for four months, including for his new club Barcelona, and eight more competition games for Uruguay for biting Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini in a World Cup group-stage game in Brazil.
The on-field clashes at last month's final — which were charged by FIFA as assault cases — came after Argentina lost a testy final to Spain where it was mostly outplayed and barely created a scoring chance.
Spain forward Ferran Torres scored the only goal of the game in the second period of extra time, after Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez was sent off.

SYKTYVKAR, August 21. /TASS/. Russia is conducting a "surgical operation" as part of its special military operation to avoid harming civilians and civilian infrastructure, TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov told reporters in Syktyvkar during the CIS International Film Festival currently taking place in the Russian northeastern Komi Region.
"When it comes to the special military operation, we are conducting a surgical operation, not a military one. We are afraid of damaging infrastructure used exclusively by civilians, not the military, and we are also afraid - God forbid - of causing completely unjustified civilian casualties. We will continue to act this way up to a certain limit. For those who are currently preparing to fight us, however, the conversation will be entirely different," Kondrashov noted.
He presented the Airport documentary film, which he directed, at the CIS International Film Festival in Syktyvkar. The film provides a detailed account of the first battle for the survival of the Donbass, drawing on archival footage and eyewitness accounts of the events. In particular, it features Donetsk Airport press secretary Dmitry Kosinov, Donetsk physician Andrey Boryak, DPR Hero and Russian presidential envoy in the Ural Federal District Artyom Zhoga, as well as residents of Donetsk.
In 2014, the Prokofiev Donetsk Airport became one of the hotbeds in the conflict between Ukrainian forces and Donbass militias. On May 26, 2014, the last flight departed from the airport, bound for Kiev. Fighting then broke out on the airport grounds and continued until mid-January 2015. The film is available to watch for free on the Russian Smotrim media platform.
The CIS International Film Festival is being held in Komi for the first time on August 17-21. Nearly 30 films from Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan were screened. As part of the festival program, viewers were offered feature-length and short films, both fiction and documentaries, as well as cultural and educational business programs.

‘Islands of biodiversity’ offer hope for recovery after High Fens fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:43:10 UTC
00:43:10 KST

Amid the charred plains of the High Fens, small areas have been largely spared by the fire that has ravaged the nature reserve over the past week. Conservationists have been able to confirm this now that the situation on the ground is under control. These “islands of biodiversity” are important for recovery in the coming years.
‘Islands of biodiversity’ offer hope for recovery after High Fens fire
Over the past week, 3,000 hectares of the High Fens in Liège province have been reduced to ashes by the fire that began on Friday. The impact is enormous, but not everything has been destroyed.
Small pockets of nature have been spared in the affected area. These form when the wind suddenly drives the fire in a different direction. The exact extent of the ecological damage will become clear in the coming weeks and months.
“Based on visual footage alone, it is difficult to form a clear picture of what the real impact is,” says Kris Verheyen, professor of forest ecology and forest management at Ghent University. “One of the things that is difficult to see is how much of the peat has actually been burnt or damaged.”
It is already clear, however, that the affected area is not a uniform whole. Some zones have been severely affected, others less so. The ground is still smouldering in various places, meaning the situation continues to evolve.
Based on visual footage alone, it is difficult to form a clear picture of what the real impact is
According to Verheyen, the fact that some areas have survived could play a key role in the area’s recovery. “If populations of certain species are still present in those areas, then the recolonisation of the burnt areas will be a lot easier,” he says. This applies not only to animals but also to rare plant species.
An iconic species of the High Fens is the extremely rare black grouse. It is doubtful whether that population survived the fire, but a male was found alive by the fire brigade on Thursday.
The exact impact on the fauna and flora will only become clear after extensive field research. Drones and aerial photographs will be used to map the site in detail.
The fact that the area has been severely affected does not mean it will remain black for years. “It will probably turn green again relatively quickly,” says Verheyen. “But that greenery will mainly be dominated by purple moor grass.”
This is a type of grass that is common in heathland and peatland areas and even benefits from large wildfires to spread further. As it is highly flammable, it increases the risk of fire during dry periods.
However, controlling the plant – for example, through grazing – is difficult in such a vast and inaccessible reserve.
“Anyone going for a walk in the High Fens in a few years’ time will, apart from the burnt trees, not notice much of the fire at first glance,” Verheyen says. “If you look more closely at the rarer species and at the peat itself, you will continue to see the traces for a very long time.”

FIFA on Friday fined the Argentine Football Association (AFA) and suspended three of its players and one team official over incidents during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, including a post-match scuffle after the final against Spain.
Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes received the heaviest punishment, with FIFA's Disciplinary Committee handing him a 10-match suspension and a fine of $90,000.
Defender Nahuel Molina was suspended for seven matches and fined the same amount, while midfielder Thiago Almada received a one-match ban and a $30,000 fine.
Argentina team official Roberto Ayala was also suspended for three matches and fined $30,000.
Spain midfielder Gavi received a one-match suspension and a $30,000 fine over his involvement in the incident.
The sanctions followed a confrontation after Spain defeated Argentina in the World Cup final in the US last month.
FIFA also fined the AFA $321,000 over several disciplinary violations during the tournament, including the display of a banner relating to the disputed Falkland Islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, following the semifinal against England.
Of the fine, $100,000 must be invested in an anti-discrimination plan, while another $100,000 has been suspended subject to a probationary period.
Argentina was also ordered to play their next two home matches with stadium capacity limited to 50%.
FIFA said the sanctions related to breaches including “using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature,” discrimination, misconduct and breaches of security regulations.
The governing body said the decisions followed disciplinary proceedings over incidents during the World Cup and were subject to appeal where applicable.

MOSCOW, August 21. /TASS/. Russian authorities have set a goal to optimize maintenance schedules of oil refineries to minimize the risk of supply shortages in the fuel market, the cabinet reported following a meeting chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak.
"The need for an even distribution of available fuel supplies among and within the regions was emphasized. A task was set to optimize planned refinery maintenance schedules to minimize the risk of supply shortages in the market," the report said.
Participants of the meeting discussed the implementation of measures aimed at ensuring sufficient fuel supplies for the domestic market, maintaining fair prices, and increasing transparency in fuel sales across both wholesale and retail segments. "Emphasis was placed on the need for an equitable distribution of available fuel supplies among regions and within them," according to the report.
On July 30, the Russian government imposed a new temporary ban on the export of gasoline, diesel, and other types of fuel, effective until January 31, 2027. The decision was made to maintain stability in the domestic fuel market. The cabinet also suspended the special rules for determining prices in state procurement of motor fuel until the end of 2026. Moreover, the government adopted a resolution aimed at ensuring agricultural producers are supplied with the necessary volumes of motor fuel.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told TASS earlier that Russia had secured sufficient fuel supplies to meet domestic market needs, but a surge in panic buying had driven up demand by around 20-30%, adding that government measures to stabilize the fuel market were yielding results as limits were already being lifted in several regions, with the number of operational filling stations increasing, and queues shortening.

North Korea has sent around 400 drone operators to Russia as part of a new deployment of approximately 8,500 troops that could support attacks on targets inside Ukraine, Maj. Gen. Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR), told CNN on Friday, Aug. 21.
The contingent is deployed primarily in Russia’s Kursk Oblast and includes about 1,000 engineers and deminers, Skibitskyi said.

Many of the drone operators have gained experience through previous North Korean deployments, according to the Ukrainian intelligence official.
Skibitskyi said their drones would likely be used for reconnaissance and attacks against targets inside Ukraine.
North Korean troops could free up Russian forces
Ukrainian intelligence assesses that the newly deployed North Korean troops are not expected to fight directly on Ukrainian territory.
Instead, they are expected to reinforce Russian rear positions, allowing Russian troops currently assigned to those areas to be redirected to assaults along the front, Skibitskyi said.
He said Russia could ask North Korea to provide up to 50,000 additional troops during a potential September meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, rejected Ukrainian claims that Pyongyang planned to send tens of thousands of additional troops to Russia, calling the estimate “groundless” and “a self-staged incident.”
North Korea supplies Russia with ballistic missiles
North Korea is also expanding its military support for Russia through ballistic missile deliveries, Skibitskyi said.
Suspected Russian Handguns Found Near Berlin: German Media
He said North Korea had sent Russia at least 150 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles for use against Ukraine between late 2023 and August 2025 and had promised another 120.
Of that new batch, 40 missiles have reportedly been delivered. Two are believed to have been used during a July 30 Russian strike on Radushne in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast that killed at least four children from the same family, Skibitskyi said.
The deliveries come as Ukraine’s stocks of US-made Patriot interceptors, which are critical for stopping ballistic missiles, have been heavily depleted.
Around 90 North Korean personnel have also been sent to Voronezh to assist with missile launches, Skibitskyi said.
He added that 10 large cargo flights had landed at the Baltimore airfield in the Voronezh area, potentially carrying North Korean missiles.
Newer versions of North Korean missiles reportedly have a range of up to 800 kilometers. However, Skibitskyi said they remain highly inaccurate and can miss their intended targets by between 15 and 19 kilometers.
He said North Korea was using missile launches against Ukraine to improve the accuracy and payload capacity of its weapons.
North Korea seeks Russian air defense technology
In exchange for supplying Russia with troops and weapons, North Korea has sought Russian air defense technology, according to Skibitskyi.
He said Pyongyang had requested Russia’s S-400 air defense system and had already received a Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile system.
Skibitskyi’s assessment suggests that North Korea’s role in Russia’s war effort is expanding beyond conventional troops and ammunition to include drone warfare, missile operations and technical cooperation.
Why North Korean troops are fighting for Russia
North Korea began sending troops to support Russia’s war against Ukraine in October 2024, when its forces were deployed to Russia’s Kursk Oblast to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion.
North Korea officially acknowledged in April 2025 that its soldiers were fighting alongside Russian forces. The initial deployment was estimated at around 10,000 troops, many of whom suffered significant casualties during fighting in Kursk Oblast.
Since then, North Korean troops have continued to be deployed or rotated through Russia. Ukrainian military intelligence estimates that around 25,000 North Korean troops have served in Russia so far, including the latest contingent of approximately 8,500.
The deployment is part of growing military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow under a mutual defense treaty signed in 2024. Ukrainian intelligence says the arrangement gives North Korean troops experience in modern drone warfare while providing Pyongyang with access to Russian military technology.

Egypt asylum shift deepens 'Fortress Europe' concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:39:45 UTC
00:39:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt asylum shift deepens 'Fortress Europe' concerns
Egypt began implementing a new state-run asylum system on Friday, as rights groups warned that the move could deepen the EU's reliance on Cairo to keep refugees and migrants away from Europe's borders despite documented abuses.
Executive regulations for Egypt's 2024 asylum law came into force on 21 August, beginning a transition that will transfer responsibility for registering asylum seekers and determining refugee status from the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) to a government committee under the authority of the prime minister.
The change comes as the EU increasingly relies on Egypt as a key partner in efforts to reduce irregular migration.
his is part of a broader policy of shifting border management beyond Europe's territory that critics have dubbed "Fortress Europe".
Under a strategic partnership agreed in 2024, the EU pledged a €7.4 billion financial package to Egypt up to 2027, including €200 million specifically for migration and mobility.
The funding covers border management, efforts against smuggling and trafficking, returns and reintegration.
Rights groups have repeatedly warned, however, that European migration cooperation with Egypt risks supporting an increasingly securitised system in which refugees and migrants have faced arbitrary arrest, detention, torture, sexual violence and deportation.
Amnesty International documented in 2024 how Egyptian Border Guard Forces, whose capabilities had been supported under an earlier €80 million EU programme, carried out mass arrests of Sudanese refugees and forcibly returned hundreds to Sudan without allowing them to seek asylum or challenge their removal.
Crackdown on refugees
Those concerns have persisted as Egypt has expanded its crackdown on refugees and asylum seekers.
In February, Amnesty documented the arrests of 22 refugees and asylum seekers, including a child and two women, between late December 2025 and early February. Fifteen were registered with UNHCR.
Human Rights Watch reported in July that refugees and asylum seekers, primarily from Sudan and South Sudan, had been subjected to months of arbitrary arrest, detention and deportation, including people with valid UNHCR cards.
Some were being given appointments as late as 2028 to renew residency documents because of government backlogs, HRW said, while remaining vulnerable to arrest for failing to possess valid permits.
The organisation also documented overcrowded detention facilities, inadequate access to food and clean water, physical abuse and racial profiling of sub-Saharan African refugees.
Egyptian authorities do not publish comprehensive figures for refugee arrests or deportations. Egyptian rights organisations cited by Amnesty estimated that between 3,000 and 5,000 refugees and asylum seekers were deported in January and February alone.
More than 1.1 million people were registered with UNHCR in Egypt as of the end of May, up around 275 percent from before the outbreak of Sudan's war in April 2023.
Around 852,000 were Sudanese, whose registered population in Egypt has increased by more than 1,300 percent since the war began. Syrians were the second-largest group, with around 98,000 registered.
The scale of Sudanese displacement has become central to Cairo's argument that Egypt is carrying a heavy economic and social burden requiring greater international support.
Egypt takes control of asylum
But the new asylum regime will also give the Egyptian state significantly greater control over those displaced populations.
For more than seven decades, refugee-status determination in Egypt has been handled by UNHCR under a 1954 agreement. Under the new system, a Permanent Committee for Refugee Affairs will ultimately determine who is recognised as a refugee and who can remain in the country.
The transfer will not happen immediately, with the regulations providing for a transitional period in which existing files and data are handed over and UNHCR continues to play a role.
Refugees Platform in Egypt has nevertheless called for implementation to be suspended, warning before Friday's deadline that there remained insufficient clarity over how responsibilities would be transferred and how international protection would be maintained.
The regulations also require people who entered Egypt irregularly to apply for asylum within 45 days, while rejected applicants can face removal.
Rights organisations have raised concerns over protections against refoulement, the forcible return of people to countries where they face persecution or serious harm, and the new committee's broad powers on national security and public order.
For critics of European migration policy, Egypt's transition illustrates a wider shift in which the EU increasingly seeks to manage migration before people reach its territory.
As Cairo assumes greater power to decide who receives protection and who does not, Europe is simultaneously investing heavily in Egypt's capacity to manage and contain migration before it reaches the Mediterranean.

Iran's president: Time to end war in 'position of strength'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:37:00 UTC
00:37:00 KST

Iran's president: Time to end war in 'position of strength'
August 21, 2026
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday that it would be an opportune moment to seek to end the war with the United States, according to state media reports.
His comments, made at a medical conference, come amid mixed messages both from officials in Tehran and from US President Donald Trump on the conflict. The partial truce agreed in June remains in a seemingly ambiguous state, having expired without progress or renewal on Monday.
Tehran continues to severely limit shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the United States is in turn trying to enforce what it refers to as a blockade of Iran's ports.
Trump this week threatened increased economic pressure on Iran. But how much further the US can turn the screws on one of the world's most heavily sanctioned countries, with which it does almost no business, is unclear.
As Pezeshkian seemingly suggested it might be a good time to negotiate peace, an Iranian military leader threatened "crushing, punishing and devastating responses" if the US did try to isolate Iran further economically.
What did Pezeshkian reportedly say?
According to IRNA's report, Pezeshkian said the war would eventually have to be brought to an end.
"It is better to end it today, as we are in a position of strength and dignity," he said.
"The whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America has attacked our schools, hospitals and infrastructure in violation of all regulations and is hated around the world," Pezeshkian said.
He also argued that the faltering 15-point Memorandum of Understanding signed by Iran and the US in June in no way signaled a defeat for Iran.
"They cannot find even a single clause in this commitment that indicates capitulation," he said. "All the commitments concern the other side."
While most concern the US, a minority of the 15 commitments do put the onus on Iran, although Tehran might argue they only constitute agreeing to return to the situation that existed before the war. The most notable examples would be allowing commercial transit without charge through the Strait of Hormuz, at least temporarily, and Iran reaffirming that it would not procure or develop nuclear weapons.
Pezeshkian also reportedly told the crowd of doctors that "under no circumstances will we bow to intimidation" and that if necessary, Iran would resist "until our last breath."
What US messaging coincides with these comments?
US President Donald Trump, after a few days dominated more by his comments on the Korean Peninsula and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, briefly returned his attention to Iran late on Wednesday.
He threatened what he referred to as the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against another country," feeling the need to write the phrase entirely in capital letters. He also referred to it as an "economic D-Day."
The message did very little to explain how the US planned to further turn the screws on Iran — which has withstood around half a century of US sanctions and does almost no trade with the US — except to say the US would look to stop Iran's trading partners from providing "any type of lifeline to Iran."
Asked to shed more light on the idea in a CNBC interview on Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed it would be the "greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world," and said it would "collapse this regime."
The economic pressure would make "large-scale" military operations unnecessary, he added.
When asked if China, Iran's most important trading partner would be asked to join in, Bessent declined to comment publicly.
What other comments are coming out of Tehran?
Not unlike the volatile US president, Iran is known for its often inconsistent and hyperbolic messaging, frequently combining apparent overtures for peace and threats on the same day or even in the same message.
It's also fairly common for the Tehran regime's political representatives like Pezeshkian and lead negotiator Mohammad Qalibaf to adopt a slightly more diplomatic posture than the military or theocratic leaders.
The chief of Iran's armed forces, Major General Ali Abdollahi, was also asked about the US economic threats on Friday and warned of a broad and decisive military response if necessary.
"With preparedness across land, sea, air, air defense and cyberspace, Iran's armed forces will respond to the enemy's new threats with crushing, punishing and devastating responses," Abdollahi was quoted as saying.
Meanwhile, chief negotiator and parliamentary speaker Qalibaf seemed to voice a similar call to intensify negotiations, claiming that Washington appeared to have concluded it could not prevail in a direct military confrontation.
"We must make plans to deal with the unjust sanctions so we can overcome them," Qalibaf said in neighboring Iraq.

Europe urged to step up mosquito controls as West Nile cases rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:36:40 UTC
00:36:40 KST

Aysu Biçer
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Europe must strengthen its efforts to control mosquitoes as the risk of mosquito-borne diseases increases, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) has warned.
Six European regions have reported locally acquired West Nile virus (WNV) infections for the first time this year. As of Aug. 13, 429 locally acquired cases had been recorded across nine countries.
Transmission usually peaks in August and early September, meaning further cases are expected, the ECDC said.
“The expansion of West Nile virus transmission as well as the spread of invasive mosquito species demonstrate why Europe needs to strengthen its mosquito-control capacity,” said Celine Gossner of the ECDC in a statement on Thursday.
The Asian tiger mosquito, which can spread dengue and chikungunya, is now established in 16 European countries – twice as many as 12 years ago.
An article published by the ECDC and EU partners in the Eurosurveillance journal has called for greater coordination and a wider range of mosquito-control measures.
The ECDC said effective control should combine mosquito and disease monitoring, management of stagnant water, community involvement and targeted measures suited to local conditions.
It also warned that insecticide resistance, environmental concerns and a limited number of authorized products were making mosquito control more difficult.
People can help reduce mosquito numbers by removing or covering stagnant water around homes, while repellents, protective clothing and mosquito-proofing can provide personal protection.
Healthcare professionals have also been urged to remain alert to local transmission and imported infections.

The designer behind the swimwear worn by Israel's top celebrities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:34:55 UTC
00:34:55 KST

When Oria Azran approached Odelia Ozel, 50, and asked her to design swimwear for an upcoming vacation in Thailand, Ozel had no idea how dramatically it would change her life.
"That was my big breakthrough, and it happened eight years ago," she says. "A mutual friend introduced us and Oria was about to leave for two weeks in Thailand. I made her an entire collection for the trip, eight or 10 swimsuits. I stopped working and focused only on her. I had expenses, but I knew it would come back to me. The people close to me didn't believe it would pay off, but they had to eat their words. She left, posted her first picture and tagged me. I woke up in the morning, opened my phone and saw a flood of new followers and tons of messages from girls who wanted to come and buy. It was amazing."
Ozel's namesake brand has become a household name among women who love swimwear and are willing to pay for it. Celebrities including Einav Booblil, Natali Dadon, Mor Silver, Romi Geyor and Frida Oziel already wear the brand. She has a large store in the Neve Tzedek area and an online store where women order swimsuits costing thousands of shekels.
"If it's a swimsuit that's not basic, and most of mine aren't, the price range is 800 to 1,400 shekels," she says. "A lot of women don't order just one but several, and they always get the matching beachwear as well."
'I designed, photographed, posted. That's it'
She was born in Bat Yam and grew up in Be'er Yaakov to a stay-at-home mother and a father who owned a large sewing workshop named after her. At its peak, Odelia Sewing employed 30 seamstresses and for years produced clothing for the country's major men's brands. When imports from China opened up, her father went bankrupt, closed the workshop and opened men's fashion stores specializing in large sizes.
"That must be in my DNA, because during all the long school vacations I worked for him. I would remove threads from the collars of men's shirts."
At first, she had no intention of following in her father's footsteps. She joined the Coca-Cola factory immediately after her military service and worked there for 20 years as a sales manager.
"I knew it wasn't my calling, but I was already a mother at 21, and it was a steady salary and a very protective environment."
At 36, however, the urge was already in her bones, and she dreamed about swimwear at night.
"I personally don't even like swimwear. I don't have a swimsuit body and I'm not the bombshell who wants to dress up for pool parties. But it was really stuck in my head. One day after work, with only a few percent battery left on my phone, I decided I was going to do it. When I was in the car, I googled 'swimwear seamstress' and drove to her. I don't know why it drew me in, but I knew I could do it and do it better than everyone else. I went to this seamstress, who had worked at Gottex for years. By coincidence, Neta Alchimister and Noa Beny from Bananhot arrived there at the same time as I did. We started that very week. We met in her living room and they told me they were new, too."
She started with a few designs and posted them on Instagram. She named the brand ODELIA OZEL and set out on her journey.
"I had 100 followers then — family and friends, that's it. I photographed the pieces on a wooden table I have on my balcony, which I call 'my blessing table,' and suddenly I started getting phone calls. One from Haifa, one from Be'er Sheva. I didn't understand where it was coming from. I didn't invest in advertising, I didn't run paid campaigns and I didn't buy followers. The simplest thing: I designed, photographed, posted. That's it."
Her romantic life had not been particularly successful. She divorced at 27 after seven years of marriage and two children, Lian, 28, who until recently worked with her in the business, and Tal, 23, who owns a cleaning company. With her second partner, whom she met at 30 and with whom she has two daughters, Sharon, 12, and Shai Li, 10, she experienced many difficulties over a decade. She does not want to go into details, saying only that "after 10 years together, I realized it was holding me back, and we separated. He went on with his life and I went on with mine. What's important is that I have two amazing girls with him."
So you built the entire business while also dealing with a complicated situation at home?
"Yes, and it wasn't easy, but to his credit, he believed in me. When he saw it was succeeding, he told me, 'Go for it,' and encouraged me to keep going. I worked at Coca-Cola during the day and designed at night. I lived like that for seven years. The business was as important to me as my children. I was completely relentless. When people would go out at night, I would drive to the seamstress with a new design. That was my happiness. During my lunch break at work, I would drive to Nahalat Binyamin to buy fabrics, and at 6 p.m., when I got home, a group of women would be waiting for me downstairs. I would receive them in an empty room at home and also do custom sewing for them, take their measurements and design according to their size — which was a nightmare. Until I realized it wasn't bridal gowns and moved to collections."
When did you decide to leave your salaried job and take the plunge?
"At 42. I was making 10,000 shekels a month at Coca-Cola and working really hard, and one evening the saleswoman at the store called and said, 'We finished the day with 10,000 shekels in sales.' I said to myself, 'What, are you a masochist? Come on, quit.' The numbers just didn't make sense anymore. Of course it's scary. In fashion, everything isn't always perfect. Suddenly there are problems with sewing workshops, suddenly there's a collection that doesn't do so well. But my belief in myself is so strong that I really never let it bring me down. So, I took a small bank loan and kept going."
Tell us a little about your close relationship with celebrities.
"Oria and I have become good friends. Since that first time, I dress her for every trip and she helps me fine-tune my work. Even though she's two decades younger than me, she's really smart and has an incredible eye. I learn from her. For example, if she's going to Tulum in Mexico, I stop everything, go to the flea market, look for 'Tulum vibes' inspiration and we actually design together. In my opinion, Oria is the person who dresses and carries clothes better than anyone in Israel, and so many girls want to dress like her. I think everyone has worn my designs except Bar Refaeli."
Do they pay?
"Of course I don't give everything away for free. I also know how to identify which of the bloggers and influencers who approach me are bogus, the ones with fake followers. I can spot it in a second. By the way, sometimes a customer who's not a celebrity brings me tons of customers because the swimsuit looks so good on her."
What sets you apart?
"I make the most beautiful, highest-quality swimwear in Israel, and the difference between me and the other two major players, Shani Shemer and Bananhot, is that I don't have an army behind me. Everything is thanks to my taste and the quality I provide. I make the craziest swimwear and I feel like I'm setting the fashion trends. I'm the first and everyone copies me. But not Shani Shemer and Bananhot — we have an unwritten agreement that we don't copy each other's designs."
What do you mean by crazy swimwear?
"I'm the first to make swimwear from real denim, because I like challenging myself and I don't hold back. I took apart jeans and washed them so the denim would have those worn-in wash marks. It's extremely complicated to make swimwear from this fabric, almost impossible, but I made an entire collection. I also make a lot of crochet swimwear. Today I have it made abroad by a specialist, but I used to buy very expensive tablecloths and take them apart. I make swimwear from real leather and lace. Right now I have a swimsuit covered entirely in gemstones that I made in Italy and it cost me a fortune. I go wild. Regular Lycra with four threads doesn't interest me. I make fashion, not swimwear. My customers travel to Mykonos and Ibiza and people chase after them asking where they got it."
And women don't think twice about spending 1,000 shekels on a swimsuit?
"Even more. I had a collection of bandanas printed on sequins. A swimsuit from that collection cost 1,300 shekels and I sold out the entire collection within five hours. I always make matching beachwear for the collection, such as jeans and sarongs, so women leave here having spent 2,500 shekels on a swimsuit plus beachwear, and they're happy. There are lots of Israelis living abroad who shop from me online. This week I had a 4,500-shekel order from Mexico from someone who isn't Jewish or anything. Who's addicted to swimwear? The hot girls who have great bodies. If I had a great body, I'd be addicted too, but where would I wear it? I've had four C-sections. They're crazy about swimwear. I have customers who bought my entire collection this year, more than 10 designs. Sometimes I have to stop them — young women come into the store and go crazy. I tell a customer, 'Wait, you haven't even worn the one you bought last time.'"
Do you still manufacture in Israel?
"Yes, but not only, because you can count the swimwear sewing workshops here on one hand. I used to manufacture in Turkey before we had our falling-out with Erdoğan, and now I manufacture in Italy. I travel to lots of fabric trade shows in Paris, Nice and Milan looking for something special, something that makes you say "wow". I was at a swimwear trade show in Paris this year, walked between the booths and simply realized that I was beating all of them."
Are your daughters proud of you?
"Very much. My oldest, Lian, became more religious after Oct. 7, so unfortunately she no longer works with me in the business. Half the country became more religious after what happened, and swimwear isn't modest, so she left. But I very much hope she'll come back one day.
"My younger girls are very independent. They order themselves food on Wolt and can cook on their own. Now that they've grown up, I feel more liberated. I can fly to a trade show and even take an extra day off. There were years when it was really hard for me. I ran the store by myself, and at 8 p.m. I'd put two little girls in pajamas in the car after their showers and drive to the sewing workshop in Ashkelon or the laundry in Rosh HaAyin. Only now have I started cutting myself some slack and allowing myself to hire a delivery person."
So what are your next dreams?
"Abroad. I'd like someone to recognize the potential because I could make a lot, a lot of money abroad. So I want an investor to come along and take me to the sky there. But I'm also good here. There's never a dull moment. I work from 8 a.m. until midnight and I'm succeeding, and that's the best feeling there is."

Syria is working to identify and prosecute Assad-era officials responsible for a 2013 chemical weapons attack that killed more than 1,400 people, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said Friday.
In a statement marking the 13th anniversary of the attack on Eastern Ghouta and Moadamiyeh in the Damascus countryside, al-Shibani said Damascus was pursuing those involved in the attacks with the aim of bringing them to trial.
Syria, he added, was also taking practical steps to address the country’s legacy of chemical weapons in cooperation with international partners.
“Syria continues working to identify those responsible for the chemical weapons massacres, holding them accountable, and bringing them to justice,” al-Shibani said, adding that the process would be carried out in accordance with the law.

Every year on Aug. 21, Syrians commemorate the massacre, saying it will never be erased from their memory and demanding accountability for those responsible.

According to the Syrian Network for Human Rights, the Assad regime carried out 217 chemical weapons attacks against residential areas under opposition control after the revolution erupted in 2011.
Syrian revolutionaries led by Ahmad al-Sharaa -- who now serves as the country’s president -- toppled the Assad regime in late 2024, ending the Assad family’s decades-long rule.
