Federal appeals court halts ruling allowing thousands of college players extra year of eligibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

NCAA gets win in court on 5-year eligibility rule, but this is hardly the end of the lawsuits
DENVER (AP) — The NCAA notched an important win in federal court Friday over its much-disputed five-year eligibility rule, though it fell short of shutting down the last-minute shuffling threatening to upend college sports rosters with football season fast approaching.
A 2-1 decision by a panel of the U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals halted, for now, a judge’s order that would have granted thousands of athletes an extra season of eligibility. But it did nothing to resolve dozens of other lawsuits and court orders piling up across the country that allow players in the same situation to join teams for the upcoming season.
Virtually all these lawsuits involve players who graduated from high school in 2022, whose college eligibility ended last season and who were not included in the NCAA’s controversial new rule — less than two months old — that grants most Division I athletes five years of eligibility over five years but doesn’t take effect until next season.
“There’s a reason we saw so many state-court lawsuits filed” after the now-paused federal court ruling that came down July 31, said Sam Ehrlich, a former lawyer who now works at Boise State and operates the College Sports Litigation Tracker. “It was a ‘just in case.’ They did it just in case what we just saw happen actually happened.”
Among the many athletes watching this unfold and wondering where it winds up are defensive linemen Kellan Wyatt and Stephan Daley, both members of the national championship team at Indiana last season who decided to return after the lower-court decision. So are former Ole Miss starters Dae’Quan Wright, Zxavian Harris and Wydett Williams, who won a ruling from a Louisiana state court giving them another season of eligibility even though they had signed with NFL teams this summer.
While some players hope to land back at their schools, whatever the impact on the rosters, how that works isn’t at all clear in many cases. The judge in the case involving the Ole Miss players, for example, gave them a week to enter the transfer portal, which for football players is only open in January.
In appealing the state court cases, the NCAA is expected to invoke parts of Friday’s ruling, which agreed with NCAA arguments that it was likely to win the case when it’s heard in full — probably several months from now — and that the NCAA would suffer more harm than the players if the court didn’t pause the order.
The NCAA can also take heart in an Ohio appeals court that paused a similar injunction involving Xavier basketball Filip Borovicanin and others.
But other than those two cases, Ehrlich said, judges across the country “are unanimous that the NCAA is in the wrong” on the five-year eligibility issue when it comes to the Class of 2022.
Plaintiffs’ attorney Rob Shelquist issued a statement calling the appeals court ruling procedural and “not a decision on the merits of the athletes’ antitrust claims.”
“We are exploring every available option given the split in the panel’s ruling and remain committed to fighting for these college athletes whose opportunities and eligibility have been unfairly restricted,” he said.
The NCAA’s chief legal officer, Scott Bearby, sent a memo to schools telling them they would not be subject to NCAA punishment for allowing any player to compete between the time the July 31 ruling came down and Friday. But he reiterated that those players are no longer eligible.
Bearby also acknowledged that the NCAA would continue to defend lawsuits around the country — a signal that the NCAA knows Friday’s ruling offers no guarantees of an end to the roster chaos.
“If anything, I do wonder if there’s a part of the NCAA that’s, like, ‘Maybe we’d have been better off not getting the stay because, boy, there’s going to be a lot of lawsuits filed over the next couple of weeks,’” Ehrlich said.
Courts that go beyond filing emergency injunctions and take up the cases in their entirety will have to decide who suffers more harm: Is it players who can’t play a fifth year and could lose educational and NIL opportunities? Or incoming freshmen who signed with the idea that they wouldn’t be competing against a class of fifth-year seniors?
When the NCAA decided to have the rule kick in next year, it also grappled with that calculation, knowing it couldn’t be perfectly fair.
“Fairness is in the eye of the beholder,” the NCAA argued in its legal brief in the appeals case. “Countless student-athletes already on campuses, and schools who built their rosters in reliance on the rules the NCAA’s membership wrote and agreed to follow, do not believe it is fair for thousands of formerly ineligible athletes to return to competition at the start of the 2026–27 season.”

Court slashes $50M judgment against Infowars’ Alex Jones over falsely calling school shooting a hoax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

Court cuts $50M judgment against Infowars’ Alex Jones over falsely labeling Newtown killings a hoax
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A Texas court on Friday slashed a $50 million judgment that conspiracy theorist Alex Jones was ordered to pay families of the 2012 Sandy Hook Elementary School massacre over his false claims that one of the deadliest mass shootings in U.S. history was a hoax.
The Infowars founder can only be forced to pay about $6 million, the Texas Third Court of Appeals ruled in a unanimous opinion, citing state laws that limit lawsuit damages.
The ruling does not affect a separate $1.25 billion judgment against Jones in Connecticut, where he was also found liable for defaming and causing emotional distress to relatives of the 20 first-graders and six educators killed in the Newtown shooting.
The punishing financial verdicts against Jones and his company, Free Speech Systems, in recent years have forced him into bankruptcy, led to some of his personal property being put up for auction and led to him leaving his Infowars platform. For decades, he used the platform to push conspiracy theories about the United Nations, the federal government, gun control and more.
Sandy Hook families have yet to collect any money from Jones, who has waged lengthy appeals in state and bankruptcy courts as his company faces liquidation. He remains on air after moving onto new websites and streaming platforms.
Friday’s ruling did not throw out the trial court’s finding of defamation against Jones. Still, he called it “a gigantic victory for the First Amendment,” and said he will continue to appeal the case to the state Supreme Court to get the remaining damages thrown out.
“I got lawyers who are good constitutional lawyers and they are not backing down,” Jones said.
Jones has already tried to appeal the Connecticut judgment to the U.S. Supreme Court but was denied last year.
The decision by the Texas Third Court of Appeals left intact more than $4.1 million in compensatory damages awarded by a jury to Sandy Hook parents Neil Heslin and Scarlett Lewis for defamation and emotional distress. But it slashed more than $45 million in additional punitive damages down to $1.5 million to comply with the state’s $750,000 cap for each plaintiff.
The court found Heslin and Lewis did not show evidence that the harassment following Jones’ hoax claims rose to a level that would allow them to exceed the cap. It also said the trial judge improperly allowed the parents to seek higher damages after trial.
Mark Bankston, an attorney for Heslin and Lewis in the Texas lawsuit, shrugged off the appeals court ruling as “irrelevant” given that Jones still faces massive financial judgments in Connecticut.
“The families care not at all about this irrelevant ruling which affects only two of the 19 claims they all share. Jones still faces over a billion dollars of liability, so this changes absolutely nothing. All it does is highlight the absurdity of Texas law,” Bankston said.
Newtown families harassed as Jones claimed the massacre was a hoax
Heslin and Lewis’s 6-year-old son Jesse Lewis was among those killed in the Sandy Hook attack. Their lawsuit against Jones and the 2022 verdict marked the first time he was held financially liable for peddling lies about the massacre, claiming it was faked by the government to tighten gun laws.
Jones portrayed the lawsuit as an attack on his First Amendment rights, but conceded during the trial that the shootings were “100% real” and that he was wrong to have lied about them.
At the Texas and Connecticut trials, victims’ relatives testified that Jones’ followers -- believing his claims that the shooting didn’t happen -- subjected them to death and rape threats, in-person harassment and abusive comments on social media. Jones argued there was no proof that linked him to those actions.
Heslin and Lewis told jurors that an apology wouldn’t suffice and initially called on them to make Jones pay more than $150 million for the years of suffering he has put them and other Sandy Hook families through.
Almost immediately after the punitive damages in Texas were announced, Jones’ trial attorney predicted the award would be reduced to $1.5 million on appeal.
Christopher Mattei, a lawyer for the Sandy Hook families in the Connecticut lawsuit, said Friday’s ruling has no bearing on the ongoing lower court proceedings in Texas involving the liquidation of Infowars’ parent company.
The Onion steps in to mock Jones and help frustrated families
Jones and his company have filed for bankruptcy, and those legal proceedings continue. The satirical website The Onion also moved to take over Jones’ Infowars platforms and turn his bullhorn of conspiracy theories into parody sites.
Jones took Infowars off the air in April and moved to a new location, switching his shows to new websites and posting them on his personal X account. The Onion, meanwhile, has set up its own Infowars webpage on its website, running videos of shows parodying Jones.
A proposed licensing deal that would give The Onion temporary authority to use Infowars’ trademarks, copyrights and intellectual property has been put on hold because the liquidation proceedings have been stayed during Jones’ appeals.
In November 2024, the Chicago-based satirical outlet was named the winner of a bankruptcy court auction of the assets of Infowars’ parent company, Free Speech Systems, aimed at helping pay some of the defamation judgments. A federal judge overturned the auction results, citing problems with the process and The Onion’s bid.

Israel will investigate Hind Rajab’s death. Her mother wants more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

Israel will investigate Hind Rajab’s killing. Her mother wants more
JERUSALEM (AP) — The mother of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed after Israeli forces fired on her family’s car in Gaza City wants an independent inquiry into her death, saying an Israeli military investigation announced this week is insufficient.
Wesam Hamada said her daughter Hind Rajab’s final pleas still haunt her.
“All I remember is her voice pleading, ‘Mama, I’m scared. Mama, I’m hungry. Mama, I’m hurt,’” she said. “Her voice keeps repeating in my ears.”
The widely publicized recording of Hind’s January 2024 phone call with her mother and emergency dispatchers made her one of the Israel-Hamas war’s most prominent casualties.
Israel’s military this week admitted to firing at the family’s car as it fled an Israeli invasion and firing toward an ambulance dispatched to help them.
It said it would launch a criminal investigation into its troops’ conduct. All six people in the car and two paramedics were killed. But both Rajab’s family and emergency responders from the Palestinian Red Crescent Society doubt the Israeli investigation can deliver justice.
“Why did the investigation and the acknowledgment of the shooting at Hind’s car and at the paramedics come only after more than two years?” Hamada said in an interview with The Associated Press. “It’s an attempt to distract from what’s happening in Gaza and improve the (Israeli) army’s image to the world. That’s it.”
A call to paramedics that was heard around the world
The story of their deaths drew international outcry after the Palestinian Red Crescent Society released recordings of Hind and her 15-year-old cousin Layan Hamada calling for help. It was further amplified by “The Voice of Hind Rajab,” a film that excerpted the recordings and was nominated for an Oscar.
On the recordings, as audible gunfire erupts around them, Hamada asks for help and tells Red Crescent dispatchers that her family had been killed. Seconds later, more gunshots are heard, and Layan’s screaming stops.
Ambulance dispatchers called back and found Hind on the other end of the line. She told them Layan was dead and Israeli tanks were advancing. The Red Crescent sent an ambulance and stayed in contact with Hind until the call dropped.
Hind and five relatives were found dead in the family car 12 days later. The two medics sent to rescue her were also found dead nearby, their ambulance blackened and destroyed.
Israel initially said its troops were not in the area. A U.N. commission of inquiry and an investigation by the research group Forensic Architecture found evidence placing Israeli forces near the car and attributed the attack to them.
Rana Al Faqih, a dispatcher who was in contact with Hind for more than three hours, said the day remains seared in her memory. She tried to calm Hind and eventually patched her mother onto the call.
“I couldn’t physically reach Hind, embrace her or help her feel safe,” she said in an interview at the Red Crescent headquarters in Ramallah, West Bank. “All I had was my voice. My voice was with her, and it might have comforted her.”
Advocates doubt an Israeli investigation can bring accountability
The investigation is one of two criminal probes the military announced Wednesday after reviewing roughly 150 incidents.
Military investigators will now take up the probes and present their findings to military prosecutors. The military advocate general can then decide to keep investigating, indict any soldiers or decline to charge them.
Israeli officials say the country’s justice system can address any violations by its troops. But such investigations rarely lead to indictments. Just 0.17% of incidents reviewed from 2014 and 2022 led to prosecution, according to an analysis by Israeli rights group Yesh Din.
The Belgium-based Hind Rajab Foundation — which campaigns for the arrest of Israeli troops it accuses of war crimes — said in a statement on Wednesday that an Israeli military investigation “should not be mistaken for a genuine step toward justice.”
“Israel’s internal investigations into the criminal conduct of its own soldiers are fundamentally flawed and cannot be regarded as credible mechanisms of accountability,” it said.
A mother says her grief is not unique
The Israel-Hamas war began on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, in southern Israel and abducted 251 others. More than 73,400 people have been killed in the Israeli offensive since, according to the health ministry in Gaza.
The ministry, part of the Hamas-led government, does not give a breakdown of civilians and militants but says women and children constitute about half the deaths.
Hamada said her pain since the killing of Hind — who had wanted to become a doctor — was not unique.
“The pain is like the pain of every mother who has lost her child in Gaza,” she said. “You wish she were in front of you, growing up and fulfilling your dreams and her dreams, and then you lose her in the most horrific circumstances.”

Türkiye and 11 other countries on Friday strongly condemned this week's Israeli airstrikes targeting the Abu al-Duhur military airbase in northwestern Syria, calling the attacks an "extreme escalation" and a violation of the country's sovereignty.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Türkiye, Algeria, Indonesia, Jordan, Lebanon, Malaysia, Mauritania, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Somalia said the strikes constituted "a flagrant violation of the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political unity" of Syria.
The ministers expressed deep concern over the continued targeting and degradation of Syrian territory and infrastructure, warning that such actions risk undermining efforts to restore security, rebuild national institutions and address the humanitarian consequences of years of conflict.
They also warned that continued Israeli violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity risk further escalating tensions, undermining regional peace and stability and eroding respect for international law and the principles of the UN Charter.
The ministers called on the international community to take a "firm, clear and principled position" against continued attacks on Syria and to take concrete steps in line with international law and the UN Charter to end the violations.
They urged full respect for the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from areas they have occupied, saying such steps are necessary to prevent further escalation and protect regional peace and stability.
The ministers reaffirmed the need to respect Syria's sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and political unity and rejected any attempt to undermine them.

People-to-people ties ‘core strength’ of India-Russia relations – envoy
People-to-people ties between India and Russia have been one of the core strengths of the relationship, Indian Ambassador to Moscow Vinay Kumar said at the four-day annual ‘India Day 2026’ festival in central Moscow.
The event, which started Thursday, is a major crowd puller that brings together hundreds of artists and artisans. Last year, over 2 million people attended.
“With technology and the creative economy, all of this is gaining more ground,” Kumar said.
He cited the countries’ cooperation in culture, academies, dance, drama, and music, and noted the “great enthusiasm” of the crowd. “On a working day, thousands of people enjoy Indian music… and see the vibrancy it generates.”
Addressing the burgeoning cooperation between the two nations, the envoy highlighted some of the key drivers they are focusing on to achieve their $100 billion bilateral trade target, which was set when Russian President Vladimir Putin visited New Delhi in December.

How a desperate Netanyahu is trying to project Türkiye as a security threat in poll-bound Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:14:28 UTC
00:14:28 KST

The already tense relations between Tel Aviv and Ankara hit a new low earlier this week when Israel attacked the Abu al-Duhur Military Airbase in Syria’s Idlib province.
The aerial strikes resulted in no casualties, even though they reduced the runway and storage facilities to rubble.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed the strike stopped Syria from allowing Turkish troops to deploy at the base, asserting that such a move would breach the security status quo.
Netanyahu also warned Türkiye against a military buildup that “descends south because it threatens us”.
Türkiye strongly condemned the attack, stating that Israel continues to target Syria’s infrastructure and capabilities, while undermining the country’s territorial integrity and unity.
Ankara also called on the international community to adopt a more resolute stance to end Israel’s aggression against Syria. Washington joined Türkiye in criticising the attacks, with US envoy to Syria Tom Barrack describing the Israeli attacks as “unnecessary escalation” that hurt regional stability.
Experts say Israeli aggression in Syria is a calculated attempt by Netanyahu to invent a Turkish security threat for domestic political gain.
Israel will hold elections in October. Already the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history, Netanyahu is fighting for his political survival – a fact reflected by his poor showing in pre-election public polls.
Israel’s rhetoric and actions risk broader confrontation with Ankara, a NATO member, that possesses military capabilities far superior to those of the rest of regional actors, analysts say.
Gokhan Batu, a Levant studies analyst at the Ankara-based Centre for Middle Eastern Studies, tells TRT World that Netanyahu has mounted an “open challenge to Türkiye’s influence” by attacking the Abu al-Duhur Military Airbase.
He says that the region and wider world are going through a period of transition amid Washington’s reluctance to remain the sole security provider.
Analysts say Netanyahu’s multiple wars across the region are part of a well-thought-out plan to bolster his chances of winning the forthcoming national elections that he is widely expected to lose.
Former Israeli premier Ehud Barak called out Netanyahu for “deliberate” escalation of tensions with Türkiye, calling the move “reckless and stupid”.
“It strongly reeks of a political motive to go into elections with a string of security tensions that would fuel public anxiety,” Barak was quoted as saying.
Similarly, opposition leader Yair Golan criticised Netanyahu for his “provocative and dangerous” decision to hit Syria.
“Military force is once again being used for political considerations,” he said, while calling Netanyahu an “extremist and unreliable” politician.
Türkiye military might: A threat to hegemon
Coming shortly after the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement – a pact between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan based on collective deterrence – the timing of the Israeli strikes is “significant”, according to Batu.
“Israel wants to signal that the (Mecca) agreement will not deter it,” he says.
Tel Aviv is “deeply unhappy” that Saudi Arabia, with which Israel has sought to normalise relations for many years, has also joined the alliance.
Türkiye has long maintained a military presence in Syria. In northern Syria, Türkiye has carried out a series of successful anti-terror operations since 2016 to prevent the establishment of a terror corridor and ensure the peaceful settlement of residents.
Since the December 2024 revolution that toppled the dictatorial Assad regime, the situation in Syria has developed “in a direction very different” from what Israel envisaged, Batu says.
Israel’s initial response challenged the legitimacy of the new government and fuelled instability. Washington’s rapprochement with Damascus, together with US efforts to limit Israeli action, is pushing Israel to find new justifications for intervention, he adds.
“Its stated justification of protecting minorities has become even less credible, particularly after stability was established in the north and different ethnic groups were integrated into the government and armed forces,” he says.
Following the fall of the Baathist regime, Israel does not want a political and security order with much stronger popular support than its predecessor to consolidate on its northern frontier, Batu says.
“It claims to view this emerging order’s close ties with Türkiye as a threat. Israel is aware that this claim is not supported by evidence, but it needs pretexts to weaken the new structure to its north,” he says.
Türkiye’s military-industrial strength further complicates Israel’s calculations.
Ankara is already the world’s largest producer of military drones. The process which gained momentum after 2015 with cost-effective and capable platforms such as the Bayraktar TB2, has expanded to include the Bayraktar Kizilelma and Turkish Aerospace’s ANKA III, with air-to-air engagement capabilities.
The indigenous fifth-generation KAAN fighter jet is also expected to enter service gradually from 2029.
“This gives Türkiye the potential to become the region’s leading air power and would confront Israel with a regional reality it has never experienced before,” Batu says.
Suggestions of outright armed conflict are not entirely without basis, he adds.
Ankara as ‘cooperative power’
Israeli strikes in Syria have also become a “reputational problem” for Türkiye, Batu says.
So far, Ankara has reacted with restraint. But it may become “increasingly difficult” for Ankara to maintain its restraint in response to continued Israeli aggression, Batu says.
Selcuk Aydin, an assistant professor at Bogazici University, says Israel’s growing anti-Türkiye stance is clearly an attempt to shore up electoral support ahead of October elections.
“Israel’s anti-Türkiye rhetoric traces back very much to the Israeli election process,” he tells TRT World.
He says the Israeli attacks in Syria appear to send a clear message to Ankara. But Türkiye is different from Iran: As a NATO ally, Türkiye has a strong defence industry and a joint defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, he says.
Netanyahu-led Israel seeks to establish hegemony and exert influence over regional politics, primarily through security-driven policies aimed at maintaining dominance, he notes.
In contrast, Türkiye’s approach in the Middle East is not solely focused on defence and security. It is deeply rooted in historical, cultural, religious, and economic cooperation, Aydin says.
Türkiye positions itself as a “cooperative power” rather than a dominant one, focusing on economic strength and stability rather than hegemony.
The two approaches are in direct conflict in the Middle East, he says.
“But I do not expect any kind of (full-on) security clash between the two countries,” he says.
Aydin also notes that recent tensions between Türkiye and Greece, along with Greece’s reactionary policies, are closely linked to Greece’s relations with Israel.
While Israel may not openly confront Türkiye, it is strengthening its alliance with Greece against Ankara and its regional challengers, including Greek-administered Cyprus, he says.
According to Batu, the Abu al-Duhur strikes have fuelled claims that the operation was partly intended to boost Netanyahu’s popularity and capitalise on public security concerns ahead of the election.
But given Türkiye’s military capabilities, what began as an electoral manoeuvre by Netanyahu could turn into political suicide, he warns.
“Türkiye is simply not a country against which military risks can safely be taken for electoral gain. The stakes are too high,” he says.

Lukoil’s Perm refinery struck 1,530 km from Ukraine’s northern border, Kyiv confirms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:14:19 UTC
00:14:19 KST

Ukraine struck one of Russia's largest oil refineries deep in the Urals and a military airfield overnight in a long-range attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on 21 August. The Ukrainian Army's General Staff confirmed the refinery and airfield hits, while Zelenskyy said the same night also reached the Black Sea and brought fresh damage from earlier strikes on a Russian warplane and a drone-launch site.
Fire at a major Lukoil refinery in Perm
Zelenskyy said the overnight drones hit the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez refinery — known as PNOS — in Perm, where the General Staff recorded a fire on the plant's grounds. The target sits more than 1,500 km from Ukraine's northern border, in a region near the Ural Mountains.
The refinery is one of Russia's largest, able to process more than 13 million tons of crude a year, with more than half its output sold abroad until recently. It supplies fuel to both Russia's economy and its army.
Ukrainian Telegram channels Supernova+ and Exilenova+ shared footage of explosions and a rising plume, with locals reporting a series of blasts at the site. Russia's Perm Krai authorities claimed they repelled the attack and downed 16 drones.
Kyiv has repeatedly hit the plant through the year. After a strike at the end of July, it had been running well below capacity.
Airfield, Black Sea, and other targets the same night
The General Staff said the same night's drones also struck the Marinovka military airfield in Volgograd Oblast, located in Russia's Volga region, with the damage still being assessed, while Zelenskyy added that Ukraine achieved unspecified results in the Black Sea. The military also reported hitting a drone storage and launch site near Donetsk, a materiel warehouse in occupied Crimea, two command posts in Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, and six relay stations in Crimea used to steer Russia's Geran and Gerbera attack drones.
Zelenskyy also confirmed damage from earlier strikes: a Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber hit at the Akhtubinsk airfield, about 600 km from the front line, and a drone store and launch site struck at Primorsko-Akhtarsk, roughly 180 km away. The strike extends a run of deep hits this month, from the TANECO refinery in Tatarstan and a Black Sea oil terminal to three refineries hit in one night and an Omsk refinery struck 2,500 km away in Siberia.

OPINION - Israeli architecture of dehumanization: Ashes in Lebanon, crocodiles in the Negev
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:14:15 UTC
00:14:15 KST

Raed Mohammed Mahmood Amer is president of the Palestinian Prisoners Association.
What connects the burning of southern Lebanon’s forests and olive groves to a plan to surround Palestinian political prisoners with crocodiles? At first glance, almost nothing. One is environmental destruction, the other is an absurd and grotesque so-called “prison security” scheme. But together they expose something deeper about Israeli policies: a conception of power in which land, nature, and human beings can all be reduced to obstacles to be removed, controlled, or punished. The question is not simply why the Israeli occupation burns land that has already been emptied. The more important question is what such destruction is intended to accomplish.
In southern Lebanon, forests and agricultural fields have repeatedly been set ablaze during Israel’s military operations. Human Rights Watch has documented Israel’s use of white phosphorus in populated areas of southern Lebanon, warning that such attacks can ignite homes, agricultural areas, and other civilian objects and may constitute unlawful, indiscriminate attacks. Lebanese government and scientific assessments have documented thousands of hectares of damaged or burned woodland and agricultural land, including tens of thousands of olive trees.
If civilians have been driven from their homes, villages have been emptied, and the territory has been brought under military control, what purpose is served by continuing to burn the forests, orchards, and farmland they depend on? Once the fighting has moved on and the land itself becomes the target, the destruction takes on a different meaning. It is no longer simply about winning a battle; it is about making the land unlivable and severing people’s connection to it. The message is stark: even if you are allowed to return, you may find that the fields, olive groves, and forests that sustained your community have been deliberately destroyed.
That is why the language of “ecocide” matters, even though it must be used carefully. Ecocide is not yet an independent crime under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. A proposal to add it as a fifth international crime remains under discussion. But the absence of a standalone ecocide offence does not mean environmental destruction is legally irrelevant. International humanitarian law already protects civilian objects and restricts attacks that cause excessive civilian and environmental harm. The destruction of the environment can also form part of conduct constituting existing war crimes or crimes against humanity, depending on the facts, intent, and scale.
The legal gap should not become a moral loophole. If international law has not yet caught up with the reality of ecological warfare, that is an argument for strengthening it—not for pretending that forests and farmland are legally invisible.
And then there is the crocodile moat. Israel has been moving toward a plan to place Nile crocodiles in a trench surrounding part of the Naqab/Negev or “Ketziot” Prison, which holds Palestinian political prisoners. The plan was promoted by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and preparations for a roughly 170-meter (558-foot) trench reportedly began in July. Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman changed the legal classification of Nile crocodiles to help clear the way for their use, despite objections from environmental authorities and legal officials.
The most revealing part came next. An Israeli court temporarily froze the plan after the animal rights group Let the Animals Live petitioned against it. The court's intervention was therefore prompted by concerns about the treatment and welfare of the crocodiles. There is something almost unbearably symbolic about this. A court can be asked to consider whether crocodiles should be subjected to an inappropriate environment. It can demand that the state account for their welfare. Yet Palestinians held in Israeli prisons have for years faced abuse, torture, degrading conditions, denial of medical care, and other severe violations. Human rights groups have documented this reality extensively. The point is not that protecting animals is wrong. Quite the opposite: protecting animals is good. The scandal lies in the contrast. The crocodiles are recognized as beings whose welfare creates a legal and political obligation. Palestinian political prisoners are bodies to be contained and populations to be punished. The moat makes that hierarchy visible.
It is difficult to imagine a more perfect metaphor for dehumanization: Place dangerous animals between the state and people whom the state already holds behind bars. The stated purpose is deterrence. But deterrence is not the only message. The imagery itself communicates contempt. It transforms imprisonment into spectacle and punishment into political theatre. That is why the two stories belong together. In Lebanon, the landscape itself becomes an enemy to be subdued. In the prison, human beings are treated as an enemy population to be surrounded by predators. In both cases, the objective is not merely military victory. It is the production of vulnerability: making return harder, making resistance harder, making ordinary life harder.
And perhaps the most disturbing question is why the international response has been so muted. There has been no shortage of evidence. International organizations have documented the environmental consequences of attacks in Lebanon. The ecological damage has been measured in burned forests, destroyed farmland, and ancient olive trees. The crocodile project has been reported openly, defended publicly, and challenged in an Israeli court. Yet neither development has produced anything resembling the political outrage that their underlying logic should provoke. That silence is not neutral.
When the destruction of ecosystems is treated as an unfortunate by-product of war, and when the degradation of prisoners is treated as a security matter, the vocabulary of accountability disappears. Everything becomes “security.” Everything becomes “necessity.” And once that happens, almost anything can be made to sound reasonable. The burning of southern Lebanon should therefore be understood not simply as damage to trees, but as damage to the possibility of return. The crocodile moat should not be dismissed merely as a bizarre idea by a far-right minister, but understood as a symptom of a political culture that increasingly turns humiliation into policy. The international community should stop waiting for these acts to become normal.
If destroying the natural foundations of civilian life is deliberate and disproportionate, it must be investigated as a possible international crime. And if a state can mobilize courts, ministries, and millions of shekels to protect crocodiles from mistreatment, the same society should be asked a much more fundamental question: What protections are being afforded to the human beings locked behind bars? The real outrage is not that Israel wants to build a crocodile moat. It is that, in a system increasingly comfortable with turning land into wasteland and political prisoners into objects, the crocodiles may receive more immediate legal protection than the people inside the prison.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Russian expert warns of impending social crisis as Ukraine death toll rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:13:31 UTC
00:13:31 KST

Russian expert warns of impending social crisis as Ukraine death toll rises
Putin’s forces continue to bring horror to Ukrainian civilians as Kyiv destroys key sections of Russian infrastructure.
Russian ballistic missile attacks have begun to cause record civilian deaths in Ukrainian cities without any Patriot interceptors to stop them, but Ukraine’s long-range strikes have destroyed Russian fuel supplies.
With the Russian economy struggling, a top expert warned that social unrest could unfold in a matter of time – and consequently lost his job.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4In Ukraine, forcible military recruitment efforts escalate into violence
- list 2 of 4Ex-defence chief’s call for wartime election raises pressure on Zelenskyy
- list 3 of 4Nord Stream bombing suspect to Hollywood fixer: Who is Volodymyr Zhuravlev?
- list 4 of 4Russia says ready for ‘new ideas’ on Ukraine war that match Putin’s goals
On Tuesday, Russian missiles killed at least 10 people in Pechenihy, a town 40km (25 miles) east of Ukraine’s northern city of Kharkiv. On Thursday, they killed 15 people in Kyiv, three in the western city of Zhytomyr and injured 40 at a border crossing between Odesa and Moldova.
Russia said it was targeting weapons manufacturing sites in Kyiv, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces struck 30 residential buildings, a school and a children’s hospital.
The United Nations said Russia killed a record 437 people in July and injured 2,610, surpassing its previous record in June by 30 percent.
Civilian casualties have continued in August, because Ukraine has run out of Patriot interceptors and has been unable to stop incoming ballistic missile attacks since the beginning of the month.
As Zelenskyy pointed out, Ukraine’s interception rate of cruise missiles and drones is still in the 90-percent range. But Russia is doubling down on the use of ballistic missiles and has brought in an additional 50 North Korean weapons, according to Ukrainian military intelligence.
Ukraine strikes back
Since June 25, Ukraine has launched a campaign of mid-range strikes to disrupt Russian logistics and has harassed fuel and ammunition supplies so effectively that it has made 233sq km (90 square miles) of territorial gains this year.
By August 16, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces announced it had put 228 supply ships out of action in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, as well as destroying 243 power stations, electricity substations and gas distribution nodes in Crimea.
They have also been striking relay antennas used to guide Russian drones and radar stations that detect Ukrainian counterstrikes. On August 20, Ukraine struck drone launch sites in Donetsk City and Primorsko-Akhtarsk on the Sea of Azov, as well as a fuel terminal in the Kerch Strait used to supply Crimea.
Ukraine’s long-range strikes have served a different purpose – to undermine the Russian economy’s ability to fund its war.
On August 15, Ukraine managed to fly two of its Flamingo cruise missiles into the Progress Rocket and Space Centre, 800km (500 miles) east of Moscow, despite Russia’s use of four A-50 early warning aircraft and its reported downing of 822 Ukrainian drones that day.
Ukraine said it hit an engine assembly workshop for Soyuz rockets, causing a fire covering half a hectare.
Russia is using Soyuz to launch satellites for its Rassvet constellation to replace dependence on the US Starlink system, after Ukraine managed to cut Russian access to Starlink on February 1 . Russia needs satellites to increase the speed and precision of its counter-battery fire on Ukrainian positions. Its loss of that capacity has been partly responsible for Ukrainian gains this year.
“One Soyuz-2.1b launch vehicle can put 20 satellites into orbit,” said Ukrainian electronics expert Serhiy Beskrestnov. “To create a basic satellite constellation in orbit, Russia needs to carry out 12-15 launches.”
The following day, Ukraine set ablaze a 25-hectare warehouse belonging to the Wildberries online retail chain, Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, and said it had destroyed seven out of Wildberries’ ten largest logistical hubs.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on July 28 that the Kremlin was monitoring the damage to Wildberries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin implied on Thursday that he might provide government funds for Wildberries to rebuild, saying “logistics and warehousing capacity certainly needs to be restored, including with government support”.
Ukraine has also succeeded in destroying Russian oil refineries and starving its economy of petrol
It has recently struck the Ust-Luga refinery, the Taneco refinery in Tatarstan and the Perm refinery, 1,500km (930 miles) from its borders.
The Izvestia newspaper reported that only 28 percent of petrol stations across the country could supply fuel this week, citing mobile app GdeBENZ, which monitors real-time fuel availability.
Izvestia said only five petrol stations in Moscow were selling high-octane AI-98 fuel. Russians posted video of Rosgvardia police units sitting outside petrol stations to avert some of the fights involving motorists in recent months.
Deputy Prime Minister, Alexander Novak, said lower-grade fuel was being supplied to ease market tensions, and confirmed that Russia is now importing refined fuel for the domestic market.
“We expect a number of oil refineries to complete maintenance work soon and the situation to improve significantly,” Novak told Vesti journalist Pavel Zarubin, but that may be wishful thinking. Ukraine has struck Russia’s largest refineries not once but repeatedly. On Wednesday [August 19 ], it struck a refining unit at Ufa, which was undergoing repairs from a previous strike. It is 1,300km (810 miles) from Ukraine.
Ukraine also struck significant military targets during the week, including the Kamenyy Kombinat plant in Rostov, which makes solid rocket fuel for missiles, and the Savasleika airfield, from where MiG fighters armed with Kh-47M2 ballistic missiles take -off.
Russian economy in trouble
Some Russian economists have begun to warn of impending social and political upheaval as a result of the slowing economy.
Andrey Klepach, chief economist at Vnesheconombank, a state bank that finances the Kremlin’s national projects, warned on August 18 that, “Losses from Ukrainian military strikes … are already becoming a significant macroeconomic barrier to Russian economic growth.
“I believe Russia won’t collapse, but I’m almost certain we’ll reach a social crisis.”
He was removed from his post after making the comments during a discussion at the Moscow Exchange’s Nikitsky Club.
Russians are withdrawing savings in increasing amounts, reported The Washington Post. While businesses are increasing “voluntary” donations to the state defence budget, in addition to having to pay for their own air defences, putting further strain on the economy.
At a meeting of the Council for Strategic Development and National Projects this week, Putin acknowledged that Ukraine’s strikes are “certainly” causing damage, adding that “overall economic performance is modest but positive”.
That damage took financial form in the $1.18bn Putin newly released to aid regional budgets, in addition to previous financial assistance. Some $52m of that was destined for Crimea.
Ukraine’s defence ministry estimated that every dollar spent on drone strikes caused five times that amount in costs to the Russian economy.

Swiss canton wants to withdraw emergency aid from dozens of Ukrainians
Canton Vaud’s population office (SPOP) has decided to stop providing emergency assistance to around 40 Ukrainians whose applications for S permits have been rejected.
As a result, they could be required to leave Switzerland and return to the countries where they first sought refuge. The decision has been condemned as “inhumane” by a coalition of organisations and political parties.
More
Go to war or stay put? Ukrainian men in Switzerland face fresh dilemmas
“Around 40 people are affected by decisions to withdraw emergency assistance. Some of those decisions have been appealed and are currently on hold pending a ruling by the Vaud Cantonal Court,” the population office of Vaud’s cantonal government said on Friday. The comments were made to the Keystone-SDA news agency through its spokesperson, Frédéric Rouyard.
+ Swiss refugee policy for Ukrainians leaves many questions unanswered
“Only the federal authorities have the power to decide whether to grant asylum or protection status. They do not grant S protection status to people from Ukraine who already hold a similar status in another European country. The cantons, meanwhile, are responsible only for implementing federal asylum decisions,” the SPOP said in a written statement.
Federal Administrative Court ruling
“It is important to note that the people currently being refused emergency assistance already have protection status in another European country. That is why the State Secretariat for Migration did not grant them S status in Switzerland, a decision that was later upheld by the Federal Administrative Court,” the statement continued.
+ Should Switzerland refuse protection to Ukrainian men of fighting age?
The individuals concerned are subject to a final federal decision ordering their return to another European country, he added, stressing that emergency aid is intended as a last resort and is provided only when a person has no other means of support.
“As the European countries that granted them protection status are required to support them, they are not eligible for emergency assistance in Switzerland,” the statement said.
It also added that this approach is consistent with current practice in other cantons, including Zurich.
More
Switzerland’s S permit for refugees from Ukraine
NGOs and political parties highly critical
This week, several organisations working in the asylum sector, along with a number of political parties, issued a joint statement condemning the practice. The signatories included Droit de rester Vaud, the Vaud Social Democrats, the Vaud Greens, the Vaud Feminist Strike and Médecins du Monde Suisse.
They called on the SPOP to “immediately reinstate emergency assistance” and “put an end to this cruel and arbitrary practice”.
The groups argue that emergency assistance is a constitutional right, enshrined in Vaud law to guarantee a minimum standard of living for anyone in need. “It can neither be restricted nor withdrawn,” they said.
They also criticised the decision for failing to take account of individual circumstances, such as health issues, or levels of integration, including those of children in the affected families.
“As the war continues to devastate Ukraine, we condemn what we see as an unacceptable and unjustified practice. It puts families who have simply tried to build a secure life in canton Vaud in serious danger. This is an inhumane measure aimed at forcing people already affected by the war to leave Switzerland,” the coalition of organisations and political groups said.
Asked about the issue, the SPOP said it would not reverse its decision in cases involving people who do not hold S protection status.

The beauty brand Neutrogena has acknowledged making its former ambassador Hayden Panettiere “feel unsupported during a very difficult time” – alluding to when the late Hollywood actor said the company severed ties with her after she spoke about enduring postpartum depression (PPD).

The aftermath of the Heroes and Nashville star’s unexpected death had seen her fans circulate a podcast interview from May in which she recounted how Neutrogena cut off its relationship with her after she had detailed her experiences with PPD.
Some of her supporters also published comments criticizing Neutrogena on social media, including calls to boycott the brand over its treatment of Panettiere, who is seen by many as only the latest victim of an industry with a history of letting its younger stars down.
Neutrogena’s statement on Thursday then said it was “deeply saddened by Hayden Panettiere’s passing” and referred to her as a “valued member of our … community” after she was affiliated with the company for a decade beginning in 2005.
“We are proud to have partnered with her and understand that we made her feel unsupported during this difficult time,” Neutrogena’s statement continued. “This is not what Neutrogena stands for or who we want to be.”
The skincare products manufacturer did not elaborate. But in an interview three months earlier with podcaster Jay Shetty, Panettiere explained how she had once made impromptu remarks about having faced PPD during a live interview in 2015 with talkshow hosts Kelly Ripa and Michael Strahan.
“When they tell you about postpartum depression, you think about – ‘OK, I feel negative feelings towards my child. I want to injure my child. I want to hurt my child,’” Panettiere said back then. “I’ve never, ever had those feelings. But you … don’t realize [how] broad of a spectrum you can really experience that on, and it’s something I think that needs to be talked about. And women need to know that they’re not alone.”
She later learned that “Neutrogena wanted to fire me over that”, she said to Shetty.
“I had no intention of or plan to talk about postpartum depression,” Panettiere said. “It just came up, and I was just being honest. And never for a second did I think that anyone – or care that anyone – would have a bad reaction to it. It was my truth.”
Panettiere added: “I had the morals clauses. They caught absolutely everything. And of all the things … that they would fire me over, this was the last thing that I thought they would ever fire me over.”
She said her representative “saved the day that year” by replying to Neutrogena with something to the effect of: “That’s illegal. You can’t do that.” Nonetheless, Panettiere said Neutrogena declined to renew her contract when it expired.
“I had worked with these people for 10 years,” Panettiere recalled to Shetty. “And I remember not hearing a word from anybody.
“Not a ‘great working with you for 10 years’. Not a nice … ‘hope you’re good. We wish you well.’ And I remember that really breaking my heart.”
In her memoir, This Is Me, which also came out in May, Panettiere documented scars from a full-time acting career that began when she was five, preceding alcohol addiction and mental health struggles.
The book said she grappled with PPD after the birth in 2014 of her daughter, Kaya, with then lineal heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko, Panettiere’s fiance at the time. Kaya, who is now 11, began living with Klitschko full-time in his native Ukraine when she was two.
PPD can affect up to 14% of people who give birth, according to the Cleveland Clinic. The clinic says PPD can be characterized by “feeling sad, worthless, hopeless or guilty” or “worrying excessively or feeling on edge”, among other symptoms.
“You may also feel that you can’t care for your baby or for yourself,” according to the Cleveland Clinic.
Panettiere, who entered rehab in 2015 while filming Nashville, told Shetty: “I think there’s been this very common misconception that I just gave up my child. That could not be farther from the truth.”
The Greenville coroner’s office completed an autopsy of Panettiere on Monday. The agency said her cause of death was pending further investigation. She would have turned 37 on Friday.
Neutrogena, meanwhile, said it initially waited on releasing its statement about Panettiere “out of respect for Hayden’s family and loved ones”.
Without elaborating, Neutrogena also promised to make “a significant investment to a longstanding community health partner to help give more women access to the support they need, including care for postpartum depression”.
“Hayden’s courage in sharing her challenges helped inspire important conversations and awareness,” the company said.

Tom Rockmore (1942-2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:07:34 UTC
00:07:34 KST

Tom Rockmore (1942-2026)
Tom Rockmore, professor emeritus of philosophy at Peking University and distinguished professor emeritus at Duquesne University, has died.
(The following memorial notice was written by Gabriel Gottlieb.)
Tom Rockmore, professor emeritus at Peking University, passed away on August 6th. He was known for his work on German Idealism, where he emphasized its constructivist methods in epistemology.
Tom’s dissertation, Man as Activity in Fichte and Marx, defended in 1973 at Vanderbilt University, was advised by John Lachs. Tom expanded his work on Fichte and Marx in his pioneering book Fichte, Marx, and the German Philosophical Tradition, published in 1980. As a prolific author (publishing more than 25 books), Tom wrote on a variety of philosophical topics, including ancient philosophy, Kant, Fichte, Hegel, Lukács and the Frankfurt School, phenomenology, Heidegger’s Nazism, Hegel and analytic philosophy, aesthetics, and constructivist epistemology, often exploring topics years prior to their becoming popular or more mainstream within the discipline. His most recent books (published by University of Chicago Press) you can find here.
While Tom taught at a number of universities, including Yale, Fordham, Université Laval, and Wesleyan, he spent much of his career as a dedicated teacher and adviser at Duquesne University (1987-2007). In 2007, he moved to Peking University in China where in 2023 he became an Emeritus Professor.
Tom’s last philosophical presentation took place during the summer of 2024 in Rome where he discussed the works of Vico and Marx, a fitting swan song.
Tom’s wife, Sylvie, reported that he died peacefully while resting after a lunch with family. He had been dealing with health issues and retired to Nice, France where he spent his final years.

Pompeii, life went on after Vesuvius: new discovery points to the Renaissance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:06:20 UTC
00:06:20 KST

New fifteenth- and sixteenth-century finds rekindle the mystery of Pompeii: the city was not forgotten after the eruption, but lived on in local memory.
Pompeii did not end in AD 79.. For centuries, while the Roman city remained buried beneath the debris of Vesuvius’ eruption, people went on living among those ruins and kept its memory alive. This surprising story is now being told thanks to a number of new finds in the Insula Meridionalis, in the southern area of ancient Pompeii.
Materials and ceramic artefacts dating from the 15th and 16th centuries have in fact provided fresh evidence of human presence on the site many centuries before the start of the Bourbon excavations, launched in 1748.
The discovery challenges the most common image of Pompeii: on the one hand the Roman city, frozen by the eruption of AD 79; on the other modern Pompeii, brought back to light almost seventeen centuries later. In between, however, lies a far more nuanced story.
The "Pompeii after Pompeii"
"The docu-drama Pompei Fuori dal tempo with Tom Hiddleston, and the work of archaeologist Steven Tuck, show how the theme of the survivors is finally becoming the focus of research and outreach initiatives," explains Gabriel Zuchtriegel, director of the Archaeological Park of Pompeii.
After the eruption, Pompeii must have looked like a truly post-apocalyptic landscape. And yet, according to new research, it was not completely abandoned. There are traces of people who returned and of communities that continued to use the area.
These, however, were fragile presences, far removed from the grand official narrative. "They are faint traces of precarious lives, in the shadow of official history," Zuchtriegel points out, explaining why they remained almost invisible for so long.
The finds from the Insula Meridionalis now add another piece to this story. The ceramics and other materials uncovered point to use of the area during the Renaissance, centuries before Pompeii officially returned to prominence with the excavations.
And the Renaissance enters Pompeii’s story
The period is particularly interesting for another reason as well. It is in roughly these same centuries that the Deposition of Christ attributed to Andrea Mantegna, recently rediscovered in the Sanctuary of the Blessed Virgin of Pompeii, was created.
The two stories are not directly connected and belong to separate historical strands. But both tell us something important: Pomeii was not a place completely erased from collective memory.
"Without detracting in any way from researchers such as Gioachino Alcubierre, who came from Spain and promoted the first archaeological excavations at Pompeii in 1748, we have to acknowledge that there was a local community here which, from the very day after the eruption, went on living in Pompeii and guarding its memory," says Zuchtriegel.
A city never truly forgotten
An apparently simple detail also reinforces this hypothesis: the place name "Civita", which, according to the director of the Park, bears witness to the local persistence of the memory of a buried city.
Farmers and shepherds who lived among the ancient ruins did not have the tools to describe that heritage in the language of modern archaeology. But that, Zuchtriegel stresses, does not mean they did not remember it.
And this is precisely where the perspective shifts: Pompeii would therefore not be a city "reborn" from nothing in the eighteenth century, but a place that continued, in different forms, to be part of the life and imagination of the local community.
"Pompeii is and has always been a genuine heritage community," says Zuchtriegel. Its name, then, would not be the outcome of a simple archaeological revival, but the sign of a memory that has remained alive in the area for centuries.
The "Pompeii after Pompeii" is still largely to be told. And the small artefacts found underground this time may prove to be among the most important clues for piecing it together.
Visits to the excavation site
Visitors can tour the Insula Meridionalis excavation site together with the archaeologists and conservators working there. Visits are available, by reservation, from Monday to Friday between 11:00 and 12:00. For information and bookings, you can call 327 2716666.

Controversial Netflix dating show sparks backlash in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:03:21 UTC
00:03:21 KST

Netflix dating show featuring cast members with criminal pasts sparks backlash in Japan
Japan's justice ministry said Friday it will cancel a collaboration with a controversial Netflix dating show featuring ex-juvenile delinquents, following backlash against what some called the glorification of crimes.
Earlier this month, the ministry launched an unusual partnership with the streaming giant's "Badly in Love," releasing a poster starring its Season 2 cast members, including heavily tattooed men and women.
"Badly in Love" spotlights Japan's so-called "yankii" (delinquent) subculture by lodging together young men and women with wild and often criminal pasts, including former yakuza gangsters and motorcycle gang members.
"In Japan's first dating show for rebellious yankiis, 11 singles butt heads, forge bonds and live together for 14 days as they go all out to find the one," the show's description reads on its website.
Since its release in December, the show has proven an unexpected global hit, with Netflix saying its Season 1 maintained a weeks-long top-10 presence in South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong. The show's Season 2 is currently the top-ranked program in Japan, Netflix said.
"At times, it feels like Japan's answer to MTV's 'Jersey Shore,' another series that centered a maligned subculture and dared viewers to look closer," according to a 2025 review of the series in the Japan Times.
The ministry's rehabilitation bureau had justified the campaign on grounds that the show's depictions of participants' harsh upbringing, atonement and personal growth jibe with its belief that "a person can change."
The ministry promoted the program – which says it aims to showcase "people who are unapologetically themselves" -- as part of the campaign, and the show will continue to air without the government's support.
"It was never the intention of this collaboration to endorse crime or delinquency, nor to glorify or trivialize these acts from someone's past," the ministry said in a statement on Friday.
"But we have received a lot of concerns and criticism that it can cause discomfort among people victimized by crimes," it said, adding that the partnership will be terminated.
"Badly in Love" Season 2 came under fire after an episode aired in which one cast member confessed that, as a teen, he had been arrested for setting someone on fire to prove he was "not chickening out."
The cancellation of the campaign, however, "isn't meant to deny efforts to help rehabilitate people who committed crimes in the past," the ministry said.
"Badly in Love" executive producer Dai Ota told AFP in April that prior to running Season 1, the production team had "extensive internal discussions" to ensure the show would not be perceived as "condoning the violence."
 "Our hope was to show that these young people — who have often been marginalized or labeled as 'social outcasts' — are simply youths who worry, struggle and genuinely grow," he said.

Italy’s largest arms maker had no plans for a Ukraine factory—a year later, it has a Kyiv subsidiary

00:02:49 KST

Italian defense giant Leonardo has quietly registered a research subsidiary in Kyiv, planting a direct corporate flag in Ukraine's wartime defense ecosystem, Euractiv reported. The move reverses the company's previous public stance against opening operations in Ukraine.
European defense firms are quickly embedding inside Ukraine's defense industry, as Ukraine's wartime manufacturing base has become a draw rather than a risk for Western capital.
Kyiv-based R&D company
Leonardo Ukraine appeared in Ukraine's business register on 20 May, but the company disclosed the step only in its H1 2026 financial report at the end of July. The subsidiary's share capital stands at about $125,000. Leonardo International wholly owns it.
"We have completed the legal process to begin operations. The new company will be used to work in this region," a Leonardo spokesperson said.
The subsidiary will focus on R&D covering communications and navigation systems, software, IT services, and electronic and optical technologies. The step brings Leonardo closer to Ukraine's drone and missile industry, which has expanded rapidly during the war.
Italy wants continental defense alliance, including Ukraine. Kyiv already out-produces all of NATO on drones
From no factory to a Kyiv office
Just over a year ago, then-CEO Roberto Cingolani said that Leonardo had no plans to open a factory in Ukraine, as Reuters reported. At the same time, Cingolani pledged to test Leonardo's Michelangelo Dome air defense system in Ukraine. The Italian government did not reappoint him in April 2026. Lorenzo Mariani took over as CEO in May.
The subsidiary is not a factory. But it gives Mariani a registered legal presence inside Ukraine's defense innovation ecosystem, positioned near the drone and electronic warfare sectors Leonardo wants to tap.
Leonardo is not the first major European defense firm to set up inside Ukraine. Germany's Quantum Systems established three joint ventures and made the country its second-largest international base. Rheinmetall is building an ammunition plant there. Ukrainian defense companies, in turn, have opened production facilities across Europe.

A tweet by Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has been visiting Iraq for the past three days, sparked an online uproar over the name of the gulf bordered by Iran, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Oman: Is it the Persian Gulf or the Arabian Gulf?
On Wednesday, the first day of Ghalibaf’s visit to Iraq — a neighbor with which Iran fought a war in the 1980s — the Iranian official posted a photo of himself on X in the evening, standing in front of a map of the gulf labeled “Persian Gulf,” as Iran calls it. The post, published while Ghalibaf was on Iraqi soil, drew widespread attention and comes amid a decades-long dispute over the gulf’s name. Iran calls it the “Persian Gulf,” a name more commonly used by international bodies when referring to the region. Other countries along the gulf, however, favor the name “Arabian Gulf” amid longstanding political tensions.
Ghalibaf thrown to the ground: 'A lesson he won't forget'
Before Ghalibaf posted the photo Wednesday, he met, among others, with his Iraqi counterpart, Mohammed al-Halbousi. According to Iraq’s official news agency, the two held talks focused on ways to strengthen relations between the two countries. Al-Halbousi stressed the importance of developing cooperation in various fields, noted that Iraq was among the countries most affected by the war and developments in the region and called on Ghalibaf to ensure that Iraq receives special status regarding its oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, in a way that protects its economic interests. According to the agency, Ghalibaf affirmed his country’s commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and the economy.
Despite the meeting being described as “positive,” the atmosphere appeared to change after Ghalibaf’s post. On Thursday, al-Halbousi posted a photo of himself on X in front of a map of the gulf labeled “Arabian Gulf.” He added the hashtag “#Arabian_Gulf.”
The issue went viral on social media following al-Halbousi’s post. Some users expressed support for the Iranian official, while others backed al-Halbousi. One user uploaded an AI-generated video to X depicting a physical confrontation between al-Halbousi and Ghalibaf, in which the Iraqi official throws his Iranian counterpart to the ground against the backdrop of a map of the gulf. The user wrote: “Iraq of honor, pride and Arab glory. Hayder al-Halbousi teaches Ghalibaf a lesson he will never forget and proves that Iraq has men who understand its deep Arab roots.”
A well-known Iraqi commentator wrote Thursday about the incident: “Ghalibaf is still in Iraq, but he posted a photo of himself for no apparent reason or purpose other than the background — a map of the gulf labeled ‘Persian Gulf.’ Shortly afterward, the speaker of the Iraqi Parliament posted a photo of himself with the gulf in the background and the words ‘Arabian Gulf.’ The two men officially met yesterday and exchanged gifts, but the Iranian official wanted to make a point and the response came quickly.”
The militias at the heart of the dispute and the disarmament deadline
The unusual confrontation comes against the backdrop of significant tensions in recent months within Iraq and between Baghdad and Tehran. Pro-Iranian Iraqi factions operate in the country and some are even part of its official security apparatus. On the other side are Iraqi factions that oppose Iranian involvement in the country.
The Iraqi government, led by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, has been trying in recent months to balance its relations with Iran while maintaining ties with the United States. Washington wants the pro-Iranian militias in the country to disarm and, in July, carried out strikes together with Saudi Arabia on positions belonging to the Popular Mobilization Forces, a major Iraqi umbrella organization considered part of the security forces that includes pro-Iranian militias. The U.S. demand is that the militias surrender their weapons and withdraw from the organization. According to a report in The New York Times, about 20 Iranian advisers were killed in the strikes, some of them members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and others technical advisers.
Iraq has set the end of September as the deadline for the militias to disarm, the same date on which the U.S.-led international coalition established as part of the war against ISIS is expected to leave the country. Some militias have already announced that they will disband and hand over their weapons, while others have firmly refused.
Iran, for its part, fears losing its influence in Iraq if the militias disarm and disengage from the Popular Mobilization Forces. Against this backdrop, senior Iranian officials have been visiting Iraq in recent weeks, and Arab media reported in recent days on a visit by Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Quds Force. Iran has repeatedly sought to highlight what it describes as the deep ties between Iran and Iraq. Funeral processions for Ali Khamenei in Iraq were also part of this effort.
According to reports Friday, Ghalibaf met during his visit to Iraq with families of those killed in the recent Saudi-American strikes against the Popular Mobilization Forces in Iraq. Ghalibaf was quoted as saying: “The resistance axis is stronger today than ever in confronting global arrogance. The U.S. and Israel must understand that the unity of the Islamic nation, especially between the Iranian and Iraqi peoples, will never be shaken or broken.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zeidi addressed the issue of militia disarmament Friday: “All political forces completely agree on continuing to concentrate weapons in the hands of the state, and work is underway on mechanisms for handing over the weapons. The presence of weapons outside state control will create an environment that deters investment, and this is unacceptable and not in the interests of Iraqis.”
Meanwhile, according to a report in the Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat, Ghalibaf discussed proposals during his visit to Baghdad aimed at preventing a confrontation between the government and Iraq’s pro-Iranian militias. Among the proposals were freezing or concealing heavy weapons, with the possibility of “transferring a large portion of those weapons to Iran temporarily, until an agreement is reached regarding the future of the weapons.”

Plants under attack leave behind a surprising call for backup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:01:03 UTC
00:01:03 KST

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
When insect pests get the munchies, some plants call in the microbes.
Gnawing fly larvae provoke cowpea plants to release chemicals into the soil that nurture a helpful community of microbes. These bacteria then prompt plants to release an airborne molecule that draws in parasitoid wasps to attack the flies, researchers report August 21 in Cell Reports. The results point toward durable protection stored in the dirt that could shield even future plantlets from the maw of an herbivore.
It’s unclear how long the microbial protection lasts, or whether other kinds of plants lean on this type of defense, says Zeng-Rong Zhu, an insect ecologist at Zhejiang University in Hangzhou, China. Uncovering how the protection works could help researchers find ways to dispatch wasps as hired assassins for pest control.
The American serpentine leafminer (Liriomyza trifolii), native to the southeastern United States and the Caribbean, is an invasive fly now found in parts of Asia, Europe and Canada. Leafminer larvae tunnel through and consume leaves from all sorts of plants. Crops including cowpeas, eggplants and beans are at risk.
Leafminers can “destroy all the leaves if we don’t use any measures to control them,” Zhu says. One tactic is to recruit Neochrysocharis formosa wasps, the fly’s natural enemy, to the scene, and let them do the dirty work. The wasp lays eggs inside leafminer larvae that, after hatching, devour the young flies.
Some plants emit chemical signals in a cry for aid, luring parasitoid wasps to leaves where an unwitting herbivore is nibbling away. Such aboveground protections are thought to be short-lived, dissipating once the pest’s feast ends. But previous studies suggest that plants can shape which microbes live around their roots, and leaf-munching insects can alter what those communities look like.
Zhu and colleagues wondered if soil microbes might help plants send SOS calls to wasps. The team grew cowpea plants and allowed leafminer larvae to dine on the leaves. The researchers then removed the original plants and used the same soil to grow other cowpeas
N. formosa wasps were more attracted to plants grown in dirt taken from leafminer-infested cowpeas. Fewer wasps visited control cowpeas grown in soil that originally hosted plants never exposed to the flies. Soil and plant analyses revealed that the leafminer larvae triggered the release of chemicals into the dirt from the plants’ roots. These chemicals cultivated bacteria that in turn directed new cowpeas to release a molecule called (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate, which pulled in wasps even when there was no herbivore to attack.
The new study suggests that plants’ microbial partners in the soil can maintain what would normally be short-lived protection for the next generation, says Michelle Afkhami, an ecologist at the University of Miami who was not involved with the work. “Even though we can’t see them with a naked eye, [microbes are] affecting quite a bit of what’s going on around us.”
Some fungi defend plants from herbivores by covering leaves with toxic alkaloid compounds, Afkhami says. But it’s fascinating that in the case of cowpeas, long-term protection seems to come from “a community that isn’t even in the area where the herbivory is happening.”
