Britain, Australia and Canada have called the decision of the Israeli military authorities not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of aid vehicles in Gaza “shameful”. The strikes killed seven humanitarian workers from the US-based World Central Kitchen (WCK) organisation.
WCK staff from the three countries were among the casualties of the attack, which prompted global outrage.
“This decision is both too little, and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf. The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability,” the countries’ joint statement said.
It continued: “In Gaza, humanitarian workers continue to work tirelessly to support civilians in desperate need, risking their lives whilst working in the most perilous conditions. Yet despite the fragile ceasefire, Gaza remains the deadliest place to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.”
On Thursday, Australia’s government expressed “outrage” over the decision, while relatives said that Zomi Frankcom, the Australian among those killed, deserved more than an “internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.”
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision.
The Polish government said on Thursday it was “very disappointed” and called for Israeli authorities to cooperate with Polish investigations into the incident. Damian Soból, a volunteer from Przemyśl, was also among the casualties.
In London, the Foreign Office said the UK was “appalled and angry” for the families of John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby, three British citizens who were killed in the attack.
WCK, which distributed food in Gaza throughout the war, said immediately after the lethal attack that it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air.
“There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.
The IDF said on Wednesday that it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the WCK convoy had deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.
One of the officers who was dismissed had reportedly signed an open letter earlier that year calling for Gaza to be deprived of aid. Israel imposed strict restrictions on the entry of humanitarian assistance during the conflict in Gaza, where experts declared a famine in August 2025.
The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday that its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing, as well as into the fatal shooting of 15 paramedics in 2025.
Hind Rajab died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as they sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.
The IDF repeatedly denied its troops had been in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.
The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”, but experts said criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians very rarely lead to convictions.

First map of Lithuanian businesses in the UK launched, companies urged to sign up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:17:00 UTC
23:17:00 KST

Hundreds of Lithuania-linked businesses operate across the United Kingdom – from small family firms to large companies, spread across different regions and sectors. But until now, there has been no single place to see the community as a whole: its scale, geography, areas of activity and strongest sectors, according to the Lithuanian Chamber of Commerce and Industry in the UK (LCCUK).
That is why the first map of Lithuanian businesses in the UK is now being created, bringing together in one place companies founded by Lithuanians, companies with Lithuanian capital, and companies closely linked to Lithuania.
The map will show which parts of the UK Lithuanian businesses operate in, what sectors they represent, and what the Lithuanian business community looks like across this market as a whole.
The map will also serve as a practical tool for businesses themselves – making it easier to find each other, identify potential partners, make new contacts and strengthen ties.
Businesses operating anywhere in the UK – England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland – are invited to register.
"The Lithuanian business community in the UK is considerably larger than is often assumed. Although the business environment changed after Brexit, thousands of Lithuanian-founded and Lithuania-linked companies continue to operate successfully here. But until now there has been no single platform to identify them, show the scale of their activity, or create more opportunities for them to collaborate," said LCCUK president Laura Budrienė.
She said the map would, for the first time, allow a fuller assessment of the Lithuanian business community in the UK – not just counting active companies, but showing where they are most numerous, which sectors Lithuanian businesses are performing best in, and where potential remains unexploited.
The UK is one of Lithuania's most important trading partners. According to Statistics Lithuania, Lithuanian exports to the UK reached nearly €1.6 billion in 2025.
Businesses are invited to register via the LCCUK website.

opposite office moves into one-square-meter treehouse at bauhaus university
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:15:19 UTC
23:15:19 KST

Munich-based architecture practice Opposite Office has opened its latest workplace inside a tree on the historic campus of Bauhaus-Universität Weimar. Named Baumhaus Office, the approximately one-square-meter structure responds to a fairly terrestrial problem: Munich’s high office rents. Since much of the studio’s work already takes place across changing international locations, the architects began questioning whether an internationally operating practice needed a large permanent headquarters at all.
The answer is a tiny elevated workspace designed for two to three architects, temporarily installed in one of the campus trees while Opposite Office works on two projects in Weimar: Fictional Infrastructures at M Books Gallery and Last Fellow II at ACC Galerie, the latter developed in cooperation with Villa Massimo Rome. The tree itself is among the oldest in Weimar and, according to the studio, was reportedly planted by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe during his time in the city. A desk, workstations, model-making area and essential infrastructure are compressed into the smallest possible footprint, turning spatial economy into both necessity and architectural proposition.
The temporary office also places itself within Weimar’s long tradition of experimental construction. On a campus historically associated with rationality, function and modern ideas of progress, Opposite Office introduces another reference point: Romanticism and its understanding of nature as something more than background, resource or object of study. Here, the tree is not simply supporting the architecture; it becomes one of its central occupants.
A skylight reinforces that shift in perspective. Rather than opening toward an abstract patch of sky, it looks directly into the tree canopy above, bringing branches and leaves into the architects’ immediate field of vision. The gesture turns the small building into an instrument for observation, briefly directing attention away from the built environment and toward something considerably older — and rather less interested in deadlines.
the one-square-meter workspace sits among the trees
HOW LITTLE OFFICE DOES AN ARCHITECTURE PRACTICE NEED?
Opposite Office draws a parallel with Cosimo, the protagonist of Italo Calvino’s The Baron in the Trees, who leaves life on the ground to inhabit the treetops. Baumhaus Office adopts the reference not as a proposal for escape but as a way of changing vantage point. Its extreme reduction of conventional office infrastructure reflects the studio’s broader working model, in which architects move between different cities, institutions and contexts rather than organizing every project from one fixed headquarters.
The treehouse consequently functions as workplace, meeting point and starting point for new projects while remaining intentionally open to visitors, clients and students. Opposite Office also describes more-than-human inhabitants as welcome, extending the idea of occupation beyond the architecture practice itself. With little more than a desk, a roof and a tree beneath it, Baumhaus Office asks how much architecture architects actually require to work — and suggests that the answer may be substantially less than the average office lease implies.

Photos: Tallinn unveils redesigned Iceland Square

Photos: Tallinn unveils redesigned Iceland Square
Iceland Square, located in front of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs building in Tallinn, was formally opened on Friday with a new Iceland‑inspired appearance.
Among those attending the opening were Iceland's president Halla Tómasdóttir, Estonia's president Alar Karis, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna and Tallinn mayor Peeter Raudsepp.
For the 35th anniversary of Estonia's restoration of independence, Iceland Square was refurbished and received a new landscape design.
The new design is inspired by Iceland's nature and architecture and helps make the symbolic meaning of the place more visible. The solution, created through cooperation between the Tallinn Urban Planning Department and the Central District Administration, gives the square a new look and creates opportunities to use the urban space more than before.
The project authors are architect Markus Puidak from the chief architect's office of the Tallinn Urban Planning Department and landscape architect Maire Suimets from the Environment and Communal Services Department. The concept authors are Artur Raik, Riina Parve, Katariina Kangro and Madis Keerd.
The landscape construction work on Iceland Square was carried out by Ardens OÜ. The cost of the work was 59,192 euros, of which 12,400 euros was co‑financed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Iceland was the first country in the world to recognize Estonia's restored independence on 22 August 1991. To commemorate this historic event, the area between Rävala Street and Theatre Square was named Iceland Square in 1998.
During the Soviet period, a statue of Vladimir Lenin stood in the same area.

A Ukrainian drone maker is taking its battle-tested technology to a European factory floor. Ukrainian producer Airlogix has agreed with Finnish technology company Innokas to establish a joint venture in Finland, the company reported.
Under the "Build with Ukraine" initiative, the partnership will manufacture uncrewed systems based on Airlogix's Ukrainian technology in Finland, scaling production of Ukrainian drones in Europe and increasing supply to Ukraine's Defense Forces.
The deal was signed in Denmark
The two companies formalized their intent at a defense event. Airlogix and Innokas signed a Letter of Intent to establish manufacturing in Finland for uncrewed systems based on Airlogix's Ukrainian technology during DALO Industry Days in Denmark.
The next stage will focus on developing the manufacturing model in Finland and establishing the joint venture, according to Airlogix.
Airlogix is a globally ranked drone maker
Airlogix is one of Ukraine's most recognized drone developers. In 2025, it ranked 84th on The Defense Post's list of the world's top 100 unmanned-systems makers, a ranking that weighed revenue, R&D investment, and growth. It was one of three Ukrainian companies on the list, alongside TAF Drones and Ukrspecsystems.
Airlogix makes the GOR unmanned aerial system, designed for reconnaissance and artillery spotting, which flies for two to two-and-a-half hours, has a range of 150 kilometers, and maintains communication at a range of 30 to 40 kilometers.
It is Airlogix's second European production deal
The Finnish venture follows a similar one across the Atlantic. In May 2026, Airlogix formed a 50-50 joint venture, Airlogix-Sentinel, with a Hamilton-based manufacturer to produce Ukrainian reconnaissance drones on Canadian soil for Ukraine's forces, under the same "Build with Ukraine" initiative.

Bolivia ousts economy minister after lawmaker pressure, in blow to Paz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:12:31 UTC

Bolivia ousts economy minister after lawmaker pressure, in blow to Paz
LA PAZ, Aug 21 - Bolivia's government has named Oscar Mario Justiniano Pinto as interim economy minister, removing Jose Gabriel Espinoza from the post, according to a presidential decree published on Friday in the Official Gazette.
On Tuesday, Bolivia's Congress voted to censure Espinoza, dealing a setback to President Rodrigo Paz's government amid mounting economic challenges.
Espinoza said on Tuesday he would take legal action against the censure, which the government called unconstitutional, and turn to the nation's top Constitutional Tribunal to review the decision.
Paz's administration initially said Espinoza would remain in office while the tribunal reviewed the dispute.
Friday's decree established that Justiniano, Bolivia's environment minister, will head the economy ministry until a permanent candidate is appointed. It did not provide a timeline.
ECONOMIC REFORMS AT STAKE
Espinoza's ouster comes at a sensitive time for Paz's government, which is seeking congressional backing for economic reforms and for a financing program negotiated with the International Monetary Fund in July that still requires approval from both Bolivia's Congress and the IMF Executive Board.
Bolivia's centrist government has been struggling to win both legislative and public support for its economic reform agenda. Widespread demonstrations and roadblocks over austerity measures earlier this year brought several cities to a standstill, prompting the government to issue emergency measures in an effort to contain the unrest.
The cabinet reshuffle deepens a confrontation between Paz and lawmakers at a time when Bolivia continues to grapple with shortages of fuel and foreign currency, and slow growth.
Espinoza had served as economy minister since Paz took office in November. He had become one of the principal architects of the administration's economic policy, playing a prominent public role in negotiations with multilateral lenders.
LAWMAKERS BACK REMOVAL
The minister's removal on Friday drew support from both opposition and ruling-party lawmakers.
Opposition lawmaker Rolando Pacheco of the leftist Popular Alliance (AP) said Paz was "showing a measure of humility and complying with the Constitution," which he said clearly grants Congress the power to question and censure ministers.
Ruling-party lawmaker Claudia Bilbao also backed the move, saying lawmakers would "not cover for anyone" and that Espinoza's departure should send a message to cabinet ministers that they must work with, and listen to, parliament.
In recent weeks, Espinoza had also faced scrutiny over the alleged purchase of an Audi vehicle at a declared value well below market price. He said the discrepancy was the result of a paperwork error. REUTERS

Russian-Australian man charged over alleged operation to gather Ukrainian military secrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:11:37 UTC
23:11:37 KST

Australian police have charged a 27-year-old Russian-Australian man with foreign interference after alleging he joined Ukraine's armed forces to obtain military information for Russian intelligence, the ABC reported.
Russia has repeatedly sought to obtain information about Ukraine's military through espionage and intelligence operations as it continues its full-scale invasion. The alleged operation also shows how Moscow can use individuals in third countries to gain access to Ukrainian military information and attempt to pass it to Russian intelligence.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) arrested Vladimir Teslov on 20 August in Sumner, a suburb of Brisbane. He appeared in Brisbane Magistrates Court on 21 August, where his case was adjourned until 2 October, according to the ABC.
Alleged operation inside Ukraine
According to the AFP, Teslov traveled to Russia in October 2024 and underwent military-style training before returning to Australia in December.
Teslov allegedly maintained contact after his return with individuals he believed were connected to Russian intelligence services, the AFP said in a press release.
Police allege he traveled to Ukraine in May 2025 and joined the Ukrainian Armed Forces, where he gained access to information about Ukrainian military personnel, units, and locations.
The AFP alleges Teslov subsequently provided, or attempted to provide, information obtained in Ukraine to people he believed were acting on behalf of Russian intelligence.
The agency said he sought to collect and communicate information about Ukrainian military personnel, locations, and operations for the benefit of Russia.
AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said the alleged activity could have endangered Ukrainian troops.
“It is alleged that this conduct created a risk to the safety and security of Ukrainian military personnel,” Barrett said, according to ABC.
The allegations have not been tested in court.
Australia has been a major supporter of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, providing about A$1.8 billion in military, economic, and humanitarian assistance.
“What happens in Ukraine matters in Indo-Pacific”: Australia pledged Ukraine another $70 million
Investigation into alleged Russian intelligence links
The AFP said its Counter Foreign Interference Task Force began Operation Woodcreeper in June 2026, following an extensive investigation by Australia's domestic intelligence agency, ASIO.
Australian authorities carried out searches at five properties in Queensland on 20 and 21 August, according to the AFP press release. Police seized electronic devices and other items relevant to the investigation, which will undergo forensic examination.
The AFP said further arrests are possible.
Barrett said there was no indication that Teslov posed a threat to Australia itself, although investigators allege parts of the activity took place both in Australia and overseas.
The foreign interference charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.
The Russian Embassy in Canberra told ABC it learned of the case through media reports and had not received an official notification from Australian authorities or Teslov. It said it was using available channels to establish the circumstances of the case.
Russian espionage cases in Australia
Australian authorities have previously warned of Russian intelligence activity in the country.
ABC noted a separate case involving Russian-born Australian citizens Kira and Igor Korolev, who were arrested in 2024 and accused of attempting to gather and send sensitive information to Russia. Their charges were upgraded to conspiracy to commit espionage in June.
In 2022, Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) Director-General Mike Burgess said the agency had disrupted a “hive of spies” from an unnamed country seeking to recruit Australians and obtain sensitive information. Multiple media reports later identified Russia as the country involved, although ASIO has not publicly confirmed this.
Last month, the Australian Signals Directorate and nearly two dozen international partner agencies warned that Russian-linked hackers were targeting Australian defense, communications, energy, and financial sectors.

Prince Harry and his fellow claimants have been ordered to pay an initial £9.54 million ($13 million) in legal costs after losing their case against the publisher of the Daily Mail.
The group of seven, which also included Elton John, Liz Hurley and Baroness Doreen Lawrence, had all its claims dismissed by Justice Nicklin last month.
Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL), the publisher of the Daily Mail, said its total legal costs were more than £34.5 million ($47.05 million).
However, the full amount will not be paid immediately.
ANL had asked for an interim payment of more than £9.9 million ($13.50 million). Lawyers representing Harry and the other claimants argued that the initial payment should be just over £7.9 million ($10.77 million).
Claims of unlawful information gathering
The claimants alleged that unlawful information gathering took place at the publisher over a 30-year period from the early 1990s.
Their allegations included voicemail interception, landline tapping and obtaining information by deception, known as "blagging."
They alleged that private investigators, freelance journalists and staff at ANL were involved. ANL strongly denied the claims.
In a 436-page ruling, Mr. Justice Nicklin said none of the claimants had proved their allegations of unlawful information gathering, including phone hacking.
Following the judgment in July, ANL described the result as an "overwhelming victory" and a "magnificent vindication of the Daily Mail's journalism."
It has described the ruling as "a devastating critique of an attempt to destroy a newspaper and the reputations of its journalists, editors and executives."
The latest order means Harry and the other claimants must now make the initial payment toward ANL's legal costs.

====================================================================================================

What does 'right-wing' actually mean in Israeli politics anymore? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:10:50 UTC
23:10:50 KST

Something peculiar has happened to Israeli politics: almost everyone’s supposedly “right-wing.” Politicians who fervently oppose Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing government claim the label, as do many others who disagree with Likud on fundamental things.
Some declare the Left-Right dichotomy obsolete, yet still seem terrified that somebody might mistake them for “left-wing.” What’s going on? What exactly does “right-wing” mean in Israel?
It certainly doesn’t mean the economic Right. I’m basically a capitalist. I may not believe the market cures all social ills, but the market, with guardrails, is the best economic principle we have. By that definition, much of Israel’s “Right” is leftist.
The constituencies most dependent on state transfers vote for parties of the Right, and unlike US working-class voters voting against their economic interests, these Israelis are being logical. They favor the huge public spending flowing to them from the pro-welfare “Right” and vote accordingly.
Fine. Perhaps being right-wing means being a Zionist.
Consider the strange case of me. I consider the Jews a people by any reasonable historical definition of that word, rather than merely adherents of a religion scattered among diasporas.
Peoples are entitled to national self-determination, and Jews, therefore, had every right to establish a nation-state in their ancestral homeland, even after a diaspora lasting 2,000 years, which I do admit is odd (many things in life are odd).
I also regard the fixation on the Nakba as disproportionate. Israel’s creation involved displacement and brutality, which was tragic for individuals, but the middle of the 20th century was filled with collapsing empires, border changes, and population movements. The partition of India uprooted many millions of Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs to create coherent states.
Elevating the Palestinian displacement into a uniquely monstrous event that confers an eternal claim against the very existence of Israel is absurd. Much more unusual was the abuse of refugees in their host societies, from which they were mostly ethnically indistinguishable.
And while Palestinian national sentiment exists powerfully today – whether Israelis like it or not – its historical claims are far weaker than advocates pretend.
Before the confrontation with Zionism helped forge a distinct Palestinian identity, the Sunni Arab inhabitants of (and migrants to) Mandate Palestine were part of the wider Arab Levant, with local and religious identities, mainly.
Being right-wing doesn’t alter the perspective on how the Palestinian identity was formed
On a national level, the differences between Palestinians and people in Jordan, Syria, and Lebanon were minor at best. There was no ancient Palestinian nation marching through history toward sovereign statehood, and the world does not owe this. I do think it may offer a way out of the conflict – but the borders must be safe for Israel, and any Palestinian statehood must be demilitarized.
I am also extremely hawkish about terrorism. When lives are in imminent danger, I favor giving the security services extreme latitude to stop the threat. My concern for the rights of terrorists resembles my concern for the rights of mobsters: minimal, and mainly because one is innocent until proven guilty in a civilized society.
By this point, I should be safely ensconced on the Right – no? Yet by the bizarre twists and turns of Israeli politics I’m a left-winger (or, via the rebrand, a “centrist”).
Why? Well, I want Israel to remain a Jewish state.
There are millions of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Israel can incorporate them with equal rights and not be a Jewish-majority state; it can rule them without equal political rights and not be a democracy; or it can attempt to remove them, which would be both immoral and strategically insane (as this would bring on global isolation on a scale that could devastate its economy, destroy crucial alliances, and undermine its ability to defend itself).
That leaves some form of partition. I have no particular attachment to the precise arrangement. The territory Israel relinquishes could become an independent Palestinian state, yes.
But one of the great missed opportunities in Israeli history was Likud’s scuttling of the 1987 London Agreement pursued by former prime minister Shimon Peres and King Hussein, which might have enabled Israel to withdraw from much but not all of the West Bank while placing it under Jordanian rather than independent Palestinian control.
Demilitarizing a region of an established country is easier than attempting to demilitarize an entire sovereign state. Likud’s
Yitzhak Shamir was not smart enough to see this.
My second “left-wing” credential is wanting Israel to remain a liberal democracy. Elections determine who governs, while democracy requires institutions that constrain what governments can do. 
Citizens possess rights that survive elections, minorities require protection from majorities, and an independent judiciary is critical in a country lacking a written constitution, a second legislative chamber, and other checks on executive power.
This was once an entirely respectable position on the Israeli Right. Former prime minister Menachem Begin’s reverence for independent courts was central to his political worldview, and Netanyahu long defended the independence and stature of Israel’s judiciary.
The strange transformation of judicial independence into a supposedly left-wing cause attaches directly to Netanyahu’s criminal trials.
My third “left-wing” offense concerns the haredim (ultra-Orthodox), and here the ideological inversion approaches absurdity. I believe children should learn mathematics and English and acquire skills needed in a modern economy.
I believe adults should support their families – not study Torah as a default vocation, receiving stipends rather than paying tuition. I believe citizens should equally share the obligations of citizenship, including military service when needed and as reasonable.
A desire to see all Israeli citizens share the military burden isn’t leftist
Yet defending an arrangement in which an ever-growing community receives enormous public support while significant parts of it minimize their participation in the productive economy and the military is now a hallmark of Israel’s Right. This arrangement will bankrupt Israel, with consequences far beyond living standards.
A poorer Israel becomes weaker and more vulnerable. Prayer will not finance Iron Dome interceptors, develop military technology, or generate the tax revenues required to sustain a first-world army.
So there we have it. My “leftism” consists principally of wanting to preserve Israel as a Jewish-majority state, prevent it from becoming an impoverished theocracy, and protect it from sliding toward elected autocracy.
I’m pretty sure most Israelis want the same – yet many of those same people insist that they are “on the Right.” The especially confused among them even vote for Likud and its allies, who undermine all these principles.
The first explanation lies partly in the failure of the peace process, the Second Intifada, and the waves of Palestinian terrorism that destroyed faith in its assumptions. October 7 deepened Israelis’ skepticism about peace.
Yet this should not logically make them want to become forever entangled with the Palestinians because of the settlements foolishly built by the Right.
Second, Netanyahu spent decades brilliantly delegitimizing “the Left.” The most revealing moment came in 1997 when he was caught on camera telling the revered Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri that “the Left forgot what it means to be Jews.” That gaslighting nonsense, repeated in different forms for decades, was politically brilliant.
This sad confusion about labels creates confusion about reality – in a country that desperately needs clear thinking.
I’m happy to call myself a capitalist, a Zionist, a security hawk, a liberal democrat, and a supporter of territorial partition. Those words convey actual information. So when someone announces they’re “right-wing,” I ask for something more useful.
I’d like to know about the Jewish-majority state, who will work and pay for it, who will defend it, and what limits will constrain its government from deciding to shut down The Jerusalem Post and calling it the will of the people.
Then we can decide who is conservative and who is radical. We can decide who wants the best for Israel. The old terms really are dead, but the disagreements are not. Resolving them requires us to end the confusion.
The writer is the former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press, the former chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem, and publisher of danperry.substack.com

‘I saw it on TikTok’: 48% of Gen Z travellers turn to the platform for travel inspiration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:10:35 UTC
23:10:35 KST

Gen Z is leading the shift in how travellers discover, book and share their holidays, with almost half citing TikTok as their source of travel inspiration.
Back in my day (not that long ago – I’m only a millennial), recommendations from family and friends, along with a YouTube vlog or a scroll through Pinterest snaps, were the go-to sources of travel inspiration. My, oh my, how things have changed since then.
Now, short-form videos on TikTok are increasingly shaping where people want to go and what they want to do abroad, especially among Gen Z travellers born between 1997 and 2012.
TUI Musement looked into how social media is influencing how travellers now discover, book, experience and share their holidays.
In the study conducted across Spain, Italy and the UK, the global tours and activities platform found that almost half (48%) of Gen Z respondents cited TikTok as a source of travel inspiration, putting the social media app ahead of recommendations from friends and family, which ranked at 43%.
According to TUI Musement, this points to visual and short-form content growing in influence for travellers seeking new destinations to visit, activities to do and bringing holiday ideas to life.
Overall, more than four in ten travellers (43%) said that seeing a viral post or video led them to either book a trip or go on an activity. This trend was especially common among us millennials at 52% – slightly more so than Gen Z, at 50%.
Influencers were also clearly found to have... influence, with 43% of respondents saying the content creators they follow are a factor in deciding where they go and what they do abroad. As many as 27% said they went as far as to change their destination because of an influencer’s recommendation.
“A single image or video can now inspire travel, and we have steadily increased our focus on how we can best reach and engage our audience through platforms such as Instagram and TikTok," Mirco Fiumene, Managing Director Experiences & CMO, TUI Musement, said.
But social media’s influence doesn’t seem to stop once a person has chosen and arrived at their destination.
In the age of scrolling, the pressure to snap the perfect holiday picture impacts how they share their experiences, with over a third (37%) feeling the need to make their trips look more exciting on their social media profiles. Among Gen Z, this figure rises to almost half, at 45%.
And for some, the search for the perfect post can impact what they do. Nearly four in ten travellers (39%) said they visited a tourist hotspot mainly to take a photo or record a video, while 37% said that, at least occasionally, they would rather go to Insta-famous places than a destination's lesser-known hidden gems.
So, is the holiday experience still about where you go, or how it looks on the social media feed once you get there?

German government seeks to calm gas storage worries as levels lag at 50%

Ayhan Şimşek
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
 Germany’s Economic Affairs and Energy Ministry moved Friday to calm concerns over the country’s unusually low natural gas storage levels, saying it is monitoring the situation closely and preparing contingency measures should supply risks grow.
“We are monitoring the filling levels of the gas storage facilities very closely,” the ministry said in a statement on social media. It is also preparing “the necessary options for action so that they can be used quickly and in a targeted manner if the situation worsens.”
German storage sites stood at 50.19% full as of Friday – well below levels typical for this point in the refill season and beneath the European average of 61.82%. The ministry acknowledged the shortfall. “Storage levels in Germany are currently significantly lower than in previous years. We take this very seriously,” it said. Yet it maintained that “based on current information, a gas shortage is not expected this coming winter.”
Officials urged against focusing on any single number. “Security of supply does not depend on a single percentage,” the ministry said, noting that Germany is now “more broadly positioned than at the beginning of the energy crisis.” What matters, it argued, is “the interaction of storage, pipeline imports, LNG, infrastructure and demand.”
At the same time, the government signaled it stands ready to step in if conditions deteriorate. “If key risk factors for security of supply worsen significantly, the state can and will respond,” the ministry said.
It argued, however, that primary responsibility still rests with the market. “As a matter of principle, winter preparedness is the task of gas companies and traders,” the statement said. Those firms have delivery obligations to municipal utilities, industry and other customers and “must ensure that they have the necessary quantities available even in winter.”
The ministry also cautioned against premature state purchases. “A hasty state intervention is not a risk-free instrument,” it said. “Government gas purchases can drive up prices and weaken the market’s preparedness.” Any intervention, it added, must be carefully weighed, with winter readiness remaining first and foremost a market task.

Changiz Sheykhli, ‘father of Iranian caving,’ dies at 99
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:08:31 UTC
23:08:31 KST

Changiz Sheykhli, ‘father of Iranian caving,’ dies at 99
TEHRAN – Changiz Sheykhli, the pioneering figure who founded Iran’s modern caving and speleology movement, died on Wednesday, August 20, in Karaj at age 99, following a period of illness.
Widely honored as the “father of Iranian caving,” Sheykhli’s death closes a formative chapter in the history of Iran’s caving community — a discipline he helped transform from an informal pastime into an organized scientific field.
Born in Mashhad in 1927, Sheykhli took up mountaineering at age 12, climbing the rocky terrain around his hometown before summiting Kolakchal (August 1945), Tochal (June 1947), and Mount Damavand. His introduction to caves came in 1943, in the Hesar region, well before caving existed in Iran as an organized pursuit.
On November 29, 1946, Sheykhli, together with S. Mostofi and A. Shafizadeh, founded Iran’s first caving association. The group adopted a motto that still guides the country’s caving community today: “The value of a discovery lies in illuminating the unknown, not in its importance.”
Over the course of his career, Sheykhli explored and documented hundreds of caves across Iran, leaving behind an extensive archive of field notes, sketches, and survey records on caves, speleology, and cave navigation. He is also historically credited with discovering the celebrated Espahbod Khorshid Cave.
Fereidoun Biglari, head of the Paleolithic Department at the National Museum of Iran, notes that as early as the 1940s and 1950s, Sheykhli was already carrying out systematic measurement, mapping, and analysis of cave formations and water systems, along with archaeological recording — methods entirely novel to Iranian caving at the time. Biglari added that Sheykhli’s legacy lives on in the dozens of Iranian caving groups whose members now volunteer their time to document caves using modern international methods, and to protect and promote the country’s natural cave heritage. “This is a generation that plays an important role in introducing this significant natural heritage,” he said, “a generation indebted to pioneers like Changiz Sheykhli.”
The culmination of Sheykhli’s lifelong dedication to documentation was The Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Iran’s Caves, published by Shalfin Publications in 2021 — a compendium of detailed entries on hundreds of caves, many personally surveyed and mapped by him.
Changiz Sheykhli’s legacy endures in the generation of Iranian speleologists he inspired to continue mapping and studying the country’s hidden underground landscape.

Burnham to dispatch 100 Whitehall officials to help regional mayors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:08:23 UTC
23:08:23 KST

Andy Burnham is to send more than 100 Whitehall officials to bolster the teams of regional mayors, after convening leaders from across England from his base at No 10 North to discuss how to spread growth.
The government described the meeting as a “situation room” to bring local and regional leaders into national decision-making.
After the call led by Burnham, the government said five to 10 civil servants would be sent to every mayoral authority for secondments of less than a year during a pilot programme in 18 mayoralties.
Mayors requested the extra capacity at the first meeting of Burnham’s National Economic Council at the end of last month.
There will also be a new civil service fast stream pilot in Yorkshire and Humber, and an expansion of the future leaders scheme, which trains high performers in the civil service, to mayoral and local authority officials.
Burnham said his No 10 North office was “bringing together mayors from different political parties to work on these challenges, because people deserve problem-solving rather than point-scoring”.
His deputy, Louise Haigh, said it marked an end to “the days of Westminster hoarding power” and would be the biggest transition of power and resources in a generation away from Whitehall.
Mayors have long been requesting more firepower from Whitehall, although on their own terms to request help and talent rather than having officials sent from London to monitor their activities – which has happened when local authorities are struggling.
Among the cabinet ministers at Friday’s meeting discussing growth across the country were Haigh, the chancellor, John Healey, the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, and Sally Jameson, a housing minister, with mayors from across the country dialling in.
Burnham’s creation of No 10 North was one of his first acts as prime minister, combining in a powerful new department with No 10 in London, and taking in parts of the Cabinet Office, Treasury and housing ministry to become the “dominant driver of the UK’s economy”.
The operation is led by his ally and enforcer Haigh, who is overseeing the No 10 operation in London, No 10 North in Manchester and parts of the Cabinet Office.
As part of the shift, Burnham has said No 10 North will take on responsibility for driving local growth, potentially weakening the power of the Treasury. However, Healey stressed on Friday that growth would be a “dual mission”.
Addressing the meeting, he said the government had “demonstrated across a range of fronts that we’re a government that just is getting on with getting things done and that includes on growth”.
“The determination to see good growth in every postcode. And that is central to the Treasury, as the government’s economics, as well as its finance ministry. But it is a dual mission between No 11 and No 10 North. And it’s a dual mission that has to become the shared endeavour of all departments in government and a shared endeavour between national, regional and local leaders.”

Turkey’s NATO membership does not protect its servicemen in Syria — Israeli expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:07:14 UTC
23:07:14 KST

TEL AVIV, August 21. /TASS/. Turkey’s NATO membership does not mean that its servicemen in Syria are automatically protected by Article 5 of the NATO Charter on collective defense, Shay Gal, founder and head of Line of State, a company specializing in strategic planning, access, and security in high-risk environments, stated.
"Just because Turkey is a member state in NATO doesn't mean it is protected in Syria," he wrote in an article for the Israel Hayom newspaper. According to Gal, Israel "studied not only how NATO's Article 5 operates, but where it applies." It "protects Turkish territory; Turkish troops do not carry that territory with them onto Syrian or occupied Cypriot soil," he noted. "Turkish vessels and aircraft operating in the Mediterranean raise separate treaty questions, but even where Article 5 applies, collective action is not automatic. NATO acts by consensus, and each member state determines the response it deems necessary," the expert noted.
He pointed out that on August 18, Israel "allegedly struck Syria's Abu al-Duhur air base before Turkish forces arrived." According to him, the apparent "doctrine" is to "deny infrastructure before the flag lands - because once Turkish troops arrive, striking also risks Turkish casualties, retaliation, American intervention." Accordingly, Israel did not wait for Turkish troops, aircraft, radar or air defense systems. It destroyed the infrastructure required to receive them before the threat became entrenched," Gal stressed.
Earlier, Syria TV reported that on Tuesday, Israeli Air Force aircraft carried out strikes on the Abu al-Duhur military airfield in the Idlib governorate. According to the TV channel, the attacks resulted in only material damage. Following this, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated that Israel would not tolerate a Turkish military presence in Syria that threatened it. In turn, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz accused Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of endangering Turkey by engaging in "dangerous gambles" in Syria. Previously, Netanyahu’s office stated that Syria was "close to undermining" the security status quo with Israel by effectively allowing the deployment of Turkish troops at an airbase in northern Syria.

Dartmoor firing times
Information on Dartmoor Training Area's firing times.
Documents
Details
Do not touch any military debris it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) or police.
Warning signals: red flags by day and red lamps by night, indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries, which are marked by red and white poles. When warning signals are displayed do not cross the range boundary.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas safely.

How Mongolia Is Diversifying Its Defense Sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

This year, Turkiye and Mongolia launched the country’s first ammunition factory, marking an elevation in bilateral relations but also jumpstarting Mongolia’s defense manufacturing capabilities. It’s part of a larger trend: in the last decade, Mongolia’s defense sector has diversified immensely.
Mongolia and Turkiye established a strategic partnership in January 2025 during Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa’s state visit to Ankara. That was followed by several high-level visits by Turkish officials.
In October 2025, Turkish Minister of National Defense Yasar Guler paid an official visit to Ulaanbaatar at the invitation of his Mongolian counterpart, Batlut Damba. The two sides discussed opportunities to deepen cooperation in military education, training, and officer exchange programs. During the same visit, Guler also participated in the inauguration of the new ammunition factory’s production line.
The Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation, or MKE, a state-owned Turkish defense company, had signed a formal contract with Mongolia’s Defense Industrial Corporation in 2024 to establish a local ammunition production line in Mongolia. It’s MKE’s second overseas facility, following a production line in Jordan – and perhaps, more importantly, Mongolia’s first domestic ammunition factory.
In August 2026, Mongolia announced that the MKE factory had officially begun production. In an interview, Batlut stated that Mongolia has now produced three types of ammunition. The government isn’t done yet; it is now looking to establish a drone factory as well.
Turkiye has long been a reliable defense partner for Mongolia. Under a 1999 agreement, Ankara provides annual grants of $1 million to Mongolia’s defense sector. The two countries regularly exchange visits and hold training of military personnel. Turkiye is also an active participant in the Khaan Quest international military exercise, which is held annually in Mongolia. As seen by the new ammunition factory, they are expanding cooperation in the defense industry, including technical assistance.
Turkiye is not the only country improving defense relations with Mongolia, either. In the last several years, Mongolia has also expanded defense and military cooperation with “third neighbors” such as Japan, India, and the United States.
The United States has not only participated in but sponsored the Khaan Quest exercises since 2003. Cooperation is expanding into new domains as well. In July 2026, Mongolia participated in the U.S.-led Cyber Shield training in Little Rock, Arkansas. NATO’s Science for Peace and Security (SPS) Program also assists Mongolia’s cybersecurity center; notably, both the U.S. and Turkiye are NATO members.
India also supports Mongolia’s cyber defense systems and participates in Khaan Quest each year. In addition, India and Mongolia conduct Nomadic Elephant, an annual joint military training exercise. In 2025, New Delhi established a defense attaché in Ulaanbaatar for the first time.
In 2025, Japan and Mongolia’s Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology Agreement came into force. Now Tokyo can supply Mongolia with non-lethal equipment such as defense hardware, surveillance, and radar systems for border security.
While Mongolia’s third neighbors help diversify and modernize the country’s military, Ulaanbaatar maintains the highest level of defense ties with its only neighbors, Russia and China. Mongolia and Russia conduct the annual Selenge military drills, focusing on tactical operations as well as counterterrorism training. With its southern neighbor China, Mongolia conducts the “Steppe Partners” military drills, training for counterterrorism, border security, and disaster relief operations.
Strategically, Mongolia refrains from joining any formal military alliances or bloc, but with Ulaanbaatar looking to modernize its military and defense sector, new initiatives and cooperation will come handy. Global military spending reached an all-time high of $2.9 trillion in 2025, and Mongolia is well aware of the new shift.
Turkiye, with its well-established defense industry, is a prime partner in Mongolia’s efforts. After Turkiye said yes to building an ammunition factory, it could also be pivotal to Mongolia’s interest in building drone technology – a step up for its defense industry, and one that’s in keeping with the trends of modern warfare.
A stronger defense relationship with Turkiye allows Mongolia to gain access to training systems and equipment to address modern day security issues. It will also create opportunities for Mongolia’s defense industry, not only shoring up self-reliance but contributing to ongoing efforts to diversify its economy away from the mining sector.

Palestine Action 'Barclays five' will not face terror sentencing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:05:44 UTC
23:05:44 KST

Breadcrumb
'Barclays five' Palestine Action activists will not be sentenced as terrorists, judge rules
Five Palestine Action activists who targeted a Barclays branch in Lancashire in 2024 will not be sentenced under terrorism legislation, a UK judge ruled on Friday.
Judge Robert Altham, sitting at Preston Crown Court, ruled that Hmeera Atiqnisar, 31; Amanda Kelly, 31; Mohammed Malik, 28; Brendon O’Hagan, 28; and Alma Yaniv, 70, will not face terrorist sentencing provisions when they are sentenced on 4 September.
"Whilst the damage is undoubtedly significant, I’m not satisfied it amounts to serious damage for the purposes of the Terrorism Act," Altham said. "Section 69 does not apply in this case."
The activists were convicted in June of causing more than £212,800 worth of damage to a Barclays branch in Burnley in 2024.
"This should never have been an option," the activists said in a joint statement. "We were on trial for charges of criminal damage, for damaging some windows and spraying red paint on a Barclays branch. At no point during the trial were we, or the jury, informed that, if convicted, we could face being sentenced as terrorists."
The group said it targeted the branch because it considered Barclays complicit in Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its occupation of Palestinian territory, citing the bank’s shareholdings in Israeli arms firm Elbit Systems at the time. The action was intended to pressure Barclays to withdraw its financial support for the company.
Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation by the UK government under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer in July 2025, marking the first time Westminster used anti-terror legislation to ban a direct-action protest group. However, the group had not been proscribed at the time of the activists’ convictions.
Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International, have sharply criticised the proscription, describing it as a dangerous escalation against civil liberties and the right to protest.
Photographs from outside Preston Crown Court on Friday afternoon showed dozens of protesters, including friends and family members of the activists, waving Palestinian flags and welcoming the decision.
Several held placards expressing support for Palestine Action, including one reading: "Saving lives is not terrorism — I support Palestine Action."
According to Defend Our Juries, a UK legal rights group, more than 3,500 people — including many aged over 60 — have been arrested for expressing support for the group.

Israeli military receives 2nd US-made refueling aircraft out of 6 purchased
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:04:34 UTC
23:04:34 KST

Lina Altawell
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
The Israeli military said Friday it had received the second of six US-made refueling aircraft set to arrive gradually, saying the planes would help extend the operational range of its air force.
In a statement, the military said a ceremony was held Thursday at Nevatim Airbase in southern Israel to receive the second “Gideon” refueling and transport aircraft for the air force.
“A Boeing KC-46 aircraft landed yesterday at Nevatim Airbase and joined the Gideon 46 refueling squadron,” the statement said.
The aircraft is the second of six refueling planes purchased through the Israeli Defense Ministry’s procurement mission in the US for the air force, the military said.
The aircraft is part of a broader effort by the Defense Ministry to strengthen the Israeli military, it added.
Refueling aircraft allow fighter jets to extend their operational range and remain airborne for longer periods, while also providing advanced transport and multi-mission capabilities, according to the military.
The Israeli military carries out long-range attacks in Iran and Yemen, operations that can require aerial refueling for fighter jets.
On May 27, the Israeli military announced that it had received the first of the six refueling aircraft purchased from the US.
Weeks earlier, the Times of Israel reported that the KC-46 aircraft were set to replace the air force’s aging Boeing 707 refueling fleet, which it said played a “major role” in Israel’s wars against Iran.
Key targets in Iran are located between 1,500 and 2,000 kilometers (932-1,243 miles) from Israeli air bases, while most fighter jets do not have sufficient range to complete a round trip without aerial refueling.
The delivery of the second refueling aircraft comes amid expectations of renewed regional escalation and the possibility of Israel again joining the US in another military confrontation with Iran.
In June 2025, Israel launched a war on Iran, before Israel and the US launched another war against Tehran on Feb. 28, which ended with a ceasefire on April 8 through Pakistani mediation.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 regarding freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled due to disagreements over security in the strait.
During the latest escalation, Israeli officials repeatedly threatened to strike Iran, though analyses and statements carried by Hebrew-language media indicated that Tel Aviv preferred not to enter that round of conflict, mainly because of Washington’s position.

Retired FSB general found dead in Moscow, Russian media report

Unknown Publisher

14:03:05 UTC
23:03:05 KST

Retired Russian FSB Major General Igor Laptev, whose business supplied communications equipment to Russia’s Defense Ministry and other state agencies, was found dead in his Moscow apartment, Russian media reported on Aug. 21.
The 83-year-old was found with a gunshot wound to the head in his apartment on Verkhnyaya Krasnoselskaya Street, according to Russian outlets Moskovsky Komsomolets and Izvestia.
The outlets, citing unnamed sources, reported that Laptev died by suicide on August 20.
Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed the reports, and the circumstances surrounding Laptev’s death remain unclear.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.
Russian independent media Mediazona reported that Laptev was chairman of the board of the Informtekhnika group, which develops secure communications systems. Companies associated with the brand supplied communications equipment to Russia’s Defense Ministry, Interior Ministry, and Voentelecom, a company that services communications infrastructure for the Russian military.
Laptev had served in the Soviet-Afghan War and later worked in the KGB and Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), where he was involved in information security.
Laptev’s reported death comes amid a series of high-profile attacks targeting Russian military officials and figures linked to Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Among the latest cases were the targeting of Russian Aerospace Forces commander Alexander Chayko in August and Russian FPV drone developer Andrey Cherezov in July.

Dizengoff attack victims’ families: Killing of terrorist’s father brings no comfort

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:02:27 UTC
23:02:27 KST

“We have no relief. Tomer isn’t coming back and we will never have relief,” Tal Morad, the sister of Tomer Morad, who was killed in the 2022 terror attack at a bar on Dizengoff Street, told ynet after the killing Friday of Fathi Hazem, the father of the terrorist who carried out the attack, Ra'ad Hazem.
“It makes us happy to know that a man who sowed so much hatred and evil among his own community is no longer alive,” she said.
“The first thing I did was check that none of our forces had been hurt,” Morad said. “To make sure there were no casualties. Revenge like this is not worth another family being destroyed. That’s the only relief, that there were no casualties.
“We miss Tomer and think about him every day and every moment. We are living that night of April 7, 2022, and praying that no other family will ever have to live the nightmare we are living. Tomer isn’t coming back. This circle will not be closed, but at least that damned man is no longer alive. That is not a consolation for us. Maybe this operation prevented painful attacks against our people in the future.”
Tomer’s mother, Eti, added: “What matters most is that nothing happened to our forces and everyone returned safely. That is the most important thing above all. We don’t concern ourselves with the terrorist or his family and everything that happens to them. It’s very difficult to concern ourselves with that. We mainly focus on and live with our loss. I’m OK with him being killed, if only so there won’t be more families like ours.”
The IDF spokesperson said Friday night that an armed terrorist with a knife tried to stab IDF troops operating in Jenin and was killed by gunfire. There were no casualties. A security official said the terrorist was Fathi Hazem, the father of the terrorist who killed Tomer Morad, Eitam Magini and Barak Lufan at the Ilka bar in Tel Aviv. Fathi Hazem had since incited against Israel and was wanted by Israeli security forces.
Eyal Magini, Eitam’s father, said: “Anyone who incites and acts against Israel, like the terrorist who killed my son, who was only 27, as well as Tomer Morad and Barak Lufan, deserves death. Just as today the terrorist’s father tried to stab a soldier, and it’s very good that they killed him. Every dog has its day.”
Dana Lufan, Barak’s widow, spoke of her pain: “My Barak went out to have a beer with friends and was murdered in a brutal terror attack, while I and our three children — Yuval, 6, Amit, 4, and Dor, 5 months old — stayed home.
“I received the news about the killing of the murderer’s father, who was an evil man in his own right. He spoke words of hatred against the Jewish people and called for us to continue being attacked. It won’t bring our Barak back. We miss him so much and long for him every single moment.”
She added: “Today, a circle has been closed, but there is no consolation. I believe there is no place for evil in the world. The most important thing is that no soldier was hurt in the operation. The children, my family and I salute the soldiers who took part in the operation.”
Fathi Hazem became known to the Israeli public shortly after his son’s identity was revealed. The father, a former senior officer in the Palestinian security services, began inciting Palestinians against Israel just hours after his son was killed.
In an impassioned speech from the balcony of his home that went viral among Palestinians, he told hundreds of people who had come to offer their condolences: “You will see the victory and the change in the coming years and in the coming days. Allah will cleanse the Al-Aqsa Mosque of the impurity of the occupiers.”
From that moment, immediately after delivering the speech, Hazem understood that he could be detained for questioning by Israel’s security establishment. He and his son, the terrorist’s brother, then went underground and began hiding under the protection of armed men from the Jenin refugee camp.

Kyiv residents were urged to be especially vigilant on the eve of and on Ukraine’s Independence Day
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
17:01:52 EEST
23:01:52 KST

Kyiv residents were urged to be especially vigilant on the eve of and on Ukraine’s Independence Day
Kyiv • UNN
The city authorities urge Kyiv residents to identify shelters, not ignore alerts, and report suspicious individuals and objects. The SBU warns about recruitment for acts of sabotage.
On August 24, Ukraine will celebrate Independence Day. Amid the full-scale war, the enemy may use mass events to carry out shelling, provocations, terrorist attacks, acts of sabotage, cyberattacks and other crimes. The Kyiv city authorities, together with law enforcement agencies, urge citizens to remain vigilant and take responsibility for their own safety, UNN reports.
As noted by the Kyiv City State Administration, on the eve of and during festive events, the following rules should be observed:
-  do not ignore air-raid alarms and identify the nearest shelter in advance; 
-  do not approach suspicious objects and do not attempt to move or inspect them yourself; 
-  if you detect suspicious individuals, objects or other signs of possible unlawful activity, report them to law enforcement; 
-  do not publish photos or videos indicating the locations of military personnel, critical infrastructure facilities, checkpoints, air defense systems, etc.; 
-  do not disseminate information about the consequences of shelling, the operation of air defense systems or the movement of Ukrainian military personnel; 
-  do not comply with requests from unknown individuals (even if they claim to be law enforcement officers) who offer to carry out questionable assignments, including photographing or filming certain facilities, delivering a package or leaving an object at a specified location. 
In addition
The Security Service of Ukraine also separately drew citizens’ attention to attempts by Russian special services to involve Ukrainians in preparing terrorist attacks and committing acts of sabotage.
If unknown individuals offer money for arson, property damage, placing unknown objects, collecting information about military facilities or other unlawful actions, do not accept such offers and immediately report them to the Security Service of Ukraine.

US flags do not protect West Bank's Palestinians from Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

Breadcrumb
US flags do not protect West Bank's Palestinians from Israeli soldiers and settlers
In one of the most contradictory scenes in the occupied West Bank, Palestinians who hold US citizenship are flying the US flag above their homes, despite knowing that the United States is the Israeli occupation's biggest supporter and arms supplier.
US flags flutter lightly above homes in the towns of Turmusaya and Qusra in the occupied West Bank, but the disappointments on the ground are heavy.
No one is protecting tens of thousands of Palestinians from settler attacks on their homes and land, so each of them has begun thinking about individual ways out, even if that means flying the US flag above their home as a last cry for help.
Businessman Louay Abdel Moneim Abu Rida, 46, from Qusra, south of Nablus in the northern occupied West Bank, arrived at Ben Gurion Airport (Lydda) on Monday evening, 17 August.
Upon his arrival, a team from the US network CNN took him to his home, which is surrounded by Israeli forces in Qusra.
The first thing Abu Rida did was raise the US flag over his home, which overlooks the settlements surrounding his town, as well as numerous outposts seeking to swallow up his home and land as they continue to expand.
In this context, Abu Rida told The New Arab, "I had a CNN team with me, and I came to my home in their car from the Israeli airport. They are a team holding US and French citizenships. Despite being with me, the soldiers stopped me for about half an hour in front of my home before allowing me to enter it."
Abu Rida, like everyone else, understands that US journalists in particular have immunity and that Israeli forces cannot target them as they do Palestinian journalists, as none of them can approach Ras al-Ain Hill.
"I am currently under siege, and I am asking the US Embassy to help lift the siege on my home," Abu Rida described. "The Israeli army is supposed to be stationed in front of my home to remove the settlers, but since 13 Aug. this year, it has been unable to do so. Last Tuesday, a settler attacked the garden of my home, and the soldiers negotiated with him to leave instead of forcibly preventing him from doing so."
Regarding the reason he raised the US flag, Abu Rida said, "This is a political message to the US government. I am a US citizen and have all the rights of a citizen, including having the US Embassy protect me and my home."
"I am a Palestinian American. I left behind a luxurious home, several cars and my family, and came to Qusra because my home in my birthplace is important to me. I asked the US Embassy to visit me at my home, and my request is being considered, according to what they told me," he added. "I want the US Embassy to come here and see the US flag raised over the home of a US citizen. If the settlers succeed in taking over my home, they will remove this flag and replace it with an Israeli flag. Is this permitted under US law?"
US flags had been flying over homes in the town of Turmusaya near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank for months, for the same reasons Abu Rida raised his flag.
Abu Rida is one of 400 Palestinians from Qusra in the occupied West Bank who hold US citizenship and live there, returning to the town during the summer holidays and on special occasions, according to Qusra Mayor Abdel Azim Wadi, who spoke to The New Arab.
Lawyer Yasser Alqam, a member of the Turmusaya municipal council and one of the Palestinian American citizens who have been flying the US flag above their homes for months, told The New Arab, "In short, we are now clinging to a straw to save our homes from the occupation and settlers."
Alqam, 58, who has held US citizenship since birth, explained, "The Palestinian American has seen that there is no one who serves as a point of reference to protect him, whether at the level of the Palestinian Authority or the occupation."
According to Alqam, "Over the long decades we lived in the United States, if we had any problem or someone attacked us, we would call the police to protect us."
"But when we come to the occupied West Bank because we live between America and here, we find that things are very different and that Israel and its army support the settlers and protect them, while no one protects us," he added.
Messages behind raising the flag
"Raising the US flag carries several messages," Alqam said. "First, for deterrence for the settlers; there could be legal consequences for burning or seizing the home of a US citizen. Second, it is an embarrassing message to the US administration and the US Embassy, whose citizens are being attacked. Third, raising the flag means asking the US administration and its embassy to stop supporting the occupation."
"I am a US citizen, and the government transfers my tax money to support Israel, and the latter uses these taxes to kill us and destroy our homes," Alqam noted. "This debate is currently growing in the United States and did not exist before in this form."
Asked whether raising the US flag had achieved its objectives and had come to provide protection, Alqam said, "First, a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step."
"There was a practical experience in Turmusaya about two weeks ago involving the famous New York neurosurgeon Hassan Shukri. After he arrived at his home in Turmusaya, where he spends the summer holiday with his family, the occupation army stormed Turmusaya and turned the house opposite his into a military post," Alqam continued. "They actually spent 72 hours in his neighbour's house and later decided to move to Dr Shukri's home. He holds US citizenship and flies the US flag above his home, and they expelled him and his family from their home."
Alqam noted, "We filmed the soldiers and sent the video to the US Embassy and the US State Department as well. We sent messages saying that the presence of the occupation army in a home flying the US flag constitutes a challenge to the United States. After four hours, the Israeli army withdrew from Dr Shukri's home and apologised to him."
He further said that "the irony is that the occupation army withdrew from Dr Shukri's home, which flies the US flag, after four hours, while it spent three days in his neighbour's home. Both neighbours hold US citizenship, but the doctor raised the flag and his neighbour did not."
"During this period, the US Embassy and State Department have become more responsive to our messages and calls because of the media focus on the presence of Palestinian Americans," Alqam said. We expect a visit early next month by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, to the town of Turmusaya."
Asked whether raising the US flag insults the Palestinian Authority, Alqam said, "Quite the opposite. There is no intention whatsoever to insult the Palestinian Authority because it is, in fact, an authority under occupation, just like any Palestinian citizen."
"The Palestinian Authority is constantly asking the European Union and the United States to help it against the brutal Israeli practices," he added.
Raising the US flag does not appear to be universally accepted in Turmusaya, where there is a heated debate in the town between those who oppose and those who support raising it.
In this context, Turmusaya municipal council member Awad Abu Samra, who is also a member of Fatah, told The New Arab, "I oppose raising the US flag over the homes of the town because America is occupying Palestine by funding Israel, and it is funding our killing."
He pointed out that months ago, there was a heated debate about a group of citizens' view that the Palestinian flag should be raised over the town's facilities funded by residents of the town.
"Most of them are US citizens and pay taxes in the United States, while the occupation comes at all times to destroy the roads and facilities. But there was opposition to this," Abu Samra remarked.
According to Abu Samra, Turmusaya is one of the Palestinian towns in the occupied West Bank with the highest number of Palestinians holding US citizenship.
"The proportion of Turmusaya residents holding US citizenship is about 90 per cent of the town's residents. The population of Turmusaya is 16,000, of whom 6,000 live in the town permanently. There are thousands of expatriates who live between the United States and the town and hold US citizenship," he said.
Anyone entering Turmusaya in the occupied West Bank may realise that they are entering a wealthy town, with buildings and luxurious villas covered in red tiles and surrounded by orchards, as well as swimming pools.
The town becomes crowded during the summer months when expatriates return for school holidays and the wedding season.
It is normal to enter any supermarket in the town and hear an American accent in everyday conversations among elderly people, children and shopkeepers or among teenagers as they talk in the street.
Notably, nine of the 11 members of the Turmusaya municipal council hold US citizenship.
Thousands of Palestinians hold dual Palestinian and US citizenship, most of them concentrated in the cities of Al-Bireh and Ramallah and their villages in the occupied West Bank, such as Turmusaya, Deir Dibwan, Silwad and Al-Mazra'a al-Sharqiya, among others.
Most of them are from families that migrated to the United States in the last century and maintained their ties with Palestine across generations.
The issue of the US flag is not the only matter of disagreement and debate among Palestinians—there is also the question of how the United States is viewed by people who lived there for decades and loved it as a country, rather than for its foreign policy.
In this context, Mohammad Rabie told The New Arab, "Before my son was killed, I used to hang the US flag on my home. Even months after his death, the flag remained raised. But my relatives and friends gently and kindly blamed me because the United States is responsible for his death just like Israel, so I removed it."
Rabie, who is from Turmusaya, recounts the day his son was killed on 6 April 2025: "Amer was no more than 14 years old, meaning he was a child."
"He was with his friends eating green almonds in one of the village's fields. Nevertheless, the occupation fired 36 bullets at him from several guns, and even after he was killed, they continued shooting at him from point-blank range while he was on the ground, on the pretext that he had thrown stones," he added.
Distinguishing Trump from America
"A senator in the state of New Jersey, where I live in the United States—the state has two senators, Cory Booker and Andy Kim—asked me if I wanted an investigation," Rabie said. "I said yes, so he sent a letter to Congress and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and another letter to President Donald Trump. So far, I have not received any response to these letters."
"No one from the embassy, State Department, or any of these official bodies has formally contacted me to take my statement legally," he said.
Rabie, 50, works as a building contractor in Turmusaya, while his older sons work in the United States and travel between Turmusaya and New Jersey.
Regarding why he placed a picture of his martyred son between the Palestinian and US flags in his living room, Rabie said, "I am a Palestinian American, and my martyred son was also one. The United States should not be reduced to Trump and his group and everyone who supports Israel. There is a wonderful country with good and honest people who genuinely stand in solidarity with Palestine. Palestine is my country and so is America."
He stressed that "there is currently a change taking place among younger generations in the United States in favour of the Palestinian cause, and I believe it will continue in favour of us Palestinians."
Sam Bahour, a businessman and expert in Palestinian-American relations, told The New Arab that he believes "what is currently happening with the raising of US flags is somewhat useful in terms of promoting the Palestinian cause to the world.
"It is a cry that attracts the attention of the press, but it will not attract serious attention from the US administration because the United States is an integral part of the occupation that we Palestinians are suffering from. Any visit by a US Embassy official to Turmusaya, Qusra or Al-Taybeh means absolutely nothing on the ground and will not stop settler attacks," Bahour said.
Asked whether there are statistics on the number of Palestinian Americans, Bahour explained that there are no accurate statistics on the number.
"What foreign agencies have published about between 45,000 and 60,000 Palestinians holding US citizenship are Israeli figures that cannot be trusted and are not from the US Embassy," he opined.
Bahour, 62, said he believes that "the US Embassy will not deal with Palestinian Americans as white American citizens."
"Everything we see in the media in terms of visits or statements is merely symbolic. At the same time, the Palestinian Authority does not properly use the presence of thousands of Palestinians holding US passports on the global stage. It is content to be a spectator. Change is currently happening in the United States, whether flags have been raised in Turmusaya or Qusra or not," he concluded.

What is Woke 2.0 and how is it linked to pro-Palestine views?
Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently said in an interview with ABC, “woke 1.0 was crazy,” but what exactly is woke 1.0, what makes woke 2.0 so different, and what role does Palestinian justice play in the newer form of woke?
According to Google Trends data, the term "Woke 1" began gaining popularity in January 2026. It describes social justice activism of the late 2010s and early 2020s. The term usually focuses on anti-racism advocacy, support for transgender people, and the overzealous use of cancel culture -- the concept of trying to 'cancel' people for perceived infractions of social justice norms by encouraging social media users to unfollow them and, at times, attempting to get people fired from their jobs or expelled from their places of education.
Another key feature of Woke 1 is the surrounding corporate culture. Following the murder of African American man George Floyd by white police officer Derek Chauvin in 2020, the Black Lives Matter movement, which was founded in 2013, became mainstream. This included major brands like cosmetics giant L'Oreal and even McDonald's.
